title: LinSpectacles Encyclopedia
scope_note: Definitions are descriptive, source-linked and inspection-oriented; availability varies by kernel, distribution, permissions, userspace version, namespace, filesystem, journal retention and hardware. Current LinSpectacles coverage includes the established inspector family plus TTY/PTY, XDG Desktop Portal, TPM/measured-boot, Linux input-device, desktop-entry/MIME integration, CPU microcode and Device Tree terminology, and Kernel Crypto API registry terminology. This revision also covers read-only KVM/libvirt/QEMU host, local domain, snapshot and current guest-environment terminology.

entries.summary: The privileged core of the operating system that manages hardware, processes, memory, filesystems and system calls.
entries.details: Linux distributions combine the Linux kernel with user-space software. The kernel exposes many inspection interfaces through procfs, sysfs, system calls and device files.
entries.why_it_matters: Kernel version and configuration influence which features and interfaces are available.
entries.caution: Do not use “Linux” and “distribution” as exact synonyms.

entries.summary: A complete operating-system distribution built around the Linux kernel plus user-space packages, configuration and tooling.
entries.details: Examples differ in package manager, defaults, release model and enabled services even when they run the same kernel.
entries.why_it_matters: LinSpectacles must distinguish kernel capabilities from distribution-specific tooling.
entries.caution: A distribution version is not the same thing as a kernel version.

entries.summary: A virtual filesystem, normally mounted at /proc, that exposes process and kernel information.
entries.details: Entries are generated by the kernel rather than stored as ordinary disk files. /proc/PID contains per-process data while many top-level files describe system-wide state.
entries.why_it_matters: A large part of Linux inspection is reading procfs safely and interpreting it correctly.
entries.caution: Some procfs files are writable controls; an inspector should not assume every /proc file is read-only.

entries.summary: A virtual filesystem, normally mounted at /sys, that represents devices, drivers and kernel objects.
entries.details: sysfs uses small attribute files and links to expose relationships such as device-to-driver binding and hardware class membership.
entries.why_it_matters: It is one of the best sources for hardware topology without parsing command output.
entries.caution: Many sysfs attributes are writable controls; read-only inspection should never write them.

entries.summary: The system’s network host name as configured for the running environment.
entries.details: A hostname is an identifier, not proof of physical machine identity, and containers may have their own hostname namespace.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for distinguishing reports from different machines.
entries.caution: Do not treat a hostname as a stable globally unique identifier.

entries.summary: A locally generated identifier commonly stored in /etc/machine-id and used by system components.
entries.details: It is intended to identify an OS installation and may be regenerated when images are cloned according to system setup rules.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for correlating local state across boots.
entries.caution: It can be privacy-sensitive and should generally be redacted from shared diagnostics.

entries.summary: The machine or execution architecture, such as x86_64 or aarch64.
entries.details: Architecture affects instruction set, ABI, kernel build and which package binaries can run natively.
entries.why_it_matters: Package and kernel-module compatibility often depends on architecture.
entries.caution: Architecture labels are not the same as CPU model names.

entries.summary: The display-session technology used by a desktop login, commonly Wayland or X11.
entries.details: Desktop environments often expose this through XDG_SESSION_TYPE and related session metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: Some app behavior, permissions and integration differ between X11 and Wayland.
entries.caution: Session type is user-session state, not a property of the kernel.

entries.summary: A name/value string inherited by processes from their parent environment unless explicitly changed.
entries.details: Variables influence program lookup, locale, desktop integration, runtime behavior and application-specific settings.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain why the same executable may behave differently in different sessions.
entries.caution: The environment can contain secrets; exports should redact sensitive values.

entries.summary: A colon-separated search list used by shells and many programs to locate executable commands.
entries.details: Order matters: an earlier matching executable is normally chosen before a later one. Empty or untrusted path elements can have security implications.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains which command binary a process is likely to launch.
entries.caution: PATH does not describe shared-library lookup.

entries.summary: An environment variable conventionally naming the current user’s home directory.
entries.details: Many applications use it to locate user data or configuration, although modern applications may also follow XDG base-directory variables.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful context for paths shown by inspectors.
entries.caution: HOME is environment data and can differ from the account database in unusual launches.

entries.summary: A set of conventions controlling language, character classification, sorting, numeric and date formatting.
entries.details: On Unix-like systems locale selection is commonly influenced by LANG and LC_* environment variables.
entries.why_it_matters: Locale can change command output and parsing behavior.
entries.caution: Machine-readable collectors should avoid depending on human-localized command output when structured interfaces exist.

entries.summary: An XDG base-directory variable that can relocate per-user configuration away from the default ~/.config location.
entries.details: Applications following the XDG Base Directory convention use it when set.
entries.why_it_matters: Portable applications should be explicit about whether they honor host XDG paths or keep their own configuration.
entries.caution: Not every application follows the XDG convention.

entries.summary: A session environment variable commonly set to values such as wayland or x11.
entries.details: Desktop software can use it to understand the current graphical session type.
entries.why_it_matters: Helpful when diagnosing display integration differences.
entries.caution: Presence and value depend on the session stack.

entries.summary: An environment variable that can add directories to the dynamic linker’s shared-library search path.
entries.details: It can override or supplement normal library lookup for dynamically linked programs.
entries.why_it_matters: Unexpected values can explain why a program loads a different library than expected.
entries.caution: Changing it globally can cause compatibility or security problems.

entries.summary: Loadable code that can extend the running kernel, often providing a driver, filesystem or protocol.
entries.details: Loaded modules appear in /proc/modules and usually have runtime state under /sys/module. Metadata may also be available from the module file through modinfo.
entries.why_it_matters: It connects kernel functionality to the code currently loaded to provide it.
entries.caution: Some kernel functionality is built in and therefore is not a loadable module.

entries.summary: Kernel functionality compiled directly into the kernel image rather than loaded as a separate module.
entries.details: Built-in drivers may serve hardware even though no corresponding entry appears in /proc/modules.
entries.why_it_matters: Prevents the false conclusion that “not listed by lsmod” means “not present.”
entries.caution: Built-in status depends on the kernel configuration.

entries.summary: A configuration value exposed by a kernel module, often under /sys/module/NAME/parameters.
entries.details: Parameters can affect driver or subsystem behavior and may have been set at load time or through the kernel command line.
entries.why_it_matters: Reading them helps explain current runtime behavior.
entries.caution: Many parameters are writable; inspection should not modify them.

entries.summary: A pattern declaring hardware or subsystem identifiers that a module can support.
entries.details: Aliases help userspace and the kernel module loader match devices or modalias strings to candidate modules.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for connecting a device identity to a driver module.
entries.caution: An alias match does not prove that the module is currently bound to a device.

entries.summary: A compatibility string embedded in many loadable kernel modules describing important properties of the kernel build they target.
entries.details: The kernel uses module compatibility checks; modinfo can display the vermagic recorded in a module.
entries.why_it_matters: A mismatch can explain why an out-of-tree module refuses to load.
entries.caution: Vermagic is not a complete guarantee of binary compatibility.

entries.summary: Signature identity recorded for a signed kernel module when module signing information is present.
entries.details: Kernel builds can enforce or verify module signatures depending on configuration and security policy.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for establishing whether a module carries a recognized signature.
entries.caution: A displayed signer name alone does not prove the running kernel accepted the signature under a particular trust policy.

entries.summary: A relationship in which one loadable kernel module relies on symbols or functionality supplied by another.
entries.details: Dependency tools and module metadata help the loader bring required modules in the correct order.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why additional modules are loaded together.
entries.caution: The /proc/modules “used by” field is runtime usage information, not a complete static dependency graph.

entries.summary: A runtime relationship indicating that another kernel object or module is holding a reference that prevents simple unloading.
entries.details: sysfs can expose holders and /proc/modules reports use counts and dependent names in its module list.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps explain why a loaded module is still in use.
entries.caution: Use counts and holder lists can change while the system is running.

entries.summary: A named kernel function or data object that may be exported or otherwise represented in the kernel symbol table.
entries.details: /proc/kallsyms can expose symbol names and addresses subject to kernel security restrictions. Modules can reference exported symbols.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for advanced module and crash analysis.
entries.caution: Kernel addresses may be hidden or zeroed by kptr_restrict; do not treat zero as a real address in that case.

entries.summary: The procfs interface that exposes the kernel symbol table subject to access restrictions.
entries.details: Entries include an address, symbol type and name, with module tags for symbols belonging to loadable modules.
entries.why_it_matters: Allows a selected kernel module to be associated with its symbols.
entries.caution: Address visibility is intentionally restricted on many systems.

entries.summary: A kernel setting that limits exposure of kernel pointer values through interfaces such as /proc/kallsyms.
entries.details: Restricting kernel addresses makes some information harder to use for attacks that rely on address disclosure.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why symbol names may be visible while addresses are hidden.
entries.caution: Its exact behavior depends on the configured value and caller privileges.

entries.summary: A set of kernel flags recording conditions that may matter when diagnosing kernel problems.
entries.details: Examples include certain proprietary or out-of-tree modules, forced module operations, hardware errors or previous kernel warnings depending on the taint bit.
entries.why_it_matters: Taint information gives maintainers context about the running kernel state.
entries.caution: “Tainted” does not automatically mean the kernel is broken or compromised.

entries.summary: Device-specific code or data loaded by a driver into hardware or used to initialize it.
entries.details: Linux drivers may request firmware files from userspace during device initialization.
entries.why_it_matters: Missing or incompatible firmware can explain otherwise functional driver modules failing to bring hardware up.
entries.caution: Firmware is distinct from the kernel driver itself.

entries.summary: Arguments passed to the Linux kernel at boot, usually visible in /proc/cmdline.
entries.details: Parameters can select root filesystems, enable or disable features, tune drivers and pass options to early userspace.
entries.why_it_matters: It records important boot-time choices affecting the running system.
entries.caution: Not every token is interpreted by the kernel itself; some are consumed by initramfs or systemd.

entries.summary: The build-time set of CONFIG_* options that determines which kernel features are built in, modular or absent.
entries.details: A distribution kernel may expose its configuration through /proc/config.gz or files under /boot, but availability varies.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why one system exposes an interface or driver while another does not.
entries.caution: Runtime state cannot always reveal every build-time option.

entries.summary: A diagnostic emitted by the kernel when it detects an unexpected or problematic condition.
entries.details: Warnings can appear in the kernel log and may set a taint flag.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful evidence when investigating driver, filesystem or hardware problems.
entries.caution: A single warning needs context; not every warning means user data is at risk.

entries.summary: The kernel’s view of physical address ranges used for RAM, firmware and device resources, commonly exposed in /proc/iomem.
entries.details: It represents address ownership and reservation rather than ordinary process virtual memory.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for low-level hardware and driver diagnostics.
entries.caution: Address visibility may be restricted; it is an expert-oriented view.

entries.summary: A process identifier assigned by the kernel within a PID namespace.
entries.details: PIDs identify running processes but can be reused after a process exits. Different PID namespaces may present different numeric IDs.
entries.why_it_matters: Most per-process inspection begins with a PID.
entries.caution: Do not use a PID alone as a permanent identity.

entries.summary: The parent process identifier reported for a process.
entries.details: It normally identifies the process that created the current process, subject to reparenting and namespace effects.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding process ancestry.
entries.caution: A parent may exit, and reparenting can change the observed relationship.

entries.summary: An execution context within a process that shares much of the process address space and resources with sibling threads.
entries.details: Linux represents threads as tasks with IDs; procfs can expose per-thread state under /proc/PID/task.
entries.why_it_matters: Thread count can explain CPU concurrency and resource use.
entries.caution: A thread ID and process ID are related but not interchangeable in every API.

entries.summary: A kernel-reported state describing what a task is currently doing, such as running, sleeping or stopped.
entries.details: The exact single-letter and textual states are documented in procfs interfaces.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for distinguishing runnable work from waiting or stopped tasks.
entries.caution: A sampled state can change immediately after it is read.

entries.summary: Accumulated time a process or thread has spent executing on CPUs in user and kernel mode.
entries.details: It is cumulative rather than an instantaneous percentage. Sampling deltas over time can produce utilization rates.
entries.why_it_matters: A stable basis for calculating process CPU activity.
entries.caution: CPU percentage conventions differ on multicore systems.

entries.summary: The set of CPUs on which a process or thread is permitted to run.
entries.details: Affinity can constrain scheduling to selected logical CPUs.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps explain why a workload does not use every available CPU.
entries.caution: Affinity is permission to run on CPUs, not a guarantee of where execution will occur.

entries.summary: A user-visible scheduling priority hint for normal time-sharing tasks.
entries.details: Higher nice values generally mean lower scheduling priority within the applicable scheduler class.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful context when comparing CPU scheduling behavior.
entries.caution: Nice does not describe real-time scheduling policies.

entries.summary: Resident Set Size: memory pages of a process that are currently resident in physical memory, with shared pages counted in the process total.
entries.details: RSS is widely available and inexpensive to read, but shared mappings mean summing RSS across processes can double-count memory.
entries.why_it_matters: Good for a quick view of resident process memory.
entries.caution: RSS is not the same as uniquely owned memory.

entries.summary: The total virtual address space mapped by a process.
entries.details: It can include executable mappings, shared libraries, anonymous mappings, reserved address ranges and mapped files whether resident or not.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding address-space layout and mapping scale.
entries.caution: A large VMS value does not mean the process is using that much physical RAM.

entries.summary: Proportional Set Size: private pages plus a proportional share of pages shared with other mappings or processes.
entries.details: PSS divides the cost of shared pages among sharers, so totals across processes are often more informative than RSS totals.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for estimating a process’s fair share of physical memory.
entries.caution: PSS requires richer mapping information and is costlier to collect than basic RSS.

entries.summary: A common user-space term for the amount of memory private to a process and not shared with other processes.
entries.details: It is typically derived from private clean and private dirty mappings reported by smaps-like interfaces.
entries.why_it_matters: Approximates memory that could be freed if that process’s private pages disappeared.
entries.caution: USS is a derived metric; the kernel does not expose a single universal field named USS.

entries.summary: Memory belonging to a process that has been moved to swap storage instead of remaining resident in RAM.
entries.details: Per-mapping swap information can be reported through smaps when available.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows whether a process has memory pressure history beyond current RSS.
entries.caution: Swap usage is not itself proof of current performance problems.

entries.summary: A page fault that requires I/O to make the referenced page available.
entries.details: Major faults can occur when data must be read from a filesystem or swap rather than satisfied from memory.
entries.why_it_matters: A high rate can indicate storage-backed memory pressure or file-access patterns.
entries.caution: “Major” describes the need for I/O, not the seriousness of an application error.

entries.summary: A page fault resolved without performing storage I/O for the page contents.
entries.details: Examples include establishing a mapping to a page already in memory or copy-on-write bookkeeping.
entries.why_it_matters: Minor faults are common and often inexpensive.
entries.caution: A high count alone is not necessarily a problem.

entries.summary: The kernel’s estimate of how much memory is available for starting new applications without swapping.
entries.details: It considers reclaimable memory and is more useful than MemFree alone for a modern Linux system.
entries.why_it_matters: A better dashboard measure of available memory than treating filesystem cache as permanently used.
entries.caution: It is an estimate, not a reservation guarantee.

entries.summary: Physical RAM that is currently completely unused.
entries.details: Linux normally uses otherwise idle RAM for caches, so MemFree can be small on a healthy system.
entries.why_it_matters: Prevents interpreting low free RAM as automatically problematic.
entries.caution: Use MemAvailable for a more practical estimate of immediately usable memory.

entries.summary: Memory used by the kernel to cache file-backed data and improve I/O performance.
entries.details: Cached pages can often be reclaimed when applications need memory.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why used RAM can remain high after file activity without indicating a leak.
entries.caution: Not every cached page is equally reclaimable at every moment.

entries.summary: Memory containing modified data that has not yet been written to its backing storage.
entries.details: /proc/meminfo exposes system-wide Dirty and Writeback counters.
entries.why_it_matters: Large or persistent dirty/writeback activity can help explain storage pressure.
entries.caution: Dirty memory is normal during writes; context and duration matter.

entries.summary: A region of a process virtual address space associated with anonymous memory, a file, shared memory or another mapping type.
entries.details: /proc/PID/maps and smaps describe mapped ranges, permissions and backing objects.
entries.why_it_matters: This is how shared libraries and many files appear in a process address space.
entries.caution: A mapping does not mean every page in the range is resident.

entries.summary: A small integer used by a process to refer to an open file, socket, pipe or other kernel object.
entries.details: /proc/PID/fd exposes descriptor links for processes you are allowed to inspect.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for finding resources a process currently has open.
entries.caution: A file descriptor is process-local; descriptor 3 in two processes need not refer to the same object.

entries.summary: A filesystem object currently referenced through a process file descriptor or mapping.
entries.details: Open paths can be inspected through procfs, subject to permissions and race conditions.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps connect processes to configuration, logs and data files.
entries.caution: An unlinked file can remain open even though its pathname no longer exists.

entries.summary: Cumulative per-process I/O accounting exposed through /proc/PID/io when permitted.
entries.details: Fields include character counts and storage-layer read_bytes/write_bytes; sampling deltas can produce rates.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides the basis for “processes with disk activity” views.
entries.caution: Counters can include effects of caching differently depending on the field; use the documented field semantics.

entries.summary: A system and service manager commonly used as PID 1 on Linux distributions.
entries.details: systemd manages units, dependencies and service processes and uses cgroups to track workloads.
entries.why_it_matters: Many LinSpectacles service and boot relationships come from systemd state.
entries.caution: Not every Linux distribution or environment uses systemd as PID 1.

entries.summary: The basic object managed by systemd, representing resources such as services, sockets, mounts, devices and targets.
entries.details: Units have names with type suffixes and can carry dependencies, conditions and state.
entries.why_it_matters: Understanding units is essential to interpreting systemd service and boot information.
entries.caution: A unit is broader than a service; not every unit runs a process.

entries.summary: A systemd unit ending in .service that describes and tracks a service process or group of processes.
entries.details: Service units define how processes are started, stopped, restarted and supervised.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides the bridge between service configuration, PIDs and cgroups.
entries.caution: Some services can be socket- or D-Bus-activated rather than started directly at boot.

entries.summary: A synchronization/grouping unit ending in .target, often used to group other units or represent milestones.
entries.details: Targets are roughly analogous to named synchronization points in the dependency graph.
entries.why_it_matters: They help explain boot sequencing without implying a process exists.
entries.caution: Targets do not themselves execute programs.

entries.summary: A high-level systemd unit state such as active, inactive, activating, deactivating or failed.
entries.details: The exact set depends on unit type; SubState provides a more specific state.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for quick classification of service health.
entries.caution: Active is not synonymous with “doing work right now.”

entries.summary: A unit-type-specific runtime state providing more detail than the high-level ActiveState.
entries.details: For a service it can distinguish states such as running or exited.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why two active units may be behaving differently.
entries.caution: SubState values are internal state names and may be more specific than users need.

entries.summary: The enablement-related state of a unit file, such as enabled, disabled, static or masked.
entries.details: This is distinct from whether the unit is currently active. A static unit lacks install information for direct enablement but can still be started as a dependency.
entries.why_it_matters: Prevents confusing “disabled” with “not running.”
entries.caution: Exact states depend on systemd version and unit configuration.

entries.summary: A unit made impossible to start through normal systemd activation by linking its unit file to /dev/null.
entries.details: Masking is stronger than disabling because even manual or dependency-driven starts are blocked until unmasked.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when interpreting why a unit refuses to start.
entries.caution: An inspector should report masking, not change it.

entries.summary: A relationship between systemd units that affects requirement, ordering, propagation or grouping.
entries.details: Directives such as Requires= and Wants= express requirement relationships, while After= and Before= express ordering.
entries.why_it_matters: Separating requirement from ordering is essential to reading the unit graph correctly.
entries.caution: After= does not mean Requires=, and Requires= alone does not define start order.

entries.summary: A systemd requirement dependency that normally causes the required unit to be started and can propagate failure under documented conditions.
entries.details: It is stronger than Wants= but still separate from ordering.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows which units are considered required for another unit.
entries.caution: Use After=/Before= separately when describing ordering.

entries.summary: A relatively weak systemd requirement dependency used to pull another unit into a transaction without the same failure coupling as Requires=.
entries.details: It is widely used for optional or desirable relationships.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps explain why a unit starts together with others.
entries.caution: Wants= does not imply ordering.

entries.summary: A systemd ordering dependency requiring one unit’s start operation to be ordered after another unit’s start operation when both are in the transaction.
entries.details: Ordering and requirement are modeled separately in systemd.
entries.why_it_matters: Critical when interpreting boot critical chains.
entries.caution: After= does not cause the other unit to be started by itself.

entries.summary: The process ID systemd considers the main process for a service when the service type has such a concept.
entries.details: systemctl show can expose MainPID along with the service cgroup containing all service processes.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for connecting service metadata to process inspection.
entries.caution: Not every service has a persistent MainPID.

entries.summary: The control group in which systemd places the service’s processes for tracking and resource control.
entries.details: On cgroup v2 systems the path maps naturally into /sys/fs/cgroup, where process membership and resource counters can be inspected.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides a reliable relationship between a service and all of its processes.
entries.caution: Cgroup paths are runtime state and can differ between system and user managers.

entries.summary: Service configuration controlling whether and when systemd automatically restarts a terminated service.
entries.details: Restart= supports policies based on clean exit, failure, abnormal termination and other conditions.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains repeated process restarts or resilience behavior.
entries.caution: Restart policy does not guarantee successful recovery.

entries.summary: A systemd execution setting that prevents the service and its descendants from gaining privileges through exec mechanisms such as set-user-ID or file capabilities.
entries.details: It maps onto the kernel no_new_privs mechanism and is one service-hardening control.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when reviewing service isolation.
entries.caution: It does not by itself create a complete sandbox.

entries.summary: A systemd sandboxing option that can give a service private /tmp and /var/tmp namespaces.
entries.details: It reduces accidental sharing of temporary files between the service and other workloads.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful hardening context in service inspection.
entries.caution: It is one control among many and does not imply full filesystem isolation.

entries.summary: A systemd sandboxing option that can make selected system filesystem areas read-only or inaccessible to a service.
entries.details: Different settings provide different levels of filesystem write restriction.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows whether a service has been hardened against modifying system files.
entries.caution: Writable exceptions and other namespace settings can alter the effective result.

entries.summary: A systemd analysis that examines service sandboxing and security-related unit settings and reports exposure findings.
entries.details: It evaluates configuration rather than proving that a service is secure or vulnerable.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful as a structured review of hardening controls.
entries.caution: Treat the exposure score as an analysis aid, not a universal security grade.

entries.summary: systemd-analyze’s view of a time-critical dependency chain for boot ordering.
entries.details: It shows when selected units became active and the time spent by units on the chain.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps identify boot dependencies contributing to the path to a target.
entries.caution: It is not simply a sorted list of the slowest units.

entries.summary: A timing list showing how long units spent in their activating state during boot.
entries.details: It is useful for spotting units that took a long time to initialize.
entries.why_it_matters: Good first-pass boot timing evidence.
entries.caution: A long activation time does not prove the unit delayed the final boot target; use critical-chain for dependency context.

entries.summary: An initial RAM filesystem used during early boot before or while the real root filesystem is located and mounted.
entries.details: It can contain storage, encryption, filesystem and discovery tools needed before the normal userspace root is available.
entries.why_it_matters: Important when boot problems happen before ordinary services start.
entries.caution: Its exact implementation varies by distribution and generator tooling.

entries.summary: A random identifier associated with the current kernel boot and exposed by Linux procfs.
entries.details: It changes on each boot and is useful for grouping logs or observations from the same boot session.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps distinguish multiple boots on the same machine.
entries.caution: It is not a permanent machine identifier.

entries.summary: systemd-journald’s structured log store queried with journalctl.
entries.details: Entries can carry metadata such as unit, PID, priority, boot ID and security context depending on the source.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides correlated evidence for service, boot and kernel problems.
entries.caution: Visibility can depend on user permissions and journal configuration.

entries.summary: An attachment of a filesystem into the process-visible directory hierarchy at a mount point.
entries.details: Linux mount state is represented per mount namespace and can be inspected through mountinfo or tools such as findmnt.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains how a path maps to a filesystem and source.
entries.caution: Mount state can differ between namespaces.

entries.summary: A directory at which a mounted filesystem is attached to the directory tree.
entries.details: A path can have another filesystem mounted over it, hiding the underlying directory contents until unmounted.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the user-visible location of a mounted filesystem.
entries.caution: The same filesystem can be mounted at more than one mount point.

entries.summary: A format and kernel driver used to organize files, directories and metadata on storage or in memory.
entries.details: Examples include ext4, XFS, Btrfs, tmpfs and procfs, each with different semantics and capabilities.
entries.why_it_matters: Filesystem type influences mount options, metadata and space accounting.
entries.caution: Not every filesystem is backed by a block device.

entries.summary: A filesystem whose contents are generated from kernel or runtime state rather than stored as ordinary persistent files.
entries.details: Examples include procfs and sysfs. tmpfs is memory-backed but behaves differently from procfs/sysfs.
entries.why_it_matters: Prevents interpreting every mount as physical storage usage.
entries.caution: “Virtual” filesystems are not all equivalent in persistence or behavior.

entries.summary: A kernel device that provides block-addressed storage and can back partitions, filesystems, swap or volume-management layers.
entries.details: Linux exposes block devices in /sys/block and under /dev.
entries.why_it_matters: Forms the physical/logical base of many storage relationships.
entries.caution: A mount source can also be network, pseudo-filesystem or another non-block source.

entries.summary: A region of a block device described by a partition table and exposed as a child block device.
entries.details: Partitions can hold filesystems, swap, encryption containers or volume-manager physical volumes.
entries.why_it_matters: Important in device-to-filesystem topology.
entries.caution: A partition is not the same thing as a filesystem.

entries.summary: An identifier stored in filesystem metadata and commonly used to refer to a filesystem independently of changing device names.
entries.details: mount and fstab tooling can resolve UUID= references to devices.
entries.why_it_matters: More stable than /dev/sdX-style names across hardware enumeration changes.
entries.caution: UUID uniqueness is expected but can be duplicated by cloning images.

entries.summary: A human-assigned filesystem identifier that can be used as a mount source tag.
entries.details: LABEL= references are supported by common mount tooling.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides a readable alternative to raw device names.
entries.caution: Labels need not be globally unique.

entries.summary: A configuration table describing filesystems and swap areas that may be mounted or activated.
entries.details: Entries normally specify source, target, filesystem type, options, dump field and fsck pass.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains persistent mount intent rather than only current runtime state.
entries.caution: Runtime mounts may exist without fstab entries, and systemd generators can interpret fstab.

entries.summary: Flags and filesystem-specific settings controlling how a mount behaves.
entries.details: Examples can affect read/write mode, execution, device files, access times and filesystem-specific features.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain security and behavior differences between otherwise similar mounts.
entries.caution: Option meaning can be filesystem-specific; do not infer semantics from names alone.

entries.summary: A mount whose VFS or filesystem state prevents ordinary writes through that mount.
entries.details: findmnt and mount information can report ro/rw state.
entries.why_it_matters: Important when diagnosing failed writes or immutable system layouts.
entries.caution: Read-only at one mount does not necessarily mean the underlying device cannot be written through another path.

entries.summary: A mount that makes an existing directory or file tree visible at another path.
entries.details: Bind mounts reuse an existing filesystem subtree rather than mounting a new filesystem format.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains duplicate-looking path trees and container/service filesystem layouts.
entries.caution: A bind mount can have mount flags distinct from the source mount in some cases.

entries.summary: A union filesystem that presents a merged view of lower and upper directory trees.
entries.details: It is widely used for containers and image-based systems to combine read-only and writable layers.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains paths whose visible content is assembled from multiple backing directories.
entries.caution: The merged view is not a simple one-to-one mapping to one disk path.

entries.summary: A memory-backed filesystem whose data is kept in virtual memory and can use swap.
entries.details: tmpfs is commonly used for runtime files and shared memory areas.
entries.why_it_matters: It consumes memory rather than ordinary persistent disk space.
entries.caution: tmpfs is not the same as procfs or sysfs.

entries.summary: A filesystem object record that stores metadata and references file data, while directory entries map names to inodes.
entries.details: Filesystems have implementation-specific inode allocation and accounting.
entries.why_it_matters: A filesystem can run out of available inodes even when byte capacity remains.
entries.caution: Inode numbers are only meaningful within their filesystem context.

entries.summary: Space reported as available to an unprivileged process after filesystem accounting and reservations.
entries.details: statvfs-like interfaces distinguish total blocks, free blocks and blocks available to ordinary users.
entries.why_it_matters: More relevant to a normal user than raw free blocks on filesystems with reserved space.
entries.caution: Exact accounting depends on filesystem semantics.

entries.summary: A mount point that has another mount placed on top of an earlier mount at the same target, hiding the lower view.
entries.details: findmnt can identify shadowed/over-mounted filesystems.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why expected files appear to vanish behind another mount.
entries.caution: The hidden lower filesystem remains mounted until explicitly unmounted.

entries.summary: A block-layer scheduling policy selected for a block device’s request queue.
entries.details: The active and available schedulers are exposed through the block queue sysfs scheduler attribute.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful context for storage latency and workload tuning.
entries.caution: The optimal scheduler is workload- and device-dependent; an inspector should not recommend changing it blindly.

entries.summary: A block-queue limit or accounting concept related to how many I/O requests may be queued or active.
entries.details: sysfs exposes attributes such as nr_requests and device-specific queue limits.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps describe storage queue configuration.
entries.caution: Different queue attributes have different meanings; “queue depth” is not one universal kernel counter.

entries.summary: A block-queue attribute indicating whether the device is treated as rotational storage.
entries.details: The kernel exposes this through /sys/block/.../queue/rotational.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for distinguishing HDD-like from non-rotational devices in topology.
entries.caution: The flag is kernel/device metadata and may not perfectly describe unusual virtual devices.

entries.summary: The block size, in bytes, presented by a block device for logical I/O addressing.
entries.details: The block queue sysfs interface exposes logical_block_size and physical_block_size separately.
entries.why_it_matters: Important for alignment and storage topology.
entries.caution: Logical and physical block sizes can differ.

entries.summary: The physical media or device block granularity reported by the block layer.
entries.details: It can differ from the logical block size presented to software.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps explain alignment and performance characteristics.
entries.caution: Virtual devices may synthesize these values.

entries.summary: A kernel network device through which packets are sent and received.
entries.details: Interfaces include physical NICs, loopback, bridges, tunnels, virtual Ethernet pairs and others.
entries.why_it_matters: The basic unit for addresses, link counters and routing decisions.
entries.caution: An interface name is not necessarily stable across all system configurations.

entries.summary: A local-only network interface used for communication within the same network namespace, commonly named lo.
entries.details: Addresses such as 127.0.0.1 and ::1 normally route through loopback.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains local services that are reachable without using a physical network link.
entries.caution: Loopback is namespace-local; containers can have their own loopback interface.

entries.summary: An IPv4 or IPv6 address assigned to an interface or otherwise used as a network endpoint.
entries.details: Linux interfaces can have multiple addresses with prefixes and lifetimes.
entries.why_it_matters: Needed to interpret routes, sockets and connectivity.
entries.caution: An assigned address does not necessarily imply Internet reachability.

entries.summary: An address plus prefix length describing a network range, such as 192.0.2.0/24 or 2001:db8::/32.
entries.details: The prefix length states how many leading address bits identify the network portion.
entries.why_it_matters: Routes and interface addresses are usually expressed with prefixes.
entries.caution: A prefix is not a subnet mask string, though they represent related information in IPv4.

entries.summary: A rule in a routing table describing where packets to a destination should be sent.
entries.details: Routes can specify destination prefixes, gateways, output interfaces, metrics and other attributes.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why traffic chooses a particular path.
entries.caution: Linux can maintain multiple routing tables and policy-routing rules.

entries.summary: A route used when no more-specific route matches a packet destination.
entries.details: IPv4 commonly represents it as default or 0.0.0.0/0; IPv6 uses ::/0.
entries.why_it_matters: Often identifies the primary path off the local networks.
entries.caution: A system can have multiple default routes with policy or metrics.

entries.summary: A next-hop router used to forward packets toward destinations not directly reachable on the local link.
entries.details: Routes can specify gateway addresses where required.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding external connectivity paths.
entries.caution: Not every route uses a gateway; directly connected routes do not.

entries.summary: A route preference value used as part of route selection when multiple otherwise applicable routes exist.
entries.details: Lower values are commonly preferred within comparable routes, subject to routing rules and protocol semantics.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why one default route wins over another.
entries.caution: Route selection is more complex than metric alone.

entries.summary: Software and configuration used to translate domain names and other DNS data through configured name servers or local resolver services.
entries.details: Traditional resolver configuration is represented in resolv.conf, though modern systems may generate it or route queries through a local service.
entries.why_it_matters: Name-resolution failures can occur even when IP routing works.
entries.caution: /etc/resolv.conf may be managed by another service and can be a symlink.

entries.summary: A DNS server address configured for resolver queries.
entries.details: resolv.conf can list nameserver entries, while system services may provide per-link DNS configuration beyond that file.
entries.why_it_matters: Identifies where name-resolution requests are intended to go.
entries.caution: The visible nameserver may be a local stub rather than the upstream recursive resolver.

entries.summary: A kernel endpoint for interprocess or network communication.
entries.details: Network sockets carry protocol, local/remote addresses and state; file descriptors refer to them in processes.
entries.why_it_matters: Connects process ownership to network activity.
entries.caution: Not all sockets are Internet sockets; Unix-domain sockets are local IPC.

entries.summary: A connection-oriented transport protocol that provides an ordered byte stream with reliability and congestion control.
entries.details: Linux exposes TCP socket state and detailed transport information through socket interfaces and tools such as ss.
entries.why_it_matters: Most long-lived network connections in desktop/server software use TCP.
entries.caution: TCP reliability does not mean the application protocol itself is trustworthy or encrypted.

entries.summary: A connectionless datagram transport protocol without TCP-style stream reliability or connection state.
entries.details: UDP sockets can be bound, connected in the socket API sense, or exchange datagrams with many peers.
entries.why_it_matters: Used by DNS, media, discovery and many other protocols.
entries.caution: A “connected” UDP socket does not create a TCP-like handshake.

entries.summary: The kernel state of a TCP socket, such as LISTEN, ESTABLISHED, TIME-WAIT or SYN-SENT.
entries.details: State reflects the TCP finite-state machine and connection lifecycle.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for distinguishing listeners, active sessions and closing connections.
entries.caution: State names describe transport state, not application health.

entries.summary: A local socket waiting for incoming connection attempts, typically TCP LISTEN or an unconnected bound datagram socket.
entries.details: ss can show listening sockets and, with sufficient permission, process ownership.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps identify services accepting network traffic.
entries.caution: A listening socket does not prove a firewall or remote network permits access to it.

entries.summary: The local IP address and port associated with a network socket.
entries.details: It may be a specific interface address or a wildcard address that accepts traffic for multiple local addresses.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows where a service or connection is bound locally.
entries.caution: 0.0.0.0 or :: means wildcard binding, not a remote destination.

entries.summary: The peer IP address and port associated with a connected network socket when one exists.
entries.details: For TCP it identifies the other endpoint of the connection.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for correlating a process with external communication.
entries.caution: Remote addresses can change rapidly and may belong to CDNs or proxies rather than the final logical service.

entries.summary: Maximum Transmission Unit: the largest packet payload size an interface/link can carry without fragmentation at that layer.
entries.details: Interface MTU is part of network-device configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: Mismatched or constrained MTUs can explain some connectivity problems.
entries.caution: Path MTU can be lower than an interface’s configured MTU.

entries.summary: A link-layer hardware or virtual address used by technologies such as Ethernet.
entries.details: Interfaces can expose a current MAC address that may be permanent, assigned or randomized.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for local-link identification.
entries.caution: Do not assume the current MAC is a globally unique permanent hardware identity.

entries.summary: Netfilter state that tracks flows and related packet tuples so firewall/NAT logic can reason about connection state.
entries.details: Conntrack records can include original and reply directions, protocol state, timeouts and counters depending on kernel configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides deeper firewall/network-flow visibility than a socket list alone.
entries.caution: Conntrack tracks network flows, not necessarily one-to-one user processes.

entries.summary: Security-Enhanced Linux, a Linux Security Module implementing mandatory access control using a loaded security policy.
entries.details: SELinux labels subjects and objects with security contexts and evaluates policy rules in addition to ordinary Unix permissions.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains access denials that persist even when mode bits appear permissive.
entries.caution: SELinux is not enabled on every Linux system.

entries.summary: SELinux mode in which policy denials are enforced as well as audited according to configuration.
entries.details: getenforce reports Enforcing, Permissive or Disabled.
entries.why_it_matters: This is the normal high-level answer to whether SELinux policy is actively blocking disallowed accesses.
entries.caution: An enforcing system can still have individual permissive domains.

entries.summary: SELinux mode in which would-be denials are logged but not enforced globally.
entries.details: Permissive mode is often used for diagnosis or policy development.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why AVC denials can be present without the operation being blocked.
entries.caution: Do not confuse global permissive mode with a single permissive domain.

entries.summary: A security label commonly represented as user:role:type:level.
entries.details: Contexts are attached to processes and objects and are central inputs to SELinux policy decisions.
entries.why_it_matters: A concise way to describe SELinux identity and type.
entries.caution: The type/domain component is often most relevant in targeted policy, but the full context carries more information.

entries.summary: The type component of an SELinux security context, used heavily by type-enforcement policy.
entries.details: Files, sockets and other objects have types; process types are commonly called domains.
entries.why_it_matters: Most targeted-policy allow rules are expressed in terms of source and target types plus object class and permission.
entries.caution: A type name alone is not a complete security context.

entries.summary: The SELinux type associated with a running process, commonly called its domain.
entries.details: Domain transitions can place executed programs into different security domains according to policy.
entries.why_it_matters: It identifies the policy confinement context of a process.
entries.caution: Being in an “unconfined” domain still occurs within an SELinux policy framework.

entries.summary: A policy switch that enables or disables predefined conditional policy behavior.
entries.details: Boolean values can alter allowed interactions without rebuilding the whole policy. semanage/getsebool tooling can list them.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding policy-supported configuration choices.
entries.caution: Changing a boolean changes security policy behavior; LinSpectacles should inspect, not toggle.

entries.summary: An SELinux access-vector-cache denial record indicating that policy denied or would deny an access.
entries.details: Audit records can include source context, target context, object class and requested permission.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides the raw evidence behind many SELinux troubleshooting cases.
entries.caution: One AVC record may be part of a larger audit event; context and grouping matter.

entries.summary: The SELinux context of the subject attempting an operation, often a process.
entries.details: AVC records identify source and target contexts for the policy decision.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows which domain initiated a denied or audited action.
entries.caution: Do not infer the human user solely from the SELinux user field.

entries.summary: The SELinux context of the object or target involved in an access decision.
entries.details: It may describe a file, socket, process or other labeled object depending on the object class.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows how the target was labeled when policy was evaluated.
entries.caution: A target path and target context are different pieces of evidence.

entries.summary: The SELinux category of object being accessed, such as file, dir, process or socket classes.
entries.details: Permissions are interpreted within an object class.
entries.why_it_matters: Necessary to understand what an AVC permission refers to.
entries.caution: The same permission word can have class-specific meaning.

entries.summary: A policy-defined operation such as read, write, execute, getattr or name_connect evaluated for an object class.
entries.details: AVC denials report the requested permission or permissions.
entries.why_it_matters: Identifies exactly what policy action was blocked or audited.
entries.caution: Permission names must be interpreted together with object class.

entries.summary: The loaded rules and labels that define SELinux access-control decisions.
entries.details: Policy can include base policy plus modules, booleans, file-context mappings, port mappings and user mappings.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the authoritative ruleset behind contexts and denials.
entries.caution: Policy layout and provided modules vary by distribution and policy package.

entries.summary: A modular policy component installed in an SELinux policy store.
entries.details: semodule can list installed modules and priorities; multiple priority levels can override lower-priority module content.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding where policy behavior originates.
entries.caution: Listing a module does not mean every rule in it is currently relevant to a selected process.

entries.summary: An SELinux process type configured so denials for that domain are logged but not enforced while other domains can remain enforcing.
entries.details: semanage permissive can list built-in and customized permissive types.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why a globally enforcing system may not enforce one domain.
entries.caution: Do not infer global mode from the presence of permissive domains.

entries.summary: A mapping from a Linux login user or group to an SELinux user.
entries.details: semanage login controls and lists these mappings.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows how an ordinary account enters the SELinux user/role model.
entries.caution: Linux usernames and SELinux users are different identity systems.

entries.summary: A policy identity that can be associated with roles and MLS/MCS ranges and mapped from Linux logins.
entries.details: semanage user lists SELinux user records and their role/range configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding confined-user policy.
entries.caution: An SELinux user is not the same record as a /etc/passwd account.

entries.summary: A policy mapping between network protocol/port ranges and an SELinux port type.
entries.details: semanage port lists these mappings.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why a confined service may be allowed to bind or connect to some ports but not arbitrary ones.
entries.caution: Port labels are policy metadata, not firewall rules.

entries.summary: A policy mapping from pathname patterns and file classes to expected SELinux file contexts.
entries.details: semanage fcontext lists configured mappings; labeling tools use policy mappings to determine expected contexts.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides the policy expectation used when checking whether a path is mislabeled.
entries.caution: The mapping is not necessarily the current on-disk label.

entries.summary: The actual SELinux security context stored for a filesystem object when the filesystem supports security labels.
entries.details: It can be compared with the policy’s expected file-context mapping.
entries.why_it_matters: Mislabeled files are a common cause of SELinux denials.
entries.caution: Do not change labels automatically based only on a mismatch report.

entries.summary: The level/range component of an SELinux context used by MLS or MCS policy features.
entries.details: Ranges can encode sensitivity levels and categories depending on policy.
entries.why_it_matters: Important on systems using MCS/MLS separation, including some container labeling schemes.
entries.caution: Meaning depends on the loaded policy; do not invent semantic labels for numeric categories.

entries.summary: A kernel framework that allows additional security modules such as SELinux or AppArmor to implement access-control hooks.
entries.details: The kernel can expose active security-module information and per-process security attributes.
entries.why_it_matters: Places SELinux within the broader Linux security architecture.
entries.caution: LSM support and active module stacking depend on kernel configuration.

entries.summary: A fine-grained privilege bit that divides traditional root powers into separately checkable capabilities.
entries.details: Processes can have permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding and ambient capability sets; executable files can also carry capabilities.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why a non-root process may perform a traditionally privileged operation.
entries.caution: Capabilities remain powerful; “not root” does not mean “unprivileged.”

entries.summary: A kernel process attribute that promises descendants will not gain new privileges through execve-based mechanisms.
entries.details: It is used by sandboxing systems and can be set by systemd’s NoNewPrivileges=.
entries.why_it_matters: A useful hardening indicator for processes and services.
entries.caution: It does not remove privileges the process already has.

entries.summary: A Linux mechanism that can restrict which system calls a process may make, commonly through filter mode.
entries.details: Sandboxed applications and services can use seccomp to reduce available kernel attack surface.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows an important dimension of process confinement beyond Unix permissions.
entries.caution: A process being in seccomp filter mode does not reveal the complete filter policy by itself.

entries.summary: Policy that filters or transforms network traffic according to rules, commonly implemented on Linux through netfilter frameworks.
entries.details: Firewall state is separate from whether a socket is listening or whether SELinux allows a port type.
entries.why_it_matters: Important when explaining why a listener is not remotely reachable.
entries.caution: Do not reduce firewall state to a single yes/no value on complex systems.

entries.summary: A domain:bus:device.function identifier for a PCI function, such as 0000:03:00.0.
entries.details: sysfs exposes PCI devices using these addresses.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides a stable runtime key for connecting hardware, drivers and resources.
entries.caution: Bus numbering can differ after hardware or firmware changes.

entries.summary: Numeric identifiers assigned to a PCI vendor and device model and exposed by PCI configuration/sysfs.
entries.details: They allow software to match hardware independent of localized product names.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for identifying devices and candidate drivers.
entries.caution: IDs identify hardware classes/models, not necessarily a unique physical serial number.

entries.summary: Kernel code bound to a device or subsystem to operate it.
entries.details: sysfs represents the driver binding for many devices; the driver may be built into the kernel or provided by a module.
entries.why_it_matters: The key relationship between detected hardware and kernel support.
entries.caution: Driver name and loadable module name are often related but not guaranteed to be identical concepts.

entries.summary: A group of devices that the kernel treats as sharing isolation constraints for I/O memory management.
entries.details: IOMMU groups are important to safe device assignment because devices in a group may not be independently isolatable.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for virtualization and passthrough diagnostics.
entries.caution: Group composition depends on platform hardware, firmware and kernel topology.

entries.summary: Non-Uniform Memory Access: a topology where memory access cost depends on the relationship between CPUs and memory nodes.
entries.details: Linux exposes NUMA nodes, CPU membership, node memory information and distance metrics on supporting systems.
entries.why_it_matters: Important for large systems and performance-sensitive workloads.
entries.caution: A single-node system can expose little or no meaningful NUMA separation.

entries.summary: The arrangement of logical CPUs into cores, packages and other topology levels exposed by the kernel.
entries.details: Topology affects scheduling, affinity and how “CPU count” should be interpreted.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when explaining multicore utilization and affinity.
entries.caution: Logical CPU count is not the same as physical core count.

entries.summary: A kernel thermal-management object representing a temperature sensor or thermal region.
entries.details: The thermal sysfs interface can expose zone type, current temperature, policy and trip points.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides a kernel-native view of thermal state.
entries.caution: Sensor names and availability vary greatly by hardware and firmware.

entries.summary: A temperature threshold associated with a thermal zone and a trip type such as passive, active, hot or critical depending on platform support.
entries.details: The kernel thermal framework exposes trip-point temperatures and types when provided by the driver.
entries.why_it_matters: Hardware-provided thresholds are more meaningful than arbitrary generic temperature colors.
entries.caution: Not every platform exposes trip points, and firmware-defined limits should not be treated as performance targets.

entries.summary: The Linux hardware-monitoring subsystem and standardized sysfs naming used for sensor readings such as temperatures, fans, voltages and power.
entries.details: Drivers expose attributes such as temp*_input, fan*_input and optional labels/limits.
entries.why_it_matters: Allows portable read-only sensor discovery across many devices.
entries.caution: A numeric sensor index does not reliably identify “CPU” or “fan 2” without labels or device context.

entries.summary: A fan speed reading in revolutions per minute exposed by supporting hwmon drivers.
entries.details: fan*_input attributes are standardized as RPM.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for thermal and cooling diagnostics.
entries.caution: Not all fans expose tachometer readings, and zero may mean stopped, unsupported or fault depending on hardware context.

entries.summary: A hardware-monitoring threshold such as max, critical, minimum or alarm limit exposed by a sensor driver.
entries.details: hwmon defines standardized attribute names but availability and exact hardware semantics vary.
entries.why_it_matters: Allows an inspector to compare a reading with hardware-provided limits.
entries.caution: Do not invent missing thresholds or assume every “max” value is a shutdown temperature.

entries.summary: A battery state-of-charge percentage exposed by the Linux power-supply class when supported.
entries.details: The CAPACITY property is defined as a percentage from 0 to 100.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides a simple battery status summary.
entries.caution: Capacity percentage is not the same as design health or remaining energy in watt-hours.

entries.summary: A power-supply state such as Charging, Discharging or Full reported by the battery driver.
entries.details: The Linux power-supply class standardizes STATUS semantics.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for interpreting whether time remaining or time to full is meaningful.
entries.caution: Drivers may report Unknown when hardware cannot determine state.

entries.summary: Energy-related battery properties measured in units such as micro-watt-hours in the Linux power-supply class.
entries.details: ENERGY_* and CHARGE_* are distinct families and should not be mixed when estimating time.
entries.why_it_matters: Correct unit pairing makes battery-time estimates more trustworthy.
entries.caution: Do not divide energy by current or charge by power; use energy/power or charge/current pairs.

entries.summary: A momentary power draw or charge rate when the power-supply driver exposes POWER_NOW.
entries.details: Together with ENERGY_NOW it can support an approximate time estimate.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for live battery consumption context.
entries.caution: Power fluctuates, so simple time estimates are inherently approximate.

entries.summary: Vendor-supplied low-level processor update data that can correct CPU errata or alter processor behavior.
entries.details: Linux distributions can apply microcode updates early in boot.
entries.why_it_matters: Relevant to firmware/security and processor behavior.
entries.caution: Microcode revision interpretation is CPU-vendor-specific.

entries.summary: A UEFI platform feature that can enforce signature-based trust during the firmware boot chain.
entries.details: On Linux it can interact with kernel/module trust and lockdown policies depending on distribution configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: Important context for why unsigned kernel components may be restricted.
entries.caution: Secure Boot being enabled does not by itself describe the security of the whole running system.

entries.summary: A Linux security mode that restricts certain kernel interfaces that could allow modification or extraction of sensitive kernel state.
entries.details: Lockdown is commonly relevant on systems booted in a trusted/verified boot configuration, depending on distribution policy.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why root or ordinary users may still be denied some low-level operations.
entries.caution: Lockdown availability and activation rules vary by kernel and distribution.

entries.summary: A distributable unit containing software plus metadata used by a package or application distribution system.
entries.details: Package systems record fields such as name, version, architecture, dependencies and provenance in system-specific ways.
entries.why_it_matters: The foundation of Installed Software inventory.
entries.caution: A package is not necessarily the same thing as one executable application.

entries.summary: A package-provided version string identifying a release according to that packaging ecosystem’s rules.
entries.details: Version syntax and comparison rules vary between RPM, Debian, Python and standalone formats.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for inventory and update comparisons.
entries.caution: Do not compare version strings lexicographically across packaging systems.

entries.summary: The target architecture recorded for a binary package, such as x86_64, aarch64 or an ecosystem-specific “noarch/all” value.
entries.details: It describes compatibility expectations for the packaged payload.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps distinguish native binaries from architecture-independent content.
entries.caution: Package architecture labels are ecosystem-specific.

entries.summary: A configured source from which a package manager can obtain package metadata and package files.
entries.details: Repository identity can help explain package provenance and update availability.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when distinguishing distribution packages from local or third-party sources.
entries.caution: A package already installed may outlive or lose access to the repository it originally came from.

entries.summary: A declared requirement or capability relationship between packages.
entries.details: RPM, Python packaging and other ecosystems encode requirements using their own syntax and semantics.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why packages are installed together and what may break when a requirement is missing.
entries.caution: Dependencies can be optional, conditional or virtual capabilities depending on the ecosystem.

entries.summary: A package or component that declares a dependency on the selected package or capability.
entries.details: Package managers can often query “what requires” relationships.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding impact before removal or replacement, even in a read-only inspector.
entries.caution: The relationship can be to a provided capability rather than directly to one package name.

entries.summary: A cryptographic signature used by a packaging ecosystem to help verify package origin and integrity.
entries.details: RPM can verify package signatures using trusted public keys in its keyring.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides provenance evidence for package files.
entries.caution: A valid signature means the signature verifies under the configured trust/policy; it does not mean the software is bug-free or safe.

entries.summary: A cryptographic hash recorded for integrity checking of package content or installed files.
entries.details: RPM verification can compare digests and other metadata with the package database.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps detect modified package-managed files.
entries.caution: A matching digest does not authenticate origin unless combined with appropriate signature/trust mechanisms.

entries.summary: A package format and database ecosystem used by RPM-based Linux distributions.
entries.details: RPM packages contain payload files and metadata; rpm can query installed packages and verify recorded file attributes.
entries.why_it_matters: Relevant on Fedora, RHEL-family and other RPM-based systems.
entries.caution: RPM is a package format/tooling layer; higher-level dependency/repository managers may sit above it.

entries.summary: A desktop application distribution and sandboxing system that uses runtimes, permissions and portals.
entries.details: Flatpak applications can be isolated from the host and use portals to request mediated desktop access.
entries.why_it_matters: Installed-software inspection should distinguish Flatpak apps and runtimes from system packages.
entries.caution: Sandbox permissions vary by application and configuration.

entries.summary: A D-Bus interface that lets sandboxed applications request desktop services such as file access or opening URIs through a mediated API.
entries.details: XDG Desktop Portal is designed for Flatpak and other containment frameworks.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains how a sandboxed app can still interact with host resources without broad filesystem access.
entries.caution: Portal availability and backend behavior depend on the desktop/session environment.

entries.summary: A shared userspace platform used by systems such as Flatpak to provide common libraries and components to applications.
entries.details: Applications target a runtime rather than bundling every host library directly.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why “runtime” entries appear separately from apps in software inventories.
entries.caution: A runtime is not the same as a running process.

entries.summary: A portable Linux application image containing an executable runtime plus an embedded filesystem image.
entries.details: Current type-2 AppImages use a runtime and SquashFS payload and launch an AppDir entrypoint.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why an AppImage can be discovered as a standalone file without being installed into a package database.
entries.caution: A file named .AppImage is not automatically trustworthy; inspecting metadata should avoid executing it.

entries.summary: A directory layout used as the source/contents model for AppImage applications, with an AppRun entrypoint and desktop metadata conventions.
entries.details: An AppImage’s embedded filesystem presents an AppDir-like application tree.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when safely extracting metadata from an AppImage without launching the application.
entries.caution: AppDir contents are application-controlled and should be treated as untrusted data.

entries.summary: A compressed read-only filesystem format used by current type-2 AppImages for their embedded filesystem image.
entries.details: The AppImage runtime mounts or otherwise exposes the SquashFS payload at execution time.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains the read-only packaged nature of many AppImages.
entries.caution: SquashFS is also used outside AppImage and does not imply a file is an AppImage.

entries.summary: An installed Python project represented by distribution metadata such as a dist-info or egg-info directory.
entries.details: Distribution names are the names used by package installers and importlib.metadata, and they do not map one-to-one to import package names.
entries.why_it_matters: Important for correctly interpreting Python Packages inventory.
entries.caution: Do not assume `pip` distribution name equals the name used in `import`.

entries.summary: A package or module name used by Python’s import system.
entries.details: One distribution can provide several import packages, and namespace packages can combine contributions from multiple distributions.
entries.why_it_matters: Prevents confusing installed project identity with import syntax.
entries.caution: Import packages and distribution packages are different concepts.

entries.summary: An installed metadata directory for a Python distribution following modern packaging standards.
entries.details: It contains core metadata and may include RECORD, entry points and installer/direct-url metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides the source for many fields shown by importlib.metadata.
entries.caution: Exact auxiliary files depend on how the distribution was built and installed.

entries.summary: The version of the Python Core Metadata specification used by a distribution’s metadata record.
entries.details: The Core Metadata specification defines required fields such as Name and Version and many optional fields.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps interpret which metadata fields may be valid.
entries.caution: It is not the Python package’s own software version.

entries.summary: Python distribution metadata declaring the Python version range supported by the project.
entries.details: Installers can use this field when deciding whether a release is compatible with the running interpreter.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for explaining environment compatibility.
entries.caution: It is a declaration by the project, not runtime proof that every code path works.

entries.summary: Core metadata fields declaring other Python distributions required by a distribution, optionally with versions, markers or extras.
entries.details: importlib.metadata can expose these requirement declarations.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides the basis for dependency inspection.
entries.caution: Environment markers can make a requirement conditional.

entries.summary: Core metadata declaring optional feature groups (“extras”) that can activate additional dependencies.
entries.details: Requirements can be conditional on a named extra.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why two installations of the same project may have different optional dependencies.
entries.caution: An extra is metadata, not a separately importable package by itself.

entries.summary: Metadata advertising a named object under an entry-point group so other software can discover plugins or launch targets.
entries.details: importlib.metadata exposes entry-point names, groups and values.
entries.why_it_matters: Used for plugin systems and command-line wrappers.
entries.caution: Loading an entry point executes/imports application code; an inspector should not load arbitrary entry points merely to list them.

entries.summary: A standard Python entry-point group used by installers to create command-line launchers that call Python objects.
entries.details: The distribution metadata identifies the command name and target object.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains where some commands installed into a virtual environment come from.
entries.caution: The wrapper executable may be separate from the import package name.

entries.summary: An isolated Python environment with its own interpreter context and site-packages location.
entries.details: Virtual environments let projects use dependency sets independent from the system interpreter environment.
entries.why_it_matters: Important when explaining why a package is visible to one Python but not another.
entries.caution: A virtual environment is not a full OS container or security boundary.

entries.summary: A conventional directory location where third-party Python distributions and import packages are installed for an interpreter environment.
entries.details: importlib.metadata searches discoverable distribution metadata on Python’s import paths.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for identifying which environment owns an installed Python package.
entries.caution: There can be multiple site directories, user sites and custom import paths.

entries.summary: A Python installation mode where project code remains linked to or referenced from a development source tree instead of being copied as an ordinary installed snapshot.
entries.details: Modern metadata can include direct-url/origin information describing editable installations.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for explaining why edits in a source checkout immediately affect an installed environment.
entries.caution: Editable implementation details vary by build backend and installer.

entries.summary: A Python package namespace that can be composed from portions provided by multiple directories or distributions.
entries.details: This is one reason import package names and distribution package names are not one-to-one.
entries.why_it_matters: Important when mapping imports back to installed distributions.
entries.caution: Do not assign a namespace import to one distribution without checking the mapping.

entries.summary: A kernel mechanism that gives a process a scoped view of a class of system resources.
entries.details: Linux provides namespace types for mount points, process IDs, networks, users, UTS/hostname, IPC, cgroups and time on supporting kernels.
entries.why_it_matters: Namespaces are a core building block of containers and service isolation.
entries.caution: A namespace isolates a view of resources; it is not by itself a complete security boundary.

entries.summary: A namespace that isolates the process ID number space and process hierarchy view.
entries.details: A process can have different PID values as seen from nested PID namespaces.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why container PIDs can differ from host PIDs.
