entries.caution: PID namespaces do not isolate filesystems or networks.

entries.summary: A namespace that gives processes an independent view of filesystem mount points.
entries.details: Mount, unmount and bind-mount changes can be isolated between namespaces depending on propagation rules.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why a service/container can see a different mount tree from the host.
entries.caution: Pathnames alone do not prove two processes see the same mounted filesystem.

entries.summary: A namespace that maps user and group IDs so processes can have different identity/privilege interpretations inside and outside the namespace.
entries.details: User namespaces underpin rootless containers and can allow a process to be UID 0 inside while unprivileged outside.
entries.why_it_matters: Important for understanding apparent root identity in containers.
entries.caution: UID 0 inside a user namespace is not automatically host root.

entries.summary: A namespace that isolates network interfaces, routes, sockets and related networking state.
entries.details: Containers can have their own loopback interface, addresses and routing tables.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why host network inspection may differ from a container’s view.
entries.caution: Network namespaces do not inherently encrypt or filter traffic.

entries.summary: A namespace that virtualizes the cgroup path view seen through procfs and cgroup mounts.
entries.details: It can hide host cgroup ancestry from a contained process.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when comparing service/container cgroup paths from different viewpoints.
entries.caution: It does not replace the cgroup resource-control mechanism itself.

entries.summary: A Linux control group: a hierarchical grouping of processes used for resource accounting, distribution and control.
entries.details: cgroup v2 provides a unified hierarchy and controllers for resources such as CPU, memory, I/O and PIDs.
entries.why_it_matters: Connects services and containers to their actual resource accounting.
entries.caution: A cgroup is not a process and can contain multiple processes or child cgroups.

entries.summary: A cgroup subsystem that accounts for or controls a particular class of resource.
entries.details: cgroup v2 controllers include CPU, memory, I/O, PIDs and others depending on kernel configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains which resource controls are available to a selected cgroup.
entries.caution: A controller can exist in the kernel but not be enabled for a particular subtree.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 interface that controls which controllers are enabled for child cgroups beneath a cgroup.
entries.details: The set determines which controller files can appear in descendants.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding why a child cgroup lacks an expected controller.
entries.caution: It is a writable control; LinSpectacles should only inspect it.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 file listing process IDs belonging directly to that cgroup.
entries.details: Reading it provides a process-membership view for the group.
entries.why_it_matters: This is the basis for connecting a systemd service cgroup to its processes.
entries.caution: PIDs can change while being read and may be recycled.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 counter reporting current memory usage for a non-root cgroup.
entries.details: The memory controller accounts major userland and kernel memory categories for processes in the cgroup.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides per-service/container memory accounting without summing process RSS.
entries.caution: It is cgroup accounting and may not equal the sum of visible process RSS values.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 hard memory usage limit when configured, or “max” when unlimited by that setting.
entries.details: It belongs to the memory controller and can constrain a workload’s memory use.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when a service is being killed or constrained despite free host memory.
entries.caution: An inspector should report the limit, not change it.

entries.summary: A cgroup PIDs-controller counter reporting the number of tasks/processes accounted in the cgroup hierarchy as defined by the controller.
entries.details: Together with pids.max it can reveal process-count constraints.
entries.why_it_matters: Helpful when services fail to create new processes or threads.
entries.caution: Controller semantics and hierarchical accounting should be interpreted from cgroup documentation.

entries.summary: A cgroup PIDs-controller limit on the number of tasks allowed for the cgroup, or “max” when unrestricted by that setting.
entries.details: It provides a resource-exhaustion guard against process creation.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains fork/thread creation failures caused by cgroup policy.
entries.caution: It is separate from system-wide PID limits.

entries.summary: Kernel metrics that quantify time tasks are stalled because CPU, memory or I/O resources are contended.
entries.details: System-wide PSI appears under /proc/pressure, with recent 10, 60 and 300 second averages and cumulative stall time.
entries.why_it_matters: It measures experienced resource contention rather than simple utilization.
entries.caution: High utilization and high pressure are related but not equivalent.

entries.summary: The PSI metric representing time when at least some tasks are stalled on the measured resource.
entries.details: It is reported as recent percentages and cumulative microseconds.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows partial resource contention affecting at least one workload.
entries.caution: It is not a percentage of hardware utilization.

entries.summary: The PSI metric representing time when all non-idle tasks are simultaneously stalled for memory or I/O; system-level CPU full is not meaningfully used in the same way.
entries.details: Full stalls identify periods where useful progress can stop across the workload set.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for detecting severe thrashing or I/O/memory stalls.
entries.caution: Interpret CPU PSI according to kernel documentation; system-level CPU full is defined specially for compatibility.

entries.summary: PSI measurements for time workloads are stalled on I/O contention.
entries.details: Available through /proc/pressure/io when PSI is enabled.
entries.why_it_matters: A stronger signal of experienced I/O contention than treating CPU iowait as a direct disk-health score.
entries.caution: It does not identify which device or process caused the pressure by itself.

entries.summary: PSI measurements for time workloads are stalled because of memory contention and reclaim pressure.
entries.details: System-wide memory PSI is available through /proc/pressure/memory when supported.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps distinguish “RAM is highly utilized” from “workloads are actually stalling for memory.”
entries.caution: It does not replace detailed OOM/reclaim evidence.

entries.summary: PSI measurements describing runnable work delayed because CPU execution resources are contended.
entries.details: CPU PSI focuses on scheduling delay rather than simple CPU percentage.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when a host is busy enough that tasks are waiting to run.
entries.caution: CPU utilization can be high without the same degree of PSI, and vice versa for short bursts.

entries.summary: Termination triggered by the kernel or cgroup memory-management path when memory requirements cannot be satisfied under applicable limits and policy.
entries.details: OOM events can be visible in kernel/journal logs and cgroup memory event counters.
entries.why_it_matters: Strong evidence of memory exhaustion or a restrictive memory limit.
entries.caution: Do not assume host-wide RAM exhaustion; cgroup limits can cause local OOM events.

entries.summary: The suffix-defined kind of object managed by systemd, such as service, socket, mount, timer or target.
entries.details: systemd uses different unit types for different resources and activation mechanisms. systemctl can filter loaded units by type.
entries.why_it_matters: Unit type determines which properties and lifecycle semantics are meaningful for a unit.
entries.caution: Do not treat every unit as a service; service-only properties may be absent on other unit types.

entries.summary: A systemd unit representing a filesystem mount point.
entries.details: Mount units normally use names derived from their mount paths and may be generated from /etc/fstab or created by other systemd mechanisms.
entries.why_it_matters: It connects filesystem mounting to systemd dependency and lifecycle management.
entries.caution: A mounted filesystem may exist without a hand-written .mount file.

entries.summary: A systemd unit representing a swap device or swap file.
entries.details: Swap units allow activation and dependency management of swap resources through systemd.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful when distinguishing memory-swap activation from ordinary services.
entries.caution: Do not confuse a swap unit with the amount of swap currently in use.

entries.summary: A systemd unit that owns or listens on an IPC or network socket and can activate another unit on demand.
entries.details: Socket activation lets systemd create a listening endpoint before the service process itself is started.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why a service may be activatable even when it is not currently running.
entries.caution: A socket unit is not the same thing as every socket opened by a process.

entries.summary: A systemd unit representing a kernel device that systemd can track through device events.
entries.details: Device units are generally synthesized dynamically rather than installed as normal unit files.
entries.why_it_matters: They expose device availability to the systemd dependency graph.
entries.caution: A device unit does not mean the device has a persistent unit file on disk.

entries.summary: A systemd unit that establishes an automount point whose corresponding mount can be triggered on access.
entries.details: Automount units are paired with mount units and can defer the actual filesystem mount until the path is used.
entries.why_it_matters: Useful for understanding delayed or on-demand mounts.
entries.caution: Do not interpret an active automount unit as proof that the backing filesystem is already mounted.

entries.summary: A systemd unit that schedules activation of another unit based on time or calendar conditions.
entries.details: Timer units can provide monotonic or calendar-based scheduling and commonly activate service units.
entries.why_it_matters: They are systemd’s native scheduled-activation mechanism.
entries.caution: A timer being active does not mean its target service is continuously running.

entries.summary: A systemd unit that watches filesystem paths and activates another unit when configured path conditions occur.
entries.details: Path units can react to a path appearing or changing without a continuously running watcher service.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain filesystem-triggered service activation.
entries.caution: They are not a general-purpose audit trail of all filesystem activity.

entries.summary: A systemd unit that groups units in the control-group hierarchy for resource organization and accounting.
entries.details: Slices form a tree and are used to organize service and scope units under cgroup resource control.
entries.why_it_matters: They connect systemd unit placement to cgroup resource management.
entries.caution: A slice is a grouping construct, not a process by itself.

entries.summary: A systemd unit that groups externally created processes so systemd can supervise and account for them.
entries.details: Unlike a service unit, systemd does not normally start the processes inside a scope; it adopts an existing process group.
entries.why_it_matters: Scopes are common for login sessions, transient workloads and externally launched process groups.
entries.caution: Do not assume every active scope has an ExecStart command.

entries.summary: systemd’s report of whether a unit definition was loaded successfully, not found, masked or otherwise unavailable.
entries.details: LoadState is distinct from whether the unit is currently active.
entries.why_it_matters: It separates definition/loading problems from runtime state.
entries.caution: Do not use LoadState as a synonym for ActiveState.

entries.summary: The filesystem path of the primary unit-file fragment systemd loaded for a unit, when one exists.
entries.details: Generated or transient units may have different provenance and some units have no ordinary fragment file.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps locate the definition that contributed the unit’s main configuration.
entries.caution: It does not include every drop-in or generated source that may affect the effective configuration.

entries.summary: A unique identifier associated with one runtime invocation of a systemd-managed unit.
entries.details: Journal entries produced during the same service invocation can carry the same invocation ID.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish separate runs of the same unit.
entries.caution: It identifies an invocation, not the permanent identity of the unit.

entries.summary: A systemd unit whose active state has entered the failed condition.
entries.details: Failure can result from unsuccessful service execution, mount failure, dependency problems, timeouts or other unit-type-specific conditions.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a strong signal that systemd recorded an unsuccessful unit outcome.
entries.caution: The failed state alone does not explain the root cause; status and journal records provide context.

entries.summary: The elapsed time attributed to activating a systemd unit during boot analysis.
entries.details: systemd-analyze blame reports per-unit activation times, while critical-chain output adds ordering context.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps identify units that consumed significant activation time.
entries.caution: A long activation time does not prove that a unit delayed the overall boot critical path.

entries.summary: One structured event stored in the systemd journal.
entries.details: A journal record normally contains MESSAGE plus metadata fields supplied by journald, the kernel or the originating process.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the atomic event inspected by Journal Inspector and other journal-backed views.
entries.caution: Not every record carries every possible journal metadata field.

entries.summary: A named metadata item attached to a journal record, such as PRIORITY, _PID, _BOOT_ID or _SYSTEMD_UNIT.
entries.details: The journal supports a defined set of trusted fields and may also contain application-supplied fields.
entries.why_it_matters: Fields let tools filter and interpret records without parsing only the human message text.
entries.caution: Field availability depends on the origin and transport of each record.

entries.summary: The standard numeric severity carried by many journal records: 0 Emergency through 7 Debug.
entries.details: Lower numbers represent more severe conditions. journalctl can filter by one priority or a priority range.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a consistent severity dimension across many journal sources.
entries.caution: Priority is supplied metadata; it should not be treated as a complete measure of user impact.

entries.summary: Metadata describing how a record entered the journal, such as kernel, syslog, journal, stdout or audit transport.
entries.details: _TRANSPORT is assigned by journald and is useful for distinguishing fundamentally different record origins.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps separate kernel-originated records from service stdout or traditional syslog input.
entries.caution: Transport is not the same thing as the application or systemd unit that emitted the message.

entries.summary: A journal/syslog field commonly used to identify the program or logical source associated with a message.
entries.details: For some records it is supplied by the application; other records may instead be better identified by systemd or process metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a useful source/filter field when available.
entries.caution: Do not assume it is globally unique or present on every record.

entries.summary: Trusted journal metadata associating a record with a systemd system unit when journald can determine that relationship.
entries.details: It is derived from process/cgroup context rather than merely copied from message text.
entries.why_it_matters: It lets journal records be grouped by the unit responsible for them.
entries.caution: Some records, including many kernel records, have no _SYSTEMD_UNIT value.

entries.summary: An opaque identifier that can be used to refer to a precise position/record in a journal stream.
entries.details: Cursors are intended for journal navigation and resumption rather than human interpretation.
entries.why_it_matters: They can anchor follow-up journal queries to an exact record position.
entries.caution: Do not parse a cursor as if its internal representation were a stable public data format.

entries.summary: A wall-clock timestamp associated with a journal record.
entries.details: Realtime timestamps are suitable for presenting calendar/date time to users.
entries.why_it_matters: They let records from a boot be placed on the human calendar timeline.
entries.caution: Wall-clock time can be adjusted; monotonic time serves a different purpose within a boot.

entries.summary: A timestamp measured on a monotonic clock and associated with a record within a boot.
entries.details: Monotonic time advances independently of ordinary wall-clock corrections and is meaningful in conjunction with the boot identity.
entries.why_it_matters: It is useful for ordering and duration reasoning inside a single boot.
entries.caution: Do not compare monotonic timestamps from different boots without their boot context.

entries.summary: A relative journal selector for a retained boot, where 0 is the current boot and negative values refer to earlier boots.
entries.details: journalctl --list-boots shows retained boots and their indices; -b can select one by index or Boot ID.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a convenient short reference for boot history.
entries.caution: Indices are relative to the journal history currently retained and should not be treated as permanent identifiers.

entries.summary: An optional stable identifier that some software attaches to a class of journal events.
entries.details: MESSAGE_ID can support machine-readable recognition of known event types without relying only on wording.
entries.why_it_matters: It can make repeated event classes easier to correlate.
entries.caution: Many journal records have no MESSAGE_ID.

entries.summary: A journalctl output mode that serializes structured record fields instead of rendering only human-formatted text.
entries.details: JSON output lets inspection tools consume field names and values directly.
entries.why_it_matters: It preserves record metadata needed for filtering and detailed inspection.
entries.caution: Some journal field values can use non-string JSON representations; consumers should parse defensively.

entries.summary: A message emitted by the Linux kernel and exposed through the kernel log/ring-buffer path and often persisted by journald.
entries.details: Kernel messages cover driver, hardware, filesystem, networking, memory and many other kernel subsystems.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence of events reported by kernel code.
entries.caution: A kernel message is not necessarily an error; severity and context matter.

entries.summary: The in-kernel buffer that stores kernel log messages for readers such as dmesg and logging daemons.
entries.details: It represents current-runtime kernel logging state and has finite capacity.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the direct live source behind dmesg-style inspection.
entries.caution: Older messages can be overwritten; it is not itself persistent boot history.

entries.summary: A userspace command that reads and formats messages from the kernel ring buffer.
entries.details: dmesg is useful for current-runtime kernel messages and supports filtering and follow modes.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a fallback when journal-backed kernel history is unavailable or restricted.
entries.caution: dmesg does not provide retained historical boots in the way a persistent journal can.

entries.summary: Journal metadata identifying a kernel subsystem associated with certain device-related kernel records.
entries.details: Examples can include subsystems such as block, net, pci or usb when the relevant metadata is available.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a reported kernel-origin grouping without guessing from message text.
entries.caution: Not every kernel record has a _KERNEL_SUBSYSTEM field.

entries.summary: Journal metadata describing a kernel device associated with certain kernel-originated records.
entries.details: The value can encode device-path information that journald derived for the event.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps connect a message to a specific device when the kernel/journal reports that association.
entries.caution: It is absent for many kernel messages and should not be inferred when unavailable.

entries.summary: A kernel diagnostic report produced when the kernel detects a serious internal fault but may continue running.
entries.details: Oops reports commonly contain register state, stack traces and taint information.
entries.why_it_matters: They are strong evidence of a kernel or driver fault.
entries.caution: Continued operation after an oops does not mean the system remains fully reliable.

entries.summary: A fatal kernel condition in which normal system operation cannot safely continue.
entries.details: Depending on configuration, a panic may halt, reboot, or leave evidence in persistent crash logging facilities.
entries.why_it_matters: It represents one of the most severe kernel failure conditions.
entries.caution: Not every crash or reboot is a kernel panic.

entries.summary: A kernel report produced by watchdog mechanisms that detect missing progress or other monitored failure conditions.
entries.details: Watchdog messages can accompany soft/hard lockups or platform-specific watchdog events.
entries.why_it_matters: They can indicate that CPUs or critical kernel execution stopped making expected progress.
entries.caution: The word watchdog covers several mechanisms; inspect the actual message before assigning a cause.

entries.summary: A condition in which a CPU or kernel execution path fails to make expected progress for a watchdog-defined interval.
entries.details: Linux can report soft and hard lockups through watchdog diagnostics when configured.
entries.why_it_matters: Lockup reports are significant evidence of scheduler, driver, firmware or hardware problems.
entries.caution: A busy system is not automatically a kernel lockup.

entries.summary: A hardware-reported machine-check condition delivered to the operating system on supported architectures.
entries.details: Machine-check reports can describe CPU, memory or platform hardware errors and may appear in kernel logs.
entries.why_it_matters: They can provide evidence of hardware-detected faults.
entries.caution: Interpretation is architecture- and hardware-specific; not every hardware problem appears as an MCE.

entries.summary: A kernel facility for exposing crash or diagnostic records retained by a persistent-storage backend across reboot.
entries.details: Backends such as ramoops can preserve kernel panic/oops output that would otherwise disappear with the volatile ring buffer.
entries.why_it_matters: It can provide post-reboot evidence of severe kernel failures.
entries.caution: Availability depends on kernel configuration, firmware/platform support and a configured backend.

entries.summary: A userspace command that reports metadata embedded in or associated with a Linux kernel module.
entries.details: Typical fields include filename, license, description, aliases, parameters, dependencies and vermagic when available.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides static module-file metadata that complements live runtime state under /sys/module and /proc/modules.
entries.caution: modinfo output describes module metadata; it does not by itself prove that the module is currently loaded.

entries.summary: A kernel object representing an opened file description that can be referenced by one or more file descriptors.
entries.details: Duplicated or inherited file descriptors may refer to the same open file description, sharing file offset and status flags.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why file-descriptor count and underlying kernel file-object allocation are related but not identical.
entries.caution: Do not use “file descriptor” and “open file description” as exact synonyms.

entries.summary: A procfs kernel interface reporting file-handle/file-table allocation values for the running system.
entries.details: The reported fields describe allocated file handles, an unused field on modern kernels, and the system maximum.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a host-level view of file-object allocation pressure.
entries.caution: It is not a list of which process owns each open file.

entries.summary: The system-wide limit used by the kernel for allocated file handles/file table entries.
entries.details: It provides the denominator for comparing current file-handle allocation with the configured host limit.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps contextualize whether file-table allocation is approaching its configured ceiling.
entries.caution: It is different from per-process file-descriptor limits such as RLIMIT_NOFILE.

entries.summary: A procfs kernel interface reporting host-level inode cache/allocation counters.
entries.details: These counters describe kernel inode objects and are distinct from per-filesystem free-inode counts.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide another host-wide kernel allocation signal alongside file-handle counters.
entries.caution: Do not interpret inode-nr as the number of free inodes on a particular mounted filesystem.

entries.summary: A captured image of process state produced when a process terminates abnormally under configured core-dump policy.
entries.details: On systemd systems, systemd-coredump can record metadata and store or forward the process core image.
entries.why_it_matters: Core dumps can preserve evidence needed to diagnose crashes.
entries.caution: A coredump can contain sensitive process memory and should be handled accordingly.

entries.summary: An asynchronous notification delivered to a process or thread using a numbered signal interface.
entries.details: Signals can request actions such as termination, stopping, continuing, or application-defined handling.
entries.why_it_matters: The terminating signal is important context for many coredumps.
entries.caution: Signal numbers and meanings can vary for some nonstandard signals across architectures.

entries.summary: The numeric identifier of a Unix signal, such as 11 for SIGSEGV on common Linux architectures.
entries.details: Tools may show both the number and symbolic name when reporting a crash.
entries.why_it_matters: Numeric sorting can group coredump records by the actual reported signal value.
entries.caution: Do not infer a signal number from its name when the record already reports the numeric value.

entries.summary: Metadata describing whether and how a process core image was stored, retained or otherwise handled by the coredump subsystem.
entries.details: coredumpctl list output can report storage/corefile information alongside process and signal metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: It tells the user whether crash metadata corresponds to an available stored core image.
entries.caution: Retention policy and permissions can make a previously recorded core unavailable later.

entries.summary: The stored process-memory image associated with a coredump when one is retained.
entries.details: systemd-coredump may store the image externally and keep metadata in the journal.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the artifact used by debuggers for post-mortem process inspection.
entries.caution: Core images may contain credentials, user data or other sensitive memory contents.

entries.summary: The systemd command-line tool for listing, inspecting, retrieving and debugging coredump records managed by systemd-coredump.
entries.details: Its list mode can emit machine-readable JSON with crash metadata such as time, PID, signal, executable and storage information.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the primary read interface used by a systemd-backed coredump inspector.
entries.caution: Availability of full core content depends on retention, permissions and system configuration.

entries.summary: The PSI moving average representing recent stall pressure over an approximately 10-second window.
entries.details: It is reported for PSI some/full lines where applicable and reflects the proportion of time tasks were stalled over that window.
entries.why_it_matters: It emphasizes very recent pressure conditions.
entries.caution: It is a reported pressure metric, not a universal good/bad threshold.

entries.summary: The PSI moving average representing stall pressure over an approximately 60-second window.
entries.details: It smooths short spikes more than avg10 while remaining responsive to recent sustained pressure.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a medium-window view of CPU, memory or I/O contention.
entries.caution: Interpret the value in workload context rather than assigning a universal health score.

entries.summary: The PSI moving average representing stall pressure over an approximately 300-second window.
entries.details: It gives a longer-window view of sustained contention than avg10 or avg60.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish persistent pressure from brief transient spikes.
entries.caution: A low long-window average does not rule out a recent short severe event.

entries.summary: The cumulative stall time reported by PSI, expressed in microseconds for the corresponding pressure line.
entries.details: Unlike avg10/avg60/avg300, total is cumulative since the counter’s lifetime began.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a monotonic amount of observed stall time suitable for calculating deltas.
entries.caution: The absolute total alone does not indicate current pressure intensity.

entries.summary: A period in which tasks cannot make useful progress because a monitored resource is unavailable or contended.
entries.details: PSI aggregates these stalls for CPU, memory and I/O and distinguishes some/full semantics where supported.
entries.why_it_matters: Stall time is the underlying phenomenon measured by PSI.
entries.caution: High utilization and pressure are related concepts but are not the same measurement.

entries.summary: A read-only comparison between a filesystem object’s actual SELinux label and the policy mapping that predicts its expected label.
entries.details: Tools can inspect the actual context and query the policy mapping without changing either one.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps identify potential mislabeling behind access denials.
entries.caution: A reported mismatch should not be automatically “fixed” without understanding local policy and intended labeling.

entries.summary: The context predicted for a path by SELinux file-context policy rules.
entries.details: It is policy-derived and can be compared with the actual label currently stored on the filesystem object.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a policy reference point for a file-context check.
entries.caution: The expected mapping is not itself proof that the object should be relabeled automatically.

entries.summary: The SELinux security context currently attached to a filesystem object.
entries.details: It is the live label observed on the object, as distinct from the context predicted by policy mapping rules.
entries.why_it_matters: It is what the kernel uses when applying SELinux type enforcement to that object.
entries.caution: Filesystems or mount options that do not support ordinary labels may behave differently.

entries.summary: An audit record or group of records containing security-relevant information, including SELinux AVC events when auditing is available.
entries.details: ausearch can retrieve AVC/USER_AVC records and associated audit fields from the audit log.
entries.why_it_matters: Audit records provide richer denial context than a short human message alone.
entries.caution: Availability depends on audit configuration, permissions and log retention.

entries.summary: The SELinux permission or set of permissions that an AVC record reports as denied for a subject/object/class combination.
entries.details: Examples depend on the object class and policy, such as read, write, getattr, connect or execute.
entries.why_it_matters: It identifies the exact operation the policy blocked.
entries.caution: A denial should be interpreted with source context, target context, object class and policy intent.

entries.summary: Software that installs, removes, queries and maintains packages using a distribution-specific package database and policy.
entries.details: Linux distributions commonly use different package-management stacks, such as RPM-based, dpkg-based or pacman-based systems.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why Installed Software must query different native package interfaces on different distributions.
entries.caution: A package manager’s database does not normally enumerate unrelated portable application formats such as arbitrary AppImages.

entries.summary: The Debian-family binary package format used by dpkg and higher-level package-management tools.
entries.details: A DEB archive carries package metadata and files intended for installation into a Debian-style package database.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the native package artifact on Debian and many derived distributions.
entries.caution: A .deb file on disk is not the same thing as an installed package record.

entries.summary: The low-level Debian package-management tool and database interface for installed DEB packages.
entries.details: dpkg can query installed package names, versions, architecture and package state.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides an authoritative native-package inventory source on Debian-family systems.
entries.caution: Higher-level tools such as APT add repository/dependency workflows but do not replace dpkg’s installed-package database.

entries.summary: The package manager used by Arch Linux and related distributions.
entries.details: pacman maintains the local installed-package database and can query installed package metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides the native package inventory source on pacman-based systems.
entries.caution: Its package database and command semantics differ from RPM and dpkg systems.

entries.summary: A packaged application format and runtime model managed by snapd.
entries.details: Installed snaps are managed separately from the distribution’s native RPM/dpkg/pacman package database.
entries.why_it_matters: It is another installed-software source that may need independent discovery.
entries.caution: Snap availability is distribution- and system-configuration-dependent.

entries.summary: A standardized classifier string published in Python project metadata to describe topics, frameworks, environments, audiences and other project attributes.
entries.details: A distribution may provide multiple Classifier fields in its metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: Classifiers can improve package categorization beyond guessing only from a project name.
entries.caution: Classifiers are author-supplied metadata and may be absent, broad or outdated.

entries.summary: Optional project metadata containing author-supplied keywords associated with a Python distribution.
entries.details: Keywords can provide additional hints about package purpose when categorizing installed distributions.
entries.why_it_matters: They complement Summary and Classifier metadata.
entries.caution: Keywords are free-form and should not override stronger exact or standardized evidence blindly.

entries.summary: A short project description stored in Python distribution metadata.
entries.details: It often describes package purpose more clearly than an opaque distribution name.
entries.why_it_matters: Summary text can support human inspection and cautious metadata-assisted categorization.
entries.caution: It is descriptive metadata supplied by the package publisher, not a security assertion.

entries.summary: Structured metadata associated with an installed Python distribution, including fields such as Name, Version, Summary, Requires-Python, dependencies and classifiers.
entries.details: importlib.metadata can expose this installed distribution metadata without importing the package’s runtime modules.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the basis for package inventory and richer categorization.
entries.caution: Distribution metadata describes packaging information; it does not guarantee import-time behavior or compatibility.

entries.summary: A firmware interface specification that defines services and data structures used during platform boot and runtime interaction with the operating system.
entries.details: On UEFI systems, firmware can load EFI executables from an EFI System Partition and stores boot-related variables in firmware-managed nonvolatile storage.
entries.why_it_matters: UEFI defines the environment in which EFI boot managers and loaders operate.
entries.caution: UEFI is a firmware interface specification, not the same thing as a particular boot loader.

entries.summary: A specially identified filesystem partition used by UEFI firmware and boot loaders to store EFI executables and related boot files.
entries.details: The ESP normally uses a firmware-readable filesystem and contains paths such as EFI/<vendor>/ as well as loader data on systems that use those conventions.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a primary on-disk source for inspecting UEFI boot-loader installations.
entries.caution: A machine can have more than one ESP, and the mounted path is not guaranteed to be /boot/efi.

entries.summary: An optional partition type defined by the Boot Loader Specification for holding boot-loader entries and related resources outside the EFI System Partition.
entries.details: XBOOTLDR can provide more space for boot artifacts while the ESP remains available for EFI executables and firmware-facing content.
entries.why_it_matters: It matters when locating boot-loader entries across systems that separate ESP and extended boot storage.
entries.caution: XBOOTLDR is optional and is not present on every Linux installation.

entries.summary: A firmware-managed variable exposed by UEFI runtime services and, on Linux, commonly surfaced through efivarfs.
entries.details: EFI variables can store boot-manager entries, boot order, Secure Boot state and other firmware-defined or vendor-defined data.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide runtime evidence of firmware boot configuration independent of files on an ESP.
entries.caution: Firmware variables can be security-sensitive and should not be modified merely for inspection.

entries.summary: The UEFI firmware mechanism that selects and launches configured EFI boot options.
entries.details: Boot options are represented through firmware variables and can reference EFI executables on suitable filesystems.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains the firmware-level boot entries that are distinct from operating-system boot-loader menu entries.
entries.caution: A firmware boot option is not the same thing as a Boot Loader Specification entry.

entries.summary: A specification for locating and describing Linux boot-loader entries and associated boot resources in a standardized filesystem layout.
entries.details: The specification defines entry formats and locations involving the ESP and optionally XBOOTLDR.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a portable vocabulary for inspecting boot-loader entries without depending entirely on one boot loader’s private configuration.
entries.caution: Not every installed boot loader or distribution uses every part of the specification.

entries.summary: A boot-loader-visible record describing a bootable operating-system/kernel choice and its associated resources or options.
entries.details: Under the Boot Loader Specification, entries can be represented by defined entry formats stored in standard locations.
entries.why_it_matters: Entries are the user-selectable boot choices distinct from firmware-level UEFI boot options.
entries.caution: Do not assume every boot-loader menu item originates from a Boot Loader Specification file.

entries.summary: A simple UEFI boot manager provided by the systemd project.
entries.details: systemd-boot reads boot entries from supported boot partitions and integrates with systemd boot-loader interfaces.
entries.why_it_matters: It is one possible current boot loader that a boot-focused inspector may detect.
entries.caution: Do not assume that every UEFI Linux system uses systemd-boot.

entries.summary: A boot-loader-managed seed file used by supported systemd-boot workflows to help carry entropy across boots into the early boot environment.
entries.details: The seed is boot-state data stored on a boot partition and is intended to be refreshed rather than treated as a readable secret or user setting.
entries.why_it_matters: Its presence is relevant when inspecting boot-loader state beyond executable files and entries.
entries.caution: A random-seed file is sensitive boot state; inspection should not expose or modify its raw contents unnecessarily.

entries.summary: The kernel message device that exposes the printk ring buffer to userspace.
entries.details: Reading /dev/kmsg yields structured kernel-message records including metadata such as sequence and timestamp information.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the direct source used by a ring-buffer inspector without relying on dmesg output.
entries.caution: Access can be restricted; a failed read is not evidence that the ring is empty.

entries.summary: The kernel logging facility used to place messages into the kernel message ring buffer.
entries.details: Kernel subsystems and drivers use printk-style logging; userspace can observe retained records through interfaces such as /dev/kmsg.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains where kernel ring-buffer messages originate.
entries.caution: The ring buffer is finite and is not the same thing as persistent journal storage.

entries.summary: A kernel-wide upper bound related to how many threads/tasks may exist.
entries.details: Linux exposes the current limit through /proc/sys/kernel/threads-max.
entries.why_it_matters: Approaching it can prevent creation of additional tasks.
entries.caution: A high task count is not itself a fault; pressure depends on the configured limit and workload.

entries.summary: The upper bound of the numeric PID allocation space.
entries.details: Linux exposes it through /proc/sys/kernel/pid_max. PIDs are reused over time.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish PID-space capacity from ordinary process count.
entries.caution: PID exhaustion and thread-capacity exhaustion are related but not identical conditions.

entries.summary: The current number of allocated asynchronous-I/O event slots reported by the kernel.
entries.details: It is exposed through /proc/sys/fs/aio-nr and can be compared with aio-max-nr.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides bounded evidence for AIO resource pressure.
entries.caution: Do not interpret a nonzero value as a problem without reference to the configured maximum.

entries.summary: The system-wide maximum number of asynchronous-I/O event slots.
entries.details: It is exposed through /proc/sys/fs/aio-max-nr.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides the capacity boundary for aio-nr.
entries.caution: It is a tunable limit, not a measure of current activity.

entries.summary: The configured maximum number of inotify watches available to a user.
entries.details: Linux exposes this in the inotify sysctl namespace.
entries.why_it_matters: Exhaustion can cause applications that monitor many paths to fail to add watches.
entries.caution: Configured capacity is not the same as current usage unless usage is measured separately.

entries.summary: The configured maximum number of inotify instances per user.
entries.details: It bounds how many separate inotify groups a user can create.
entries.why_it_matters: It is relevant when applications fail to initialize filesystem watching.
entries.caution: Do not confuse instances with individual watches.

entries.summary: A clock identified by a clock ID and queried through interfaces such as clock_gettime().
entries.details: Different clocks represent wall time, monotonic elapsed time, boot-inclusive time or other time domains.
entries.why_it_matters: Knowing the clock type prevents comparing timestamps with different semantics.
entries.caution: Clock IDs differ in whether they are settable, adjusted, suspend-aware or wall-clock based.

entries.summary: The nominal granularity reported for a POSIX clock by clock_getres().
entries.details: Resolution describes the clock interface granularity, not a guarantee that every read advances by that amount.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain the precision available from a particular clock.
entries.caution: Resolution is not scheduler latency and should not be treated as a performance benchmark.

entries.summary: The POSIX wall-clock time source representing calendar time.
entries.details: It can be adjusted and can jump when system time is changed.
entries.why_it_matters: It is appropriate for calendar timestamps but not for measuring uninterrupted elapsed time.
entries.caution: Clock adjustments can make differences between two realtime readings surprising.

entries.summary: A nonsettable monotonic clock used for elapsed-time measurement.
entries.details: On Linux it advances monotonically while the system is running and is not subject to wall-clock jumps.
entries.why_it_matters: It is suitable for ordering and elapsed-time measurements.
entries.caution: It normally excludes time spent suspended; CLOCK_BOOTTIME differs here.

entries.summary: A monotonic Linux clock that includes time spent suspended.
entries.details: It is useful for measuring elapsed time across system sleep.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes boot-relative elapsed time from CLOCK_MONOTONIC behavior.
entries.caution: It is not the same as wall-clock calendar time.

entries.summary: A kernel timekeeping source used to read a continuously advancing hardware or virtual counter.
entries.details: Linux can expose the current and available clocksources through sysfs.
entries.why_it_matters: Clocksource selection affects the kernel timekeeping foundation.
entries.caution: A clocksource is not a POSIX clock and is not the same as an RTC.

entries.summary: The clocksource currently selected by the Linux kernel for timekeeping.
entries.details: It is commonly exposed in /sys/devices/system/clocksource/clocksource0/current_clocksource.
entries.why_it_matters: It tells an inspector which low-level source is currently active.
entries.caution: Do not infer quality merely from the clocksource name.

entries.summary: The clocksources the running kernel reports as available for selection.
entries.details: The set depends on hardware, architecture, virtualization and kernel configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides context for the current clocksource without changing it.
entries.caution: Availability does not mean every source is equally suitable.

entries.summary: Kernel time-discipline state exposed through the adjtimex system call.
entries.details: A read-only adjtimex query can report status, frequency/offset-related fields and synchronization flags without changing time.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides kernel-level synchronization evidence independent of a particular time-sync daemon.
entries.caution: Reading state is distinct from using adjtimex modes that modify time and require privilege.

entries.summary: Kernel-reported state indicating whether the system clock is considered synchronized by the time discipline.
entries.details: It is one piece of synchronization evidence and may be complemented by userspace daemon state.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish a synchronized clock from merely having a time-sync service installed.
entries.caution: An unsynchronized state may be intentional on isolated or offline systems.

entries.summary: A hardware or virtual real-time clock exposed by Linux through RTC class devices.
entries.details: RTC devices can retain calendar time independently of the main system clock.
entries.why_it_matters: They help establish the hardware-clock side of Linux timekeeping.
entries.caution: RTC time is not the same object as CLOCK_REALTIME and multiple RTC devices may exist.

entries.summary: Common name for a platform real-time clock used to retain time across reboots or power cycles.
entries.details: On Linux it is typically represented by an RTC class device such as /dev/rtc0.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains the persistent clock source inspected separately from system time.
entries.caution: The system can have more than one RTC and the designated system RTC can vary.

entries.summary: A running systemd manager instance that loads units and manages their state.
entries.details: Linux systems commonly have one system manager plus per-user manager instances.
entries.why_it_matters: Manager scope determines which units and properties an inspection refers to.
entries.caution: System and user managers are distinct and should not be silently merged.

entries.summary: The system-wide systemd manager, normally PID 1 on a systemd-based host.
entries.details: It manages system units and exposes the system manager D-Bus object model.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the authoritative scope for system services and many boot-time units.
entries.caution: User-manager units are not part of this scope.

entries.summary: A per-user systemd manager that manages units in a user session/account scope.
entries.details: User services and timers can exist independently of similarly named system units.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why a user can have failed or active units while the system manager is healthy.
entries.caution: Do not assume the user manager is always running or available.

entries.summary: A unit object currently known to a running systemd manager.
entries.details: Runtime-unit state includes load, active and sub-state information even when no persistent unit file exists.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes manager runtime objects from unit-file inventory.
entries.caution: A runtime unit is not the same thing as an enabled unit file.

entries.summary: A systemd unit definition or installation link discoverable in the manager unit-file search paths.
entries.details: Unit files provide configuration/provenance and have states such as enabled, disabled, static or masked.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain persistent configuration separately from current runtime state.
entries.caution: A unit file can exist without a currently loaded runtime unit and vice versa.

entries.summary: A unit relationship viewed from the unit that is depended on toward units that reference it.
entries.details: For example, reverse requirements answer which units require a selected unit.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps investigate the impact of a unit on other units.
entries.caution: Reverse dependency is a view of relationship direction, not a separate dependency type.

entries.summary: A systemd ordering dependency requiring one unit to be ordered before another when both are activated.
entries.details: Ordering and requirement dependencies are separate concepts.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain activation order and critical paths.
entries.caution: Before= does not by itself cause the other unit to be started.

entries.summary: The outcome recorded by systemd for a service activation or run, such as success, exit-code, signal or timeout.
entries.details: It complements active/sub-state by describing why the most recent service run ended.
entries.why_it_matters: It is useful when a service is no longer running but systemd retained an outcome.
entries.caution: Exact result values depend on systemd version and service type.

entries.summary: The status value recorded for the service main process when it exited or was terminated.
entries.details: Its interpretation depends on the accompanying exit-code classification.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides concrete process-outcome evidence in service diagnostics.
entries.caution: A numeric status alone is ambiguous without the associated exit-code semantics.

entries.summary: The next activation time computed for a systemd timer unit when available.
entries.details: Timer units can be based on monotonic events, calendar events, or both.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps answer when a timer is expected to trigger next.
entries.caution: A timer can have no next elapse if it is inactive or its conditions do not yield one.

entries.summary: The systemd service that manages login sessions, logged-in users and seats.
entries.details: It exposes the org.freedesktop.login1 D-Bus object model.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the authoritative userspace manager behind Login Inspector inventories.
entries.caution: It is not the same as the systemd service manager unit model.

entries.summary: A login session object reported by systemd-logind.
entries.details: Sessions carry properties such as identity, user, seat, type/class, state and leader where available.
entries.why_it_matters: It represents the session object directly rather than inferring logins from process lists.
entries.caution: Session availability and properties depend on logind and the active login stack.

entries.summary: A user object currently known to systemd-logind.
entries.details: It represents logged-in/login-managed user state and associated sessions.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a runtime login view distinct from the static account database.
entries.caution: A user existing in /etc/passwd does not imply a current login1 User object.

entries.summary: A seat object grouping hardware devices and sessions for local login purposes.
entries.details: Seats can report active sessions and graphical/TTY capabilities.
entries.why_it_matters: It is important on multi-seat and local-session systems.
entries.caution: A seat is not a CPU or NUMA hardware topology object.

entries.summary: The top-level org.freedesktop.login1.Manager D-Bus object.
entries.details: It lists sessions, users and seats and exposes manager-wide login properties.
entries.why_it_matters: Manager Details can inspect these properties without invoking control methods.
entries.caution: The D-Bus interface also has mutating methods; a read-only inspector should not call them.

entries.summary: A systemd service exposing system time, timezone, local-RTC and network-time configuration properties.
entries.details: Its D-Bus interface is org.freedesktop.timedate1.
entries.why_it_matters: Read-only properties complement kernel timekeeping state.
entries.caution: The service exposes control methods too; inspection should not use them.

entries.summary: systemd's network time synchronization service implementing SNTP/NTP-style clock synchronization.
entries.details: Where present, org.freedesktop.timesync1 exposes read-only synchronization properties.
entries.why_it_matters: It adds daemon-specific context to generic kernel time-discipline state.
entries.caution: Not every Linux system uses timesyncd; chrony, ntpd or no network synchronizer may be used instead.

entries.summary: The D-Bus interface exposing systemd-timesyncd manager properties.
entries.details: It can report server and synchronization-related state without parsing command output.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a structured source for timesyncd-specific inspection.
entries.caution: Its absence does not mean the system clock is unsynchronized.

entries.summary: A freedesktop.org .desktop metadata file describing an application, launcher or related desktop integration entry.
entries.details: Desktop entries use key/value groups to describe names, executable commands, icons, visibility and other desktop behavior; XDG autostart reuses this format.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the underlying file format for XDG autostart entries inspected by Autostart Inspector.
entries.caution: A .desktop file is not automatically an autostart entry; its location and autostart-specific keys determine that role.

entries.summary: Desktop-session autostart entries described by .desktop files in standard XDG autostart locations.
entries.details: User-level entries can override system entries with the same desktop file name according to the specification.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain programs configured to start with a graphical desktop session.
entries.caution: XDG autostart is distinct from systemd services and shell profile startup.

entries.summary: A time-based job scheduler traditionally used to run commands according to recurring schedules.
entries.details: System and per-user cron sources can coexist.
entries.why_it_matters: Cron entries are one source of automatically executed work.
entries.caution: Cron is scheduling, not proof that a job successfully ran.

entries.summary: A table of cron schedule entries for a user or system context.
entries.details: Fields describe when a command should run and what command is invoked.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the principal configuration object inspected for cron-based autostart/scheduling.
entries.caution: Syntax and special fields vary somewhat between cron implementations.

entries.summary: A conventional directory containing system cron fragments.
entries.details: Files commonly use a system crontab-style format that includes the target user.
entries.why_it_matters: It is an important system-wide cron source.
entries.caution: A file present here does not prove the command currently succeeds.

entries.summary: A scheduler designed to run periodic jobs even when a machine was not continuously powered on.
entries.details: Anacron uses period-based jobs rather than requiring the machine to be running at an exact minute.
entries.why_it_matters: It complements cron on intermittently running systems.
entries.caution: Anacron semantics are not identical to ordinary cron schedules.

entries.summary: A legacy local startup script convention executed during boot on systems that support it.
entries.details: Its exact path and integration depend on distribution/init configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: It remains relevant when auditing legacy startup behavior.
entries.caution: Many modern systems do not enable rc.local by default.

entries.summary: A legacy S-prefixed symbolic link selecting a SysV init script for startup in a runlevel.
entries.details: Traditional rc directories encode ordering and enablement through link names.
entries.why_it_matters: It captures legacy automatic startup that may coexist with systemd compatibility.
entries.caution: Presence and interpretation are distribution-dependent on modern systems.

entries.summary: A systemd utility for inspecting and managing boot loader and EFI-related state.
entries.details: Read-only status output can report firmware, ESP, boot loader and loader-entry information.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a structured source used by Boot Loaders inspection.
entries.caution: bootctl also has mutating commands; an inspector should restrict itself to read-only acquisition.

entries.summary: An external early-userspace image loaded by the boot process for use before the real root filesystem is available.
entries.details: Linux commonly uses compressed cpio content as an initramfs image.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the inspectable artifact associated with a kernel version in Initramfs Inspector.
entries.caution: The exact image format and tooling vary by distribution.

entries.summary: An archive format used by Linux initramfs to package early-userspace files.
entries.details: The kernel can unpack newc-style cpio archives into the initial root filesystem.
entries.why_it_matters: Recognizing cpio explains the internal form of many initramfs images.
entries.caution: An initramfs file may also be compressed and may contain concatenated components.

entries.summary: Compression applied to an external initramfs image, such as gzip, xz, zstd or other kernel-supported formats.
entries.details: Compression reduces image size while the kernel or boot path expands it for early userspace.
entries.why_it_matters: It is useful metadata when inventorying initramfs images.
entries.caution: Supported formats depend on kernel build and distribution choices.

entries.summary: The procfs interface describing mounts visible in the current process mount namespace.
entries.details: It reports mount IDs, parent IDs, major:minor device identity, roots, mount points, options, propagation fields, filesystem type and source.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the authoritative primary inventory source for Mounted Filesystems.
entries.caution: It is namespace-specific and is richer than /proc/mounts.

entries.summary: The identifier assigned to a mount record in mountinfo.
entries.details: The ID identifies a mount within the current namespace view and may be reused after unmount.
entries.why_it_matters: It allows parent/child and stacked-mount relationships to be reconstructed.
entries.caution: It is not a persistent filesystem UUID.

entries.summary: The mountinfo identifier of a mount's parent in the mount tree.
entries.details: It establishes mount hierarchy and helps represent over-mounted/stacked mounts.
entries.why_it_matters: It makes mount topology explicit.
entries.caution: The root of a mount namespace has special parent semantics.

entries.summary: The path inside the mounted filesystem that forms the root exposed at the mount point.
entries.details: It is particularly important for bind mounts and subdirectory mounts.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes the filesystem-internal root from the namespace mount point.
entries.caution: Do not assume every mount exposes the filesystem's own / root.

entries.summary: The device number pair reported by mountinfo for files on the mounted filesystem.
entries.details: It corresponds to st_dev-style device identity and can help correlate mounts with block devices where applicable.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a stable kernel identity within the running system.
entries.caution: Pseudo and network filesystems may not map to a conventional disk device.

entries.summary: The rules that control how mount and unmount events propagate between related mount trees/namespaces.
entries.details: mountinfo optional fields can describe shared, master and unbindable relationships.
entries.why_it_matters: It is important for containers, bind mounts and namespace topology.
entries.caution: Propagation state is not the same as read/write access.

entries.summary: A mount belonging to a shared peer group in the Linux mount-propagation model.
entries.details: Mount events under one peer can propagate to other peers in the group.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains shared mount relationships reported by mountinfo.
entries.caution: Shared does not mean a network share.

entries.summary: A mount-propagation relationship in which a slave receives events from a master peer group.
entries.details: mountinfo can expose master and propagate_from identifiers.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains one-way propagation relationships.
entries.caution: The terminology is specific to mount propagation, not device hierarchy.

entries.summary: A mount marked so that it cannot be the source of a bind mount.
entries.details: mountinfo can report the unbindable propagation flag.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a special mount-propagation state worth preserving in metadata.
entries.caution: It does not mean the filesystem is inaccessible.

entries.summary: A standard interface for obtaining mounted-filesystem capacity, inode and flag information.
entries.details: It reports values such as block counts, free/available blocks, file counts and maximum filename length.
entries.why_it_matters: It enriches mount inventory with filesystem capacity without parsing df output.
entries.caution: Not every returned field is meaningful on every filesystem.

entries.summary: The major and minor device numbers identifying a Linux block device.
entries.details: The pair is exposed by sysfs and device metadata and is used by the kernel to identify device nodes.
entries.why_it_matters: It enables exact block-device identity and mount correlation.
entries.caution: It is not the same as partition number or filesystem UUID.

entries.summary: The Linux kernel framework for creating virtual block devices from mapping targets.
entries.details: It underlies technologies such as LVM logical volumes and some encrypted/multipath mappings.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains stacked block devices and holder/slave relationships.
entries.caution: A device-mapper node alone does not identify the higher-level semantic technology that created it.

entries.summary: The Linux multiple-device (MD) subsystem for assembling software RAID arrays from block devices.
entries.details: MD exposes array level, member, state and synchronization metadata through sysfs.
entries.why_it_matters: It allows Block Devices and Problem Finder to identify array topology and degradation state.
entries.caution: MD RAID is distinct from device-mapper and hardware RAID.

entries.summary: A higher-level block device that holds or depends on another block device in sysfs topology.
entries.details: Holder relationships help represent stacked mappings such as DM or MD.
entries.why_it_matters: They show which block objects consume a lower device.
entries.caution: Holder/slave direction must not be reversed when presenting topology.

entries.summary: A lower-level block device used by a higher-level block mapping.
entries.details: The slaves relationship exposes dependencies beneath stacked block devices.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps answer what storage objects lie underneath a selected mapping.
entries.caution: Terminology reflects kernel/sysfs relationship naming and may differ from user-facing storage vocabulary.

entries.summary: A block device whose storage is backed by a regular file or another block device.
entries.details: Loop devices are commonly used for filesystem images and package/container image mounting.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain block objects that do not correspond directly to physical disks.
entries.caution: The backing file and access flags are part of loop-device state, not filesystem identity.

entries.summary: A RAM-backed compressed block device provided by the Linux kernel.
entries.details: zram is commonly used for compressed swap or temporary block storage.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains block devices whose capacity is backed by compressed memory rather than persistent media.
entries.caution: Reported virtual size is not the same as physical RAM consumed.

entries.summary: The starting sector offset of a partition relative to its parent block device.
entries.details: Linux sysfs exposes partition start and size values in sectors.
entries.why_it_matters: It allows exact partition geometry and proportional layout rendering.
entries.caution: Sector units must be interpreted with the correct kernel/sysfs conventions.

entries.summary: The number of sectors occupied by a partition according to the block layer.
entries.details: Combined with the start sector it defines the partition range.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides exact geometry without parsing partitioning CLI output.
entries.caution: It does not by itself describe filesystem allocation inside the partition.

entries.summary: The directed relationships between stacked block devices, including parents, partitions, holders and slaves.
entries.details: A mapping graph represents kernel block-layer topology rather than filesystem mount relationships.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain stacked storage such as DM and MD arrays.
entries.caution: It should not be confused with file-to-physical-block mapping.

entries.summary: A recognizable on-device signature identifying content such as a filesystem, RAID metadata, crypto container or partition table.
entries.details: libblkid can probe selected devices read-only and report usage/type/UUID/label and partition metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: It tells what content a block device appears to contain without mounting it.
entries.caution: A signature is evidence of format, not proof that the content is healthy or mounted.

entries.summary: The util-linux library for probing block-device content signatures and tags.
entries.details: It can perform low-level read-only probing without parsing the blkid command output.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a direct library source for selected-device signature inspection.
entries.caution: Probing reads device content and may require access even though it does not modify the device.

entries.summary: An identifier associated with a partition-table entry rather than the filesystem stored inside the partition.
entries.details: It can be reported by partition metadata and used to identify a partition independently of filesystem UUID.
entries.why_it_matters: It prevents conflating partition identity with filesystem identity.
entries.caution: PARTUUID semantics depend on partition-table type.

entries.summary: A partition label stored in partition-table metadata where the table format supports it.
entries.details: It names the partition entry independently of any filesystem label inside it.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish partition metadata from filesystem metadata.
entries.caution: PARTLABEL and filesystem LABEL are different namespaces.

entries.summary: A major ext4 allocation structure dividing filesystem space into groups of blocks and metadata.
entries.details: Runtime allocator information can expose free-space characteristics per group.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the native allocation-unit concept used when deepening an ext4 mount.
entries.caution: Runtime allocator output is not a raw on-disk group-descriptor dump.

entries.summary: The /proc/fs/ext4/<device>/mb_groups runtime view of the ext4 multiblock allocator buddy cache.
entries.details: It reports allocator/free-block information for mounted ext4 filesystems.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides kernel-reported ext4 allocation detail without reading raw media.
entries.caution: Fields are allocator runtime information and can vary with kernel implementation.

entries.summary: A top-level allocation unit in an XFS filesystem.
entries.details: XFS geometry ioctls can report AG length, free blocks, inode counts and health flags.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the natural row object for XFS allocation inspection.
entries.caution: An XFS AG is not equivalent to an ext4 block group in every implementation detail.

entries.summary: XFS geometry health flags indicating which allocation-group structures have been checked.
entries.details: Checked flags provide context for interpreting corresponding sick flags.
entries.why_it_matters: They prevent an inspector from calling an unchecked structure healthy.
entries.caution: Not checked is not the same as checked and healthy.

entries.summary: XFS health flags reporting structures that the kernel has marked sick.
entries.details: Flags can identify affected metadata families such as AG headers or btrees.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide explicit kernel-reported filesystem problem evidence.
entries.caution: Absence of a sick bit does not prove unexamined structures are healthy.

entries.summary: A Btrfs allocation class such as Data, Metadata or System.
entries.details: Btrfs space-info interfaces report totals/usage by class and allocation profile.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the filesystem-native allocation concept used instead of inventing numbered groups.
entries.caution: Classes and profiles are separate dimensions.

entries.summary: The redundancy/placement profile associated with Btrfs allocated space, such as single, DUP or RAID variants.
entries.details: Profiles describe how a Btrfs space class is laid out across member devices.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain allocation behavior on single- and multi-device filesystems.
entries.caution: A profile name is not the same as Linux MD RAID topology.

entries.summary: A device reported by Btrfs as belonging to a particular Btrfs filesystem.
entries.details: BTRFS_IOC_DEV_INFO can expose device ID, UUID, total size and bytes used.
entries.why_it_matters: It is intrinsic filesystem membership information.
entries.caution: It should not be expanded into generic partition/DM/MD topology, which belongs to block-device inspection.

entries.summary: A Linux ioctl that retrieves physical extent mappings for a filesystem where supported.
entries.details: The API reports physical ranges, owner identifiers and flags without requiring a recursive file walk.
entries.why_it_matters: It supports an explicit read-only Physical Map view of filesystem allocation.
entries.caution: Support is filesystem-specific and owner identifiers do not automatically map to pathnames.

entries.summary: A snapshot of physical ranges and ownership classes reported by a filesystem mapping API.
entries.details: It can distinguish free space, filesystem metadata and other owner categories defined by the API.
entries.why_it_matters: It reveals filesystem-level physical allocation without parsing raw media.
entries.caution: It is not a per-file pathname-to-sector map unless an explicit file-mapping API is used.

entries.summary: A filesystem that has entered a read-only state because of an explicitly reported error condition.
entries.details: This is different from a filesystem intentionally mounted read-only by configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: It can explain sudden write failures and is a strong fault signal when the provider reports the cause explicitly.
entries.caution: A generic ro mount must never be assumed to be error-forced without authoritative evidence.

entries.summary: The traditional Unix/Linux access-control model based on ownership, permission bits and ACLs.
entries.details: DAC decisions are made separately from mandatory access-control systems such as SELinux.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the correct domain for ordinary file access checks.
entries.caution: A DAC allow does not guarantee SELinux or another LSM will also allow access.

entries.summary: The owner/group/other read, write and execute permission bits stored for a filesystem object.
entries.details: Mode bits are one input to discretionary access checks and are represented by stat metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide the basic access baseline for files and directories.
entries.caution: ACLs and capabilities can add semantics beyond the familiar rwx display.

entries.summary: An access control list providing more fine-grained discretionary file permissions than owner/group/other mode bits alone.
entries.details: Access ACLs can name additional users/groups and use a mask entry to constrain effective permissions.
entries.why_it_matters: They are essential for accurate file access inspection on ACL-enabled filesystems.
entries.caution: Displayed mode bits alone may not reveal all effective ACL permissions.

entries.summary: The POSIX ACL entry that limits effective permissions for named users, named groups and the owning group class.
entries.details: The mask participates in the ACL access-check algorithm.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why an ACL entry can show permissions that are not all effective.
entries.caution: The file owner entry and other entry are treated differently by the ACL algorithm.

entries.summary: The access a particular account would receive after applying DAC ownership, groups, mode bits and ACL rules.
entries.details: It is account-specific and differs from merely displaying metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: It answers whether a named account can read, write or execute/search a path under DAC/ACL rules.
entries.caution: SELinux and other LSM decisions are separate layers and can still deny access.

entries.summary: Linux capability data attached to an executable file, commonly stored in a security extended attribute.
entries.details: File capabilities can grant selected privilege bits when an executable is run.
entries.why_it_matters: They are important integrity/security metadata for selected executable files.
entries.caution: A capability stored on a file is not the same as a capability currently held by a running process.

entries.summary: A cryptographic hash value commonly used to fingerprint file contents.
entries.details: For the same byte sequence SHA-256 deterministically produces the same 256-bit digest.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides content-integrity evidence for a selected file.
entries.caution: A matching hash proves equality to the compared digest, not that the file is trustworthy or malware-free.

entries.summary: A directory entry that refers to the same filesystem inode as another directory entry.
entries.details: Multiple hard-link names share the same underlying inode and file contents.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why counting paths can overcount allocated storage unless inode identity is deduplicated.
entries.caution: Hard links normally cannot cross filesystem boundaries.

entries.summary: A filesystem object containing a pathname reference to another path.
entries.details: Unlike a hard link, a symlink has its own inode and the target may be missing or on another filesystem.
entries.why_it_matters: Explicit symlink handling prevents recursive scans from unexpectedly crossing boundaries.
entries.caution: Following a symlink changes which object is being inspected.

entries.summary: The inode metadata count of hard links referring to a filesystem object.
entries.details: For regular files it helps detect whether multiple directory entries reference the same inode.
entries.why_it_matters: It is useful for hard-link discovery and allocation deduplication.
entries.caution: The semantics for directories and special files can differ from simple regular-file expectations.

entries.summary: A name/value pair attached to a filesystem object outside the ordinary stat metadata.
entries.details: xattrs are used for ACLs, SELinux labels, capabilities and application/filesystem metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: They are useful integrity/provenance evidence for selected paths.
entries.caution: Namespaces and permission rules restrict which xattrs can be read or changed.

entries.summary: A file whose logical size includes regions that do not have physical storage blocks allocated.
entries.details: Sparse files can have a large apparent size while consuming much less allocated space.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains differences between apparent and allocated size.
entries.caution: Copying a sparse file with unsuitable tools can allocate the holes and increase storage use.

entries.summary: The logical byte length of a file as reported by its size metadata.
entries.details: For sparse files and some filesystem objects it can differ substantially from allocated storage.
