entries.why_it_matters: It is the user-visible content length used in Path Inspector Usage accounting.
entries.caution: Summing apparent sizes does not equal physical storage consumption.

entries.summary: An estimate of filesystem blocks allocated to a file, commonly derived from stat st_blocks units.
entries.details: It better reflects storage allocation than apparent size for sparse files.
entries.why_it_matters: It supports disk-usage accounting and hard-link deduplication.
entries.caution: Filesystem compression, sharing/reflinks and metadata can make allocated-byte interpretation more complex.

entries.summary: The device identity reported by stat for the filesystem containing a path.
entries.details: Recursive scans can compare st_dev with the starting object to avoid crossing filesystem boundaries.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a kernel-level boundary for selected-path scans.
entries.caution: st_dev identifies the mounted filesystem/device view, not necessarily a physical disk.

entries.summary: The Executable and Linkable Format used for Linux executables, shared libraries, object files and core files.
entries.details: ELF headers describe object class, machine architecture, type, program headers, sections and notes.
entries.why_it_matters: Direct ELF parsing provides executable identity without running external file-inspection commands.
entries.caution: Not every executable on Linux is ELF.

entries.summary: An identifier commonly stored in an ELF note to distinguish a particular built binary or library.
entries.details: Build IDs are often used by debugging and symbol infrastructure to correlate binaries with separate data.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide stronger build identity than a filename alone.
entries.caution: Presence and algorithm are toolchain-dependent; a build ID is not a package signature.

entries.summary: The association recorded by a native package manager between an installed package and filesystem paths it owns.
entries.details: A selected file can be queried against native package metadata to determine whether it belongs to a package.
entries.why_it_matters: It links path-level inspection to installed-software provenance.
entries.caution: Files can legitimately be unowned, generated after installation, or managed outside the native package database.

entries.summary: The native package manager's local record of installed packages and associated metadata.
entries.details: RPM, dpkg and pacman maintain different database formats and semantics.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the authority for installed-package inventory and native package checks.
entries.caution: A package database does not continuously monitor whether installed files later change.

entries.summary: A native package-manager condition in which installed package dependency requirements are not satisfied.
entries.details: The exact audit mechanism and semantics are package-manager specific.
entries.why_it_matters: It can explain software that is installed but not in a coherent dependency state.
entries.caution: Do not infer dependency health by simply checking whether a package name exists.

entries.summary: A package-manager state indicating package unpack/configuration work did not finish cleanly.
entries.details: dpkg-based systems can retain packages requiring configuration or repair after an interrupted transaction.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a concrete package-management problem distinct from file integrity verification.
entries.caution: The concept and native recovery mechanisms are backend-specific.

entries.summary: A Linux namespace that isolates System V IPC objects and POSIX message queues.
entries.details: Processes in different IPC namespaces can see different IPC object sets.
entries.why_it_matters: It defines the scope for /proc/sysvipc and mqueue views used by IPC inspection.
entries.caution: IPC namespace identity is separate from the IPC objects contained within it.

entries.summary: A Linux namespace that isolates hostname and NIS domain-name identifiers.
entries.details: Processes in different UTS namespaces can observe different host naming state.
entries.why_it_matters: It is one of the namespace identities discoverable through /proc/<pid>/ns.
entries.caution: It does not isolate networking by itself.

entries.summary: A Linux namespace that can virtualize certain monotonic/boottime clock offsets for processes.
entries.details: Current membership and child-namespace targets can be exposed through proc namespace handles.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why time-related process views can differ between namespace contexts.
entries.caution: It does not virtualize every clock or wall-clock setting.

entries.summary: A file-like reference such as /proc/<pid>/ns/mnt that refers to a Linux namespace object.
entries.details: The link target includes a namespace type and inode-like identifier; open descriptors can keep namespaces alive.
entries.why_it_matters: Handles provide direct identity references for namespace inspection.
entries.caution: A visible process-handle inventory is not guaranteed to discover namespaces kept alive only by other references.

entries.summary: The inode-style identifier shown for a namespace handle, commonly rendered like mnt:[4026531841].
entries.details: Within a namespace type it can be used to group processes sharing the same namespace object.
entries.why_it_matters: It enables deduplication of namespace memberships.
entries.caution: It is not a globally persistent identifier across reboots.

entries.summary: The Linux pseudo-filesystem used to represent namespace file descriptors and namespace relationships.
entries.details: Namespace ioctls can operate on namespace FDs to discover owning user namespaces or parents for hierarchical namespaces.
entries.why_it_matters: It supports relationship metadata without entering a namespace.
entries.caution: Using nsfs inspection is distinct from setns(), which changes namespace membership.

entries.summary: The parent relationship exposed for hierarchical namespace types such as PID and user namespaces.
entries.details: NS_GET_PARENT can return a file descriptor for the parent where the operation is supported.
entries.why_it_matters: It adds hierarchy context to namespace identity.
entries.caution: Not every namespace type has a parent relationship exposed this way.

entries.summary: The user namespace that owns another namespace object.
entries.details: NS_GET_USERNS can return a handle for this relationship.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain privilege/ownership context of namespace objects.
entries.caution: This is not the same as listing the user IDs inside that namespace.

entries.summary: A proc namespace handle indicating the PID namespace that newly created children will enter.
entries.details: It can differ from the process's current PID namespace in specific namespace setups.
entries.why_it_matters: It prevents conflating current membership with child namespace targets.
entries.caution: It is a target for future children, not the current PID namespace identity.

entries.summary: A proc namespace handle indicating the time namespace that newly created children will use.
entries.details: It is analogous to pid_for_children for time namespaces.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes child-target state from current membership.
entries.caution: It should not be displayed as the current time namespace when they differ.

entries.summary: A process chosen to provide a stable human-readable representative for a namespace group in an inventory snapshot.
entries.details: A representative can be selected deterministically, for example the lowest visible member PID.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps label namespace rows without claiming the process owns the namespace.
entries.caution: The representative may exit after acquisition and is not a namespace authority.

entries.summary: An unnamed unidirectional byte-stream IPC channel with a read end and a write end.
entries.details: Linux exposes open anonymous pipes through process file descriptors with targets such as pipe:[inode].
entries.why_it_matters: It allows active pipes to be deduplicated and correlated with visible process references.
entries.caution: The inode-style number identifies the pipe object for correlation but is not a filesystem path.

entries.summary: A filesystem node that provides pipe semantics through a pathname.
entries.details: Processes open the FIFO for reading and/or writing; the node can exist even when no process currently has it open.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains the difference between active FIFO references and dormant FIFO nodes.
entries.caution: A FIFO is not a regular file even though it has a filesystem pathname.

entries.summary: A named FIFO filesystem node with no visible active process file-descriptor reference at scan time.
entries.details: It can be discovered only by an explicit bounded filesystem scan rather than procfd correlation alone.
entries.why_it_matters: It completes FIFO inventory without requiring a whole-filesystem crawl.
entries.caution: Dormant means no visible active reference, not that the FIFO can never be opened.

entries.summary: A file descriptor referring to the read end, write end, or in some cases a read/write reference associated with a pipe/FIFO.
entries.details: File-descriptor flags can help classify visible references.
entries.why_it_matters: It allows IPC Inspector to summarize readers, writers and reference counts.
entries.caution: Reference direction reflects accessible descriptor state and can race with process changes.

entries.summary: A socket in the AF_UNIX/AF_LOCAL address family for local IPC on the same system.
entries.details: Unix sockets may use filesystem pathnames, Linux abstract names, or no bound name.
entries.why_it_matters: They support bidirectional local IPC and can be correlated with process socket FDs.
entries.caution: They are scoped by the network namespace despite being local IPC.

entries.summary: A Linux Unix-domain socket address in the abstract namespace rather than the filesystem pathname namespace.
entries.details: Abstract names do not correspond to filesystem nodes and are represented specially in /proc/net/unix.
entries.why_it_matters: It prevents treating every Unix socket name as a path on disk.
entries.caution: Abstract-socket lifetime follows sockets, not persistent filesystem nodes.

entries.summary: A Unix-domain socket without a bound pathname or abstract name visible in the socket table.
entries.details: Such sockets can still have active process references.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains socket rows where inode/type/state exist but no name is present.
entries.caution: Lack of a name is not evidence that the socket is unused.

entries.summary: A named kernel message queue provided by the POSIX message-queue API.
entries.details: Queues have attributes such as maximum messages, message size and current message count and are commonly represented through mqueuefs.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide message-oriented IPC distinct from System V queues.
entries.caution: They are scoped by IPC namespaces and may be unavailable if mqueuefs is not mounted.

entries.summary: The special filesystem normally mounted at /dev/mqueue that exposes POSIX message queues.
entries.details: Queue entries and read-only pseudo-file metadata make the current IPC-namespace queue view inspectable.
entries.why_it_matters: Its presence is needed for pathname-style enumeration of POSIX queues.
entries.caution: An unmounted mqueue filesystem means the view is unavailable, not necessarily that no queues exist.

entries.summary: The family of System V shared-memory, semaphore and message-queue mechanisms.
entries.details: Linux exposes current objects through /proc/sysvipc in the current IPC namespace.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a coherent object family for IPC inventory.
entries.caution: System V IPC and POSIX IPC are separate APIs with different identifiers and semantics.

entries.summary: A System V IPC object that allows processes to attach the same kernel-managed memory segment.
entries.details: Segments have an IPC ID, key, ownership/permissions and size-related metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain shared-memory objects listed under /proc/sysvipc/shm.
entries.caution: A segment can persist beyond individual process attachments until removed according to SysV semantics.

entries.summary: A System V IPC object containing one or more semaphores used for process synchronization.
entries.details: The set is identified by an IPC ID and carries ownership/permission metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the correct inventory object rather than pretending each semaphore is a separate top-level IPC object.
entries.caution: Inspecting set existence does not necessarily expose every individual semaphore value.

entries.summary: A System V IPC object for exchanging discrete messages.
entries.details: Queues are identified by IPC IDs and can report message/count/byte and ownership metadata.
entries.why_it_matters: It is distinct from POSIX message queues.
entries.caution: Keys are not guaranteed to be unique permanent identities; IPC IDs identify current objects.

entries.summary: A key value used by System V IPC APIs to find or create IPC objects.
entries.details: Different object types can use keys and special values such as IPC_PRIVATE have defined semantics.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides source metadata for SysV objects.
entries.caution: The key is not the safest deduplication identity for a current object; the kernel IPC ID is stronger for inventory.

entries.summary: The kernel identifier returned for a current System V IPC object.
entries.details: Operations on SysV shared memory, semaphores and queues use these IDs.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the natural per-type object identity for a current snapshot.
entries.caution: IDs can be reused after objects are removed; they are not persistent identifiers.

entries.summary: A locality domain grouping CPUs and memory in a Non-Uniform Memory Access system.
entries.details: Linux exposes per-node CPU association, memory, distance, allocation statistics and huge-page state in sysfs.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the primary object for richer NUMA inspection.
entries.caution: A node can exist without CPUs or without normal memory on some systems.

entries.summary: The list-form CPU mask associated with a NUMA node.
entries.details: It names the logical CPUs assigned to that node by the kernel topology.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides readable CPU placement context for the node.
entries.caution: It is topology, not CPU-affinity policy for a process.

entries.summary: The bitmap-form representation of CPUs associated with a NUMA node.
entries.details: It expresses the same association as cpulist in a machine-oriented mask format.
entries.why_it_matters: It preserves the exact kernel-reported node CPU map.
entries.caution: Do not treat a bitmap as a scheduling-affinity mask for an individual process.

entries.summary: A kernel-reported relative cost from one NUMA node to each node in the system.
entries.details: Local distance is typically lower than remote distance, but values are abstract relative costs.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain memory/CPU locality relationships.
entries.caution: Distance values are not metres, latency measurements or bandwidth measurements.

entries.summary: NUMA allocation hit/miss counters exposed for each node.
entries.details: Counters include numa_hit, numa_miss, numa_foreign, interleave_hit, local_node and other_node.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide evidence about allocation locality.
entries.caution: They are cumulative page counters, not live percentages.

entries.summary: A per-node counter incremented when a process wanted memory from a node and the allocation succeeded there.
entries.details: It is reported in pages.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a direct locality-success counter.
entries.caution: A large absolute number has no meaning without workload and time context.

entries.summary: A per-node counter incremented when an allocation landed on this node even though another node was preferred.
entries.details: It is reported in pages and paired conceptually with numa_foreign on the preferred node.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps identify nonpreferred NUMA allocation activity.
entries.caution: Nonzero misses are not automatically a fault.

entries.summary: A per-node counter indicating allocations intended for this preferred node that were satisfied elsewhere.
entries.details: It complements numa_miss recorded on the node where allocation actually succeeded.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps interpret NUMA allocation locality.
entries.caution: It is cumulative and workload-dependent.

entries.summary: A NUMA counter for allocations made from a node by a CPU local to that node.
entries.details: It reflects CPU-local allocation rather than process preferred-node policy.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides another locality perspective alongside numa_hit.
entries.caution: It should not be equated exactly with numa_hit.

entries.summary: A NUMA counter for allocations satisfied on a node for a CPU located on another node.
entries.details: It reflects remote CPU-to-memory locality.
entries.why_it_matters: It complements local_node in node allocation statistics.
entries.caution: Nonzero values can be normal under memory policy and workload pressure.

entries.summary: Per-node virtual-memory statistics exposed through nodeN/vmstat.
entries.details: It provides a large set of allocation/reclaim/page-state counters for that node.
entries.why_it_matters: It enables advanced node metadata without crowding the main NUMA inventory.
entries.caution: Counters are kernel implementation details and should not be converted into a generic health score.

entries.summary: A memory page larger than the normal base page size, used to reduce page-table overhead and support specific workloads.
entries.details: Linux supports explicit HugeTLB pools and also separate transparent-huge-page mechanisms.
entries.why_it_matters: Per-node huge-page pools are useful NUMA context.
entries.caution: HugeTLB and Transparent Huge Pages are related but distinct mechanisms.

entries.summary: A configured pool of persistent/reserved huge pages of a particular size.
entries.details: Per-node sysfs can report total, free and surplus huge pages for supported sizes.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides capacity evidence for huge-page workloads.
entries.caution: A zero pool can be intentional; it is not automatically a problem.

entries.summary: Kernel-reported status for a speculative-execution or other processor vulnerability exposed in sysfs.
entries.details: Linux reports per-vulnerability text such as Not affected, Vulnerable, Mitigation: ... or other qualified states.
entries.why_it_matters: It exposes the running kernel's own assessment without external vulnerability guessing.
entries.caution: The complete kernel text should be preserved because states can contain important qualifications.

entries.summary: A kernel-reported mitigation active for a CPU vulnerability.
entries.details: Mitigation status is commonly included in /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities/* text.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains what protection the running kernel says is enabled.
entries.caution: A mitigation label is not a general guarantee that every attack path is impossible.

entries.summary: The Linux Error Detection And Correction subsystem for reporting hardware error information, especially memory-controller errors.
entries.details: EDAC sysfs can expose corrected and uncorrectable error counters where supported by hardware/drivers.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides structured RAS evidence without log keyword scanning.
entries.caution: Not all systems expose EDAC counters and counter availability depends on drivers/firmware.

entries.summary: A memory error that ECC hardware detected and corrected.
entries.details: EDAC can accumulate corrected-error counts per controller/DIMM where supported.
entries.why_it_matters: Nonzero counts can provide early reliability evidence while data was corrected.
entries.caution: Corrected and uncorrectable errors have very different severity.

entries.summary: A memory error that ECC mechanisms could not correct.
entries.details: EDAC may expose uncorrectable-error counters when platform support is available.
entries.why_it_matters: It is strong hardware fault evidence.
entries.caution: Some platforms may react immediately (including panic), so a running-system counter is not guaranteed to capture every event.

entries.summary: The PCI Express mechanism for reporting correctable, non-fatal and fatal link/device errors.
entries.details: Linux can expose AER statistics for PCIe devices and handles recovery for error classes.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides structured PCIe reliability evidence.
entries.caution: Correctable AER events are not equivalent in severity to fatal errors.

entries.summary: A thermal-zone trip point classified as critical by the platform/kernel thermal framework.
entries.details: Reaching or exceeding such a trip is stronger evidence than merely observing a high absolute temperature.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides hardware-defined thermal problem semantics.
entries.caution: Trip-point availability and accuracy depend on platform firmware and drivers.

entries.summary: A health status reported through the Linux power-supply class for a battery or other supply.
entries.details: Values can describe good health or explicit fault conditions such as overheat depending on driver support.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides direct platform-reported evidence for power problems.
entries.caution: Absence of a health property does not imply either healthy or faulty state.

entries.summary: A terminated process whose parent has not yet collected its exit status.
entries.details: Linux process state Z represents a zombie task.
entries.why_it_matters: A large or persistent zombie population can indicate parent-process cleanup problems.
entries.caution: A single transient zombie can be normal and should not automatically be treated as a severe fault.

entries.summary: A task state in which a process is sleeping in an uninterruptible kernel wait, commonly while waiting for I/O or kernel resources.
entries.details: Linux typically labels this process state D.
entries.why_it_matters: A persistent or large D-state population can help explain hangs or blocked I/O.
entries.caution: Short-lived D state is normal and a one-time snapshot cannot prove a task is permanently stuck.

entries.summary: The per-process soft/hard resource limit governing the maximum file descriptor number a process may allocate.
entries.details: It can be compared with a process's open descriptor count to diagnose descriptor exhaustion.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides process-specific capacity context beyond the system-wide file-handle limit.
entries.caution: Soft and hard limits differ, and the limit is not the number of descriptors currently open.

entries.summary: The kernel-reported memory commit limit used by Linux virtual-memory overcommit accounting.
entries.details: It can be compared with Committed_AS to assess commitment pressure under relevant overcommit modes.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a capacity boundary different from physical free RAM.
entries.caution: Commit accounting semantics depend on vm.overcommit settings and do not equal resident memory usage.

entries.summary: The amount of virtual memory the kernel has committed to supplying under its overcommit accounting model.
entries.details: It appears in /proc/meminfo and can be compared with CommitLimit.
entries.why_it_matters: It can reveal commit-space pressure that ordinary free-memory views miss.
entries.caution: Committed_AS is not the same as currently resident or allocated physical RAM.

entries.summary: A running process whose executable pathname refers to a file that has since been unlinked or replaced.
entries.details: Linux can reveal this through procfs executable links ending in a deleted marker.
entries.why_it_matters: It can indicate a process still running old code after an upgrade.
entries.caution: The condition is not automatically an error; long-running services can legitimately retain old mappings until restarted.

entries.summary: A filesystem object that has been unlinked from directory names but remains open through one or more process file descriptors.
entries.details: Its storage may remain allocated until the last open reference is closed.
entries.why_it_matters: Large deleted-open files can explain space usage that pathname-based scans cannot find.
entries.caution: The deleted marker is procfs evidence about pathname removal, not proof the descriptor is faulty.

entries.summary: Receive errors reported by a network interface.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: Transmit errors reported by a network interface.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: Received packets dropped by the interface/network stack counters.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: Transmit packets dropped according to interface counters.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: Transmit carrier-related errors reported by an interface.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: Receive or transmit FIFO/overrun errors reported by an interface.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: Receive frame/alignment errors reported by an interface.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: Collision events reported by an interface where the link technology exposes them.
entries.details: These are cumulative interface statistics exposed by Linux and can be inspected without active probing.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide direct evidence for network-interface error/drop conditions.
entries.caution: Counters are usually cumulative since interface/reset/boot; a nonzero value does not identify when the event occurred.

entries.summary: The current number of entries in the netfilter connection-tracking table.
entries.details: It can be compared with nf_conntrack_max when conntrack is enabled.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides current capacity usage for a finite networking resource.
entries.caution: Conntrack can be absent or disabled; that is Unavailable rather than zero usage.

entries.summary: The configured maximum number of netfilter connection-tracking entries.
entries.details: Together with nf_conntrack_count it defines connection-tracking capacity pressure.
entries.why_it_matters: Reaching the limit can cause new flows to fail to be tracked.
entries.caution: It is a configured capacity, not a measure of traffic throughput.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 file reporting hierarchical memory-controller event counters such as high, max, oom and oom_kill.
entries.details: The counters provide explicit evidence that a cgroup crossed memory-control boundaries.
entries.why_it_matters: They allow Problem Finder to detect cgroup-local OOM/limit events without monitoring.
entries.caution: Counters are cumulative and describe the cgroup hierarchy semantics defined by cgroup v2.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 file reporting events such as attempts blocked by the pids.max controller limit.
entries.details: It provides direct evidence of process-count limit enforcement in a cgroup.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes configured limits from actual limit-hit events.
entries.caution: It is available only when the pids controller/interface is present.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 CPU-controller statistics file that can include usage and throttling counters.
entries.details: Where bandwidth control applies it can report periods and throttled time/events.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides historical evidence that CPU bandwidth limits affected a cgroup.
entries.caution: Any single nonzero cumulative throttling counter needs workload/time context before being called a current fault.

entries.summary: An MD RAID array operating with fewer healthy active members than its fully functional configuration expects.
entries.details: Linux MD reports array/member state through sysfs.
entries.why_it_matters: It is strong storage-redundancy problem evidence.
entries.caution: Meaning and tolerance depend on RAID level; degraded does not always mean the array is immediately inaccessible.

entries.summary: An MD RAID member explicitly marked faulty by the MD subsystem.
entries.details: Member state can be inspected through the array sysfs hierarchy.
entries.why_it_matters: It identifies a specific storage member problem rather than inferring from aggregate I/O counts.
entries.caution: Faulty and missing are distinct states.

entries.summary: The MD array state describing resync, recovery, check, repair or idle synchronization activity.
entries.details: It is exposed in the MD sysfs hierarchy for relevant RAID levels.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains whether an array is rebuilding or checking redundancy.
entries.caution: An active resync/recovery is not itself a failure; failed/interrupted conditions require separate evidence.

entries.summary: Kernel/sysfs state describing whether an NVMe controller is live, resetting, connecting, deleting or otherwise unavailable depending on driver version.
entries.details: It provides direct controller-state evidence for NVMe problem checks.
entries.why_it_matters: A non-live/dead state can explain inaccessible namespaces/devices.
entries.caution: State names and availability are driver/kernel specific.

entries.summary: A condition in which a filesystem has no allocatable inodes remaining even if data blocks are still available.
entries.details: statvfs file-count fields can expose total/free inode capacity where meaningful.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains failures to create new files on filesystems that still show free bytes.
entries.caution: Some filesystems allocate inodes dynamically, so inode counts may not be meaningful everywhere.

entries.summary: A condition in which a mounted filesystem has no usable data-block capacity remaining for the relevant allocation context.
entries.details: statvfs distinguishes free blocks from blocks available to unprivileged users.
entries.why_it_matters: It is one of the most actionable storage-capacity problems.
entries.caution: Reserved blocks and filesystem semantics mean raw free and available values can differ.

entries.summary: A condition where allocated kernel file handles approach or reach the system-wide configured maximum.
entries.details: /proc/sys/fs/file-nr and file-max provide the relevant global capacity evidence.
entries.why_it_matters: It can explain failures to open files or sockets system-wide.
entries.caution: The kernel may dynamically manage allocation, and near-limit warnings are threshold-based rather than explicit faults.

entries.summary: The relationship between current task/thread population and the kernel threads-max limit.
entries.details: A near/exhausted condition can prevent creation of additional tasks.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a bounded resource-exhaustion check.
entries.caution: The configured limit can change and process count alone is not a problem.

entries.summary: A Linux monotonic clock based on raw hardware time without NTP frequency adjustments.
entries.details: It advances monotonically and exposes a lower-level hardware-based elapsed-time view than CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain differences between raw counter time and disciplined monotonic time.
entries.caution: It normally excludes suspend time and is not a wall clock.

entries.summary: A Linux clock representing International Atomic Time derived from wall-clock time without UTC leap-second discontinuities.
entries.details: It is system-wide and not directly settable through clock_settime.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a distinct timescale for applications that need TAI semantics.
entries.caution: TAI and UTC are different timescales; the offset depends on leap-second history/configuration.

entries.summary: A POSIX clock measuring CPU time consumed by the calling process.
entries.details: It advances according to processor time used rather than wall elapsed time.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes execution CPU time from realtime/monotonic clocks.
entries.caution: It is not a measure of total elapsed runtime or system-wide CPU usage.

entries.summary: A POSIX clock measuring CPU time consumed by the calling thread.
entries.details: It provides per-thread execution-time accounting through the clock API.
entries.why_it_matters: It complements process CPU-time inspection for multithreaded workloads.
entries.caution: It is CPU time, not scheduler wait time or wall time.

entries.summary: The source paths and drop-in fragments that contribute to a systemd unit definition.
entries.details: systemctl cat and manager properties can reveal the main fragment and additional drop-ins.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain where a unit's effective configuration came from.
entries.caution: A displayed unit file may be supplemented or overridden by drop-ins and generated units.

entries.summary: A NUMA counter incremented when an interleave memory policy allocates on the intended interleave target.
entries.details: It is reported per node in numastat and measured in pages.
entries.why_it_matters: It completes the common node allocation-locality counter set.
entries.caution: It is policy-dependent and cumulative; nonzero values are not a fault.

entries.summary: Per-node memory statistics exposed through nodeN/meminfo.
entries.details: It reports node-local totals and memory classes similar to selected /proc/meminfo fields.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides memory-distribution context for NUMA nodes.
entries.caution: Fields vary by kernel and should be reported only when present.

entries.summary: A kernel vulnerability-file status stating that the processor/system is not affected by the named vulnerability.
entries.details: The wording comes from the running kernel's sysfs vulnerability interface.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the strongest non-vulnerable classification that Hardware Topology can display without external inference.
entries.caution: It applies to the specific vulnerability file, not to all CPU security issues.

entries.summary: A kernel vulnerability-file status indicating the system is vulnerable or has incomplete mitigation according to the reported text.
entries.details: Qualified Vulnerable strings can include details such as missing microcode.
entries.why_it_matters: It preserves explicit kernel-reported vulnerability evidence.
entries.caution: The complete raw status matters; do not reduce qualified text to a simple Boolean.

entries.summary: A kernel vulnerability-file status in which the kernel cannot provide a definitive affected/mitigated conclusion.
entries.details: Reasons can include virtualization or servicing/microcode uncertainty depending on vulnerability.
entries.why_it_matters: It prevents unknown state from being mislabeled safe.
entries.caution: Unknown is not equivalent to vulnerable or not affected.

entries.summary: Btrfs-reported counters for device read, write, flush, corruption and generation errors where the kernel interface exposes them.
entries.details: These counters provide filesystem/device-specific error evidence without running a repair or scrub.
entries.why_it_matters: They underpin Problem Finder checks for Btrfs storage errors.
entries.caution: Counters are historical/cumulative evidence and availability depends on kernel/Btrfs interfaces.

entries.summary: A threshold condition in which configured swap usage is at or near total swap capacity.
entries.details: It is derived from current swap totals/usage rather than merely observing that swap is in use.
entries.why_it_matters: It can warn of limited remaining swap headroom.
entries.caution: Using swap is normal; only the explicitly defined capacity threshold should be called pressure.

entries.summary: A read-only scan that extracts runs of printable text-like bytes from a selected file.
entries.details: It can reveal embedded paths, identifiers or messages as supplementary integrity evidence.
entries.why_it_matters: It is useful as an explicit file-inspection action without executing the file.
entries.caution: Extracted text is not a semantic parser and can include false positives or sensitive content.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 attribute describing the cgroup type and whether it participates normally in the unified hierarchy.
entries.details: The value is exposed by the cgroup v2 filesystem and helps describe how a selected cgroup participates in controller and thread placement semantics.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides structural context before interpreting controller files and membership.
entries.caution: Do not infer controller availability from cgroup.type alone.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 event file reporting selected state transitions such as whether a cgroup is populated or frozen.
entries.details: The values are kernel-maintained state indicators for the selected cgroup and are separate from resource-accounting counters.
entries.why_it_matters: They help distinguish an empty cgroup from one that currently contains descendants or tasks.
entries.caution: An event state is not a health verdict.

entries.summary: The cgroup v2 freezer control/state interface for stopping or resuming execution of processes in a cgroup.
entries.details: A read-only inspector may report the exposed value without changing it. Freeze state is also reflected through cgroup event reporting.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why tasks in an otherwise populated cgroup may not be progressing.
entries.caution: Reading freeze state is not the same as changing it.

entries.summary: The cgroup v2 CPU bandwidth limit expressed as quota and period, or max for an unlimited quota.
entries.details: The interface constrains CPU time available to the cgroup over a scheduling period; the two values should be kept distinct rather than collapsed into a guessed percentage.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the authoritative cgroup v2 CPU-limit interface exposed by the kernel.
entries.caution: A quota does not describe actual CPU consumption.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 memory-throttling boundary intended to apply reclaim pressure when usage exceeds the configured level.
entries.details: Unlike memory.max, memory.high is primarily a throttling/reclaim mechanism rather than the final hard memory ceiling.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes soft pressure control from the hard memory limit.
entries.caution: Do not describe memory.high as identical to memory.max.

entries.summary: A cgroup v2 interface for per-device I/O bandwidth or IOPS limits.
entries.details: Limits can be expressed independently for read/write bytes per second and I/O operations per second for a device.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides controller-level context when an I/O workload is constrained by its cgroup.
entries.caution: Configured limits do not by themselves prove that the workload is currently saturated.

entries.summary: Pressure Stall Information exposed for CPU, memory or I/O within a cgroup.
entries.details: cgroup v2 can expose pressure files such as cpu.pressure, memory.pressure and io.pressure, using the PSI reporting model for that cgroup scope.
entries.why_it_matters: It lets an inspector distinguish system-wide pressure from pressure attributable to a selected cgroup.
entries.caution: Pressure is stall-time evidence, not a direct utilization percentage.

entries.summary: A brokered D-Bus communication environment that routes messages between connected applications and manages bus names.
entries.details: Linux desktops and system services commonly use separate system and session/user buses. Connections exchange method calls, replies, errors and signals through the bus.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides the context for names, object paths, interfaces and members shown by D-Bus Inspector.
entries.caution: A bus inventory is not a traffic trace.

entries.summary: A name used on a D-Bus message bus to address a connection or service.
entries.details: D-Bus distinguishes unique connection names from well-known names that may be owned by a connection.
entries.why_it_matters: Name type and ownership explain whether a displayed service endpoint is currently connected and addressable.
entries.caution: A listed name does not by itself prove that a service was activated by the inspector.

entries.summary: A human-meaningful D-Bus bus name that can be owned by a connection, commonly using reversed-domain notation.
entries.details: Messages addressed to a well-known name are routed to its current primary owner when one exists.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the stable service identity users usually recognize in D-Bus inventories.
entries.caution: A well-known name can be unowned even if it is activatable.

entries.summary: The bus-assigned unique name identifying one live D-Bus connection.
entries.details: Unique names normally begin with a colon and remain associated with that connection for its lifetime.
entries.why_it_matters: They let an inspector connect well-known names to the actual live connection that owns them.
entries.caution: A unique name is connection identity, not an application package name.

entries.summary: A D-Bus service name for which the bus has activation information available.
entries.details: An activatable service may not currently have a live owner. D-Bus Inspector can report activation availability without intentionally starting the service.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes “known to the bus for activation” from “currently running and owning the name.”
entries.caution: Do not treat activatable as equivalent to active.

entries.summary: A slash-separated path identifying an object instance exposed through D-Bus.
entries.details: Object paths form a hierarchical namespace such as /org/freedesktop/example and provide the location at which interfaces and members are exposed.
entries.why_it_matters: They are the navigation layer beneath a selected D-Bus service name.
entries.caution: An object path is not a filesystem path.

entries.summary: A named API contract grouping methods, properties and signals on a D-Bus object.
entries.details: An object can implement multiple interfaces, including standard interfaces and application-specific interfaces.
entries.why_it_matters: Interface boundaries explain which members belong together and what API surface an object declares.
entries.caution: Declared interface shape does not prove that every operation is safe or authorized for the current caller.

entries.summary: A callable member declared by a D-Bus interface.
entries.details: Methods have names and type signatures for their input/output arguments and are invoked using method-call messages.
entries.why_it_matters: Inspecting method declarations reveals API shape without needing to invoke the method.
entries.caution: D-Bus Inspector should not call arbitrary methods merely to inspect them.

entries.summary: A named value declared by a D-Bus interface, with an associated type and access mode.
entries.details: Properties are conventionally accessed through the standard org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties interface. A read-only inspector can perform explicit bounded reads where appropriate.
entries.why_it_matters: Property declarations and values expose service state without implying permission to modify it.
entries.caution: A readable property is not necessarily stable over time.

entries.summary: An asynchronous D-Bus message emitted by an object/interface to announce an event or state change.
entries.details: Signals have names and type signatures but are not method calls and do not have replies.
entries.why_it_matters: Declared signal metadata describes the API without requiring traffic monitoring.
entries.caution: Seeing a signal declaration does not mean the inspector observed that signal being emitted.

entries.summary: The standard D-Bus mechanism for obtaining XML that describes an object’s child objects, interfaces and members.
entries.details: The org.freedesktop.DBus.Introspectable interface returns declarative API information for a selected object path.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the basis for bounded read-only exploration of object/interface/member structure.
entries.caution: Introspection metadata is an API description, not a live traffic capture.

entries.summary: A Linux interrupt request identifier associated with delivery of a hardware or kernel-managed interrupt source.
entries.details: The generic IRQ layer maps interrupt descriptors and handlers onto architecture-specific interrupt-controller mechanisms.
entries.why_it_matters: IRQ identity links per-CPU counts, affinity and source/device context in Interrupts Inspector.
entries.caution: IRQ numbering and controller details are platform-dependent.

entries.summary: A procfs inventory of interrupt sources and their per-CPU delivery counters.
entries.details: Rows identify interrupt vectors/sources where the architecture exposes them, while columns show counts attributed to CPUs.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the primary current-state inventory used to show how interrupts have been distributed across CPUs.
entries.caution: Counters are cumulative and do not directly represent an interrupt rate without comparing observations over time.

entries.summary: A Linux soft interrupt class used for deferred kernel work outside the immediate hard-interrupt handler path.
entries.details: The kernel exposes per-CPU SoftIRQ counters for classes such as networking, timers and RCU-related work.
entries.why_it_matters: SoftIRQ distribution complements hardware IRQ inspection by showing deferred interrupt-related work.
entries.caution: A high cumulative counter is not by itself evidence of a problem.

entries.summary: A procfs table of cumulative SoftIRQ class counts split by CPU.
entries.details: Each row is a SoftIRQ class and each CPU column records how many times that class has been handled on the CPU.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a bounded kernel interface for comparing deferred-work distribution.
entries.caution: The values are cumulative counters, not percentages.

entries.summary: The set of CPUs permitted to service a configurable IRQ.
entries.details: Linux exposes configured affinity through /proc/irq/<irq>/smp_affinity and smp_affinity_list where supported.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains the intended CPU placement of interrupt delivery.
entries.caution: Some managed interrupts have kernel-controlled affinity that cannot be changed through the normal procfs interface.

entries.summary: The CPU set on which the kernel currently considers an IRQ effectively deliverable.
entries.details: For some interrupts the effective mask can differ from the configured affinity, particularly with managed interrupts or CPU hotplug.
entries.why_it_matters: Comparing configured and effective affinity avoids treating requested placement as guaranteed current routing.
entries.caution: An effective affinity value does not describe the per-CPU count distribution by itself.

entries.summary: The Linux runtime kernel-parameter mechanism exposed primarily through the /proc/sys hierarchy.
entries.details: sysctl names map to files beneath /proc/sys; tools may present dotted names while procfs uses path components.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides the conceptual model for Kernel Tunables without implying that the inspector changes values.
entries.caution: A tunable being readable does not mean it is safe to change.

entries.summary: The procfs namespace exposing many live kernel runtime parameters.
entries.details: Top-level areas commonly include kernel, vm, fs, net and other subsystem-specific namespaces depending on the running kernel.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the direct runtime inventory used by a read-only Kernel Tunables browser.
entries.caution: Availability and permissions vary by kernel configuration, namespace and policy.

entries.summary: A kernel parameter whose current value is exposed at runtime through a sysctl/procfs interface.
entries.details: The observed value is current state; it may have come from defaults, boot-time configuration, a service or a later runtime change.
entries.why_it_matters: Separating current state from persistent evidence prevents overclaiming where a value came from.
entries.caution: Current value alone does not prove which configuration file set it.

entries.summary: A configuration-file assignment intended to apply a sysctl value during boot or device availability.
entries.details: On systemd systems, sysctl.d files are one common source of persistent assignments; other distributions or tools may use additional mechanisms.
entries.why_it_matters: It is useful provenance evidence when comparing a live /proc/sys value with configuration intended to persist across boots.
entries.caution: A matching file assignment does not prove that it successfully applied to the current runtime value.

entries.summary: A cooling control object exposed by the Linux thermal framework.
entries.details: Cooling devices expose current and maximum states and can be associated with thermal zones/trip points by kernel thermal policy.
entries.why_it_matters: They show what cooling mechanisms the kernel has exposed alongside thermal-zone measurements.
entries.caution: A cooling state is framework state, not necessarily a direct fan-speed percentage.

entries.summary: A CPU Performance Scaling policy object controlling a set of CPUs that share a frequency-scaling interface.
entries.details: The kernel exposes policy directories under /sys/devices/system/cpu/cpufreq/policyX with related CPUs, limits, current/requested frequency, driver and governor information.
entries.why_it_matters: Policy scope prevents treating every logical CPU as independently frequency-controlled when hardware coordinates them together.
entries.caution: Reported scaling_cur_freq may not always equal the exact instantaneous hardware frequency.

entries.summary: The kernel driver that implements the frequency-scaling mechanism for a CPUFreq policy.
entries.details: The active driver is reported through the policy interface and determines which controls and measurements are available.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides hardware/platform context for interpreting policy ranges and governor behavior.
entries.caution: Driver name alone does not describe the current frequency-selection algorithm.

entries.summary: The policy/algorithm used by CPUFreq to choose requested CPU frequencies within allowed limits.
entries.details: Generic governors include performance, powersave, userspace, schedutil and others; availability depends on kernel and scaling driver.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain why a policy may request different frequencies under changing load.
entries.caution: Governor behavior and actual hardware frequency are related but not identical.

entries.summary: A power source or sink represented through the kernel power_supply class, such as a battery, mains source or USB supply.
entries.details: The class can expose attributes such as type, status, health, capacity and online state when supported by the driver.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a common read-only inventory for battery and external-power state.
entries.caution: Not every device exposes every attribute, and units depend on the documented class interface.

entries.summary: A power zone/domain exposed by the Linux power-capping framework.
entries.details: Domains are arranged beneath a control type and can represent power-controllable parts of the system, with energy monitoring and optional constraints.
entries.why_it_matters: It exposes the topology used by kernel power-capping drivers such as RAPL without assuming a particular vendor.
entries.caution: A domain being present does not mean an active power limit is configured.

entries.summary: A configurable limit exposed for a power-cap domain by the kernel power-capping framework.
entries.details: Depending on the driver, constraints can include power limits and time windows and are represented as attributes under the domain.
entries.why_it_matters: Read-only inspection can report the available constraint set and current values without modifying them.
entries.caution: Constraint semantics vary by power-capping driver and domain.

entries.summary: A cumulative energy measurement exposed by some Linux power-cap domains, commonly through energy_uj.
entries.details: The power-capping framework may also expose the maximum energy-counter range so software can account for wraparound.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides direct energy-accounting evidence where supported.
entries.caution: A cumulative energy counter is not an instantaneous power reading.

entries.summary: The systemd network name-resolution service providing DNS, LLMNR and mDNS resolution plus caching and optional DNSSEC validation.
entries.details: It can maintain global and per-link resolver state and expose that state through the org.freedesktop.resolve1 D-Bus API.
entries.why_it_matters: Resolver Inspector can use its already-running state without intentionally activating the service.
entries.caution: Not every Linux system uses systemd-resolved.

entries.summary: The D-Bus API exposed by systemd-resolved for resolver configuration, state and lookup operations.
entries.details: The Manager and per-link interfaces expose DNS servers, domains, protocols, DNSSEC state and other resolver information.
entries.why_it_matters: It is an authoritative structured source when systemd-resolved is already running.
entries.caution: Inspecting the API should not be confused with issuing DNS queries or changing resolver configuration.

entries.summary: DNS Security Extensions that allow DNS data to carry cryptographic authenticity evidence validated along a chain of trust.
entries.details: systemd-resolved can expose DNSSEC mode/state and validation statistics when DNSSEC support is in use.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes ordinary DNS transport/resolution from validation of signed DNS data.
entries.caution: DNSSEC validation status is not the same thing as transport encryption.

entries.summary: A domain suffix that a resolver may append when attempting to resolve suitable relative or single-label names.
entries.details: Search domains can be configured globally or per-link depending on the resolver stack.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain why an unqualified name may be tried with one or more suffixes.
entries.caution: Search domains affect name lookup behavior but are not default routes for ordinary IP packets.

entries.summary: A domain used by systemd-resolved to decide which link or DNS servers are appropriate for lookups within a DNS suffix.
entries.details: Routing domains participate in resolver routing; the special ~. route can make a link preferred for all suitable DNS traffic.
entries.why_it_matters: They explain split-DNS behavior where different links handle different namespaces.
entries.caution: A DNS routing domain is not an IP routing-table prefix.

entries.summary: DNS server and domain configuration associated with a particular network link.
entries.details: systemd-resolved can combine per-link DNS servers, routing/search domains, default-route eligibility and protocol settings when routing lookups.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides context for machines with VPNs, multiple interfaces or split DNS.
entries.caution: Per-link DNS state may be absent when a different resolver stack is in use.

entries.summary: Stored name-resolution results retained temporarily by a resolver to answer repeated queries without repeating all upstream work.
entries.details: systemd-resolved maintains caches per lookup scope and exposes cache-related state/statistics.
entries.why_it_matters: Cache information helps explain why current resolver behavior may reflect earlier responses until their validity expires.
entries.caution: A cache entry is not permanent configuration.

entries.summary: The libc mechanism that selects ordered sources for databases such as hosts, users and groups according to nsswitch.conf.
entries.details: For host name lookups, NSS configuration can route applications through modules such as files, dns or systemd-related resolver modules.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides fallback/provenance context when a resolver inspector is not using only systemd-resolved state.
entries.caution: NSS source order is configuration, not a guarantee that every application uses libc name-resolution APIs.

entries.summary: The kernel scheduling policy associated with a Linux thread and used as part of deciding when it may run.
entries.details: Linux exposes normal, batch, idle, real-time, deadline and newer extensible scheduling policies depending on kernel support.
entries.why_it_matters: Policy is central context for interpreting priority, nice value, affinity and scheduler-specific attributes.
entries.caution: Policy name alone does not establish how much CPU time the thread is currently receiving.

entries.summary: The standard Linux time-sharing scheduling policy for ordinary threads.
entries.details: SCHED_OTHER uses dynamic scheduling behavior influenced by factors such as nice value rather than a positive real-time static priority.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes normal time-sharing workloads from real-time and deadline classes.
entries.caution: SCHED_OTHER is also referred to as SCHED_NORMAL in kernel code.

entries.summary: A fixed-priority real-time scheduling policy without round-robin time slicing among equal-priority threads.
entries.details: A runnable SCHED_FIFO thread can preempt normal-policy threads and runs until it blocks, yields, or is preempted by a higher-priority real-time thread.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why a thread’s static real-time priority matters differently from a normal nice value.
entries.caution: Real-time policies can severely affect system responsiveness when misconfigured; inspection does not imply changing them.

entries.summary: A round-robin real-time scheduling policy based on SCHED_FIFO with a time quantum among equal-priority runnable threads.
entries.details: Threads retain real-time static priorities but rotate after consuming their round-robin quantum.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes FIFO and round-robin behavior for real-time threads.
entries.caution: The quantum and behavior should not be inferred from cumulative runtime alone.

entries.summary: A Linux deadline scheduling policy using runtime, deadline and period parameters.
entries.details: The kernel implements deadline scheduling with bandwidth control and earliest-deadline-first concepts; attributes are obtained through sched_getattr where supported.
entries.why_it_matters: It exposes scheduling guarantees/constraints that cannot be represented by only nice value or static FIFO/RR priority.
entries.caution: The configured parameters are not proof that application-level deadlines are always met.

entries.summary: The Linux extensible scheduler class that can run scheduling logic supplied through BPF sched_ext programs when supported and active.
entries.details: The kernel can expose global sched_ext state and threads may report SCHED_EXT policy context depending on configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: It identifies systems using the extensible scheduler framework rather than assuming only traditional scheduler classes exist.
entries.caution: Kernel support for sched_ext does not mean a BPF scheduler is currently active.

entries.summary: Kernel scheduler statistics exposing cumulative per-CPU, per-thread or scheduling-domain counters where enabled.
entries.details: The /proc/schedstat format is versioned and includes counters that must be interpreted according to the reported version.
entries.why_it_matters: It supports read-only accounting such as runtime, runqueue wait, schedule calls and load-balancing activity.
entries.caution: Counters are cumulative; rates require comparison between observations, and field layouts can change by schedstat version.

entries.summary: A kernel grouping of CPUs used by scheduler load-balancing topology on SMP systems.
entries.details: schedstat can expose per-domain CPU spans and balancing counters, with one or more domain levels associated with a CPU.
entries.why_it_matters: Domains explain the topology across which scheduler balancing decisions are accounted.
entries.caution: Scheduler domains are kernel scheduling topology, not cgroups or hardware NUMA nodes, though they may reflect topology.

entries.summary: Accumulated time a schedulable thread or CPU workload spent runnable but waiting for CPU service, where the relevant scheduler accounting exposes it.
entries.details: Scheduler Inspector can report schedstat-derived wait alongside runtime and slice counts without converting it into a health judgement.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish time executing from time ready-to-run but not executing.
entries.caution: Cumulative wait requires time-window context before comparing workloads of different ages.

entries.summary: A scheduler event in which a task becomes runnable and is considered for placement/execution.
entries.details: Per-CPU scheduler statistics can expose wakeup-related counters including local and cross-CPU activity depending on schedstat version.
entries.why_it_matters: Wakeup counters provide scheduler activity context beyond only runtime.
entries.caution: A wakeup count alone does not identify latency or performance problems.

entries.summary: A display protocol and architecture in which graphical clients communicate with a compositor that coordinates presentation and input.
entries.details: A Wayland session can still run X11 applications through XWayland. Session evidence such as XDG_SESSION_TYPE and WAYLAND_DISPLAY describes the graphical environment but does not by itself identify every compositor capability.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes native Wayland graphical sessions from native X11 sessions and explains which inspection sources are meaningful.
entries.caution: The presence of DISPLAY in a Wayland session can come from XWayland and must not be used to reclassify the session as X11.

entries.summary: The X Window System protocol and server model used by traditional Unix/Linux graphical sessions.
entries.details: In a native X11 session, tools such as xrandr can query X server output and mode state. X11 can also be provided inside a Wayland session through XWayland.
entries.why_it_matters: It determines whether X server output information represents the native graphical session or only an XWayland compatibility layer.
entries.caution: An X11 endpoint being present does not prove that the desktop session itself is native X11.

entries.summary: An X server that runs as a Wayland client so X11 applications can operate inside a Wayland session.
entries.details: XWayland provides X11 compatibility while the underlying desktop remains Wayland. Its RandR view can be an emulated representation rather than authoritative physical-output state.
entries.why_it_matters: It prevents a Wayland session from being misidentified as X11 merely because DISPLAY or an X server process exists.
entries.caution: Do not infer physical monitor ownership or native output configuration from XWayland alone.

entries.summary: The graphical-session component that combines client surfaces for presentation and, under Wayland, acts as the protocol server.
entries.details: Compositors may expose monitor state through compositor-specific interfaces such as Mutter DisplayConfig, KScreen tooling, or wlroots output-management protocols.
entries.why_it_matters: Display Server Inspector may need compositor-specific sources because ordinary Wayland clients are not guaranteed access to full monitor-management state.
entries.caution: A candidate compositor process discovered in /proc is not automatically proven to belong to the active session.

entries.summary: A display endpoint reported by the active graphical stack, such as a monitor connector or compositor-managed output.
entries.details: Depending on the session, output state may come from native XRandR or compositor-specific Wayland interfaces. Different sources are not necessarily interchangeable or equally authoritative.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the object to which modes, scale and current display state are attached.
entries.caution: An output record does not by itself prove which GPU physically owns the connector.

entries.summary: A display timing choice, normally identified by pixel dimensions and refresh characteristics.
entries.details: A graphical stack can advertise several modes for one output and identify one as current or preferred where the source provides that information.
entries.why_it_matters: Modes explain the resolution and timing combinations the current source reports for an output.
entries.caution: Advertised or preferred does not necessarily mean currently active.

entries.summary: The reported frequency at which a display mode presents frames, commonly expressed in hertz.
entries.details: Display tools and protocols may report the rate directly or in units that require conversion before presentation.
entries.why_it_matters: Two modes with identical pixel dimensions can differ in refresh rate.
entries.caution: A reported mode refresh rate is not a measurement of application frame rate or GPU rendering performance.

entries.summary: A graphical-session scaling value used to map logical interface dimensions to displayed pixels.
entries.details: Compositors can apply output-specific scaling; the available precision and semantics depend on the display protocol and compositor interface.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why logical desktop size and physical pixel resolution may differ.
entries.caution: Scale is session/compositor state and should not be inferred from monitor pixel dimensions alone.

entries.summary: An interface name and version advertised by a Wayland server through the registry.
entries.details: Registry inspection can show which protocol interfaces the server advertises to that client connection.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides evidence about protocol availability without changing compositor configuration.
entries.caution: Advertisement is not proof that a feature is enabled, usable for every client, or sufficient to establish monitor-management authority.

entries.summary: Firmware that initializes the platform and provides boot/runtime interfaces before and alongside the operating system.
entries.details: On Linux, firmware identity and interface evidence can be exposed through DMI/SMBIOS data and the /sys/firmware hierarchy, including EFI runtime presence on UEFI systems.
entries.why_it_matters: It establishes the firmware environment in which boot, ACPI and firmware-update mechanisms operate.
entries.caution: A firmware version string is vendor-reported identity, not a health or security verdict.

entries.summary: Platform-management structures that report system, BIOS, baseboard and chassis identity information supplied by firmware.
entries.details: Linux exposes commonly used DMI identity fields through sysfs, which can include firmware vendor/version and system or board identifiers.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides firmware-origin identity data without requiring the inspector to probe hardware directly.
entries.caution: Serial numbers, UUIDs and other identifiers can be privacy-sensitive and may be missing or vendor-populated incorrectly.

aliases: Advanced Configuration and Power Interface table
entries.summary: A firmware-provided data table used by ACPI to describe platform configuration, devices, power-management and related interfaces.
entries.details: Linux can expose firmware ACPI tables under /sys/firmware/acpi/tables; table headers include signature, length, revision and OEM/creator identifiers.
entries.why_it_matters: The table inventory shows what ACPI data the running kernel has made visible from platform firmware.
entries.caution: Presence of a table does not by itself prove that every feature described by it is active or working correctly.

entries.summary: The Linux filesystem interface commonly mounted at /sys/firmware/efi/efivars for UEFI variables.
entries.details: Each file combines EFI variable attributes with variable data. Variables can contain boot, Secure Boot and vendor-defined firmware state.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides the read-only evidence used to inspect variables such as SecureBoot and SetupMode when exposed.
entries.caution: EFI variables are writable firmware state; inspection code should not modify or delete them.

entries.summary: A UEFI-defined table through which firmware resources and update-related status can be exposed to the operating system.
entries.details: Linux surfaces ESRT entries under /sys/firmware/efi/esrt/entries, including resource class/type, current and lowest-supported versions, capsule flags and last-attempt information where provided.
entries.why_it_matters: It links platform firmware resources to firmware-update capability and reported update state.
entries.caution: An ESRT entry is not itself proof that a newer firmware release exists or that an update should be installed.

entries.summary: A device known to the fwupd service with firmware identity and update-related metadata.
entries.details: fwupd can enumerate devices and expose information used by clients such as fwupdmgr without requiring an inspector to perform an update.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides userspace firmware-update context alongside kernel/firmware interfaces such as ESRT.
entries.caution: Being known to fwupd does not mean an update is available, applicable or recommended.

entries.summary: Locally recorded information about firmware update attempts/results maintained by fwupd.
entries.details: fwupdmgr can query the history stored by fwupd without refreshing remotes or installing firmware.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides historical evidence that is separate from current firmware identity and update availability.
entries.caution: History is local recorded state and may be incomplete if fwupd was not responsible for an update.

entries.summary: The Linux kernel graphics subsystem that exposes GPU/display interfaces and device nodes to userspace graphics software.
entries.details: DRM provides device nodes and userspace interfaces for rendering and display-related operations, with driver-specific capabilities layered on the common subsystem.
entries.why_it_matters: GPU Inspector uses DRM/sysfs and process file-descriptor evidence rather than vendor utilities as its common inspection base.
entries.caution: DRM here means Direct Rendering Manager, not digital-rights management.

entries.summary: A device file under /dev/dri that provides a userspace entry point to a DRM device.
entries.details: DRM devices can expose primary card nodes and render nodes with different access and control roles.
entries.why_it_matters: It connects filesystem-visible device nodes to the GPU and DRM driver reported through sysfs.
entries.caution: Node presence alone does not prove that the current user can open it or that a process is actively using it.

entries.summary: A DRM device node traditionally used for display/KMS control and DRM-master semantics.
entries.details: Primary nodes are commonly named cardN. Access to master-only operations is separate from render-node access.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes display-control-facing DRM access from render-only nodes.
entries.caution: A card node being present does not mean the inspecting process is or can become DRM master.

entries.summary: A DRM device node intended for render/compute access without DRM-master display-control privileges.
entries.details: Render nodes provide a safer userspace entry point for rendering workloads and are distinct from primary card nodes.
entries.why_it_matters: Many ordinary GPU clients use render nodes even when they have no display-control role.
entries.caution: Render-node access still depends on device permissions and driver support.

entries.summary: A userspace open DRM file represented in the kernel by per-open client state.
entries.details: DRM fdinfo can expose a client ID, driver/device identity and optional usage counters for a readable process file descriptor.
entries.why_it_matters: It lets GPU usage evidence be associated with visible processes without treating every duplicated descriptor as a separate client.
entries.caution: Inspector visibility is limited to process descriptors and fdinfo that the current user is permitted to read.

entries.summary: Standardised and driver-specific DRM key/value statistics exported through /proc/<pid>/fdinfo/<fd>.
entries.details: Standard DRM keys use the drm- prefix and can include client identity, device identity, engine counters and memory-region accounting when the driver reports them.
entries.why_it_matters: It is GPU Inspector’s ordinary-user source for per-client memory and engine records.
entries.caution: Fields are optional and driver-dependent; missing fields must not be converted into invented zeros or unsupported claims.

entries.summary: A named memory region for which a DRM driver may report per-client buffer accounting.
entries.details: DRM fdinfo can report total, shared, resident, purgeable and active amounts for a region, depending on driver support.
entries.why_it_matters: It separates reported per-client memory accounting from whole-device memory totals.
entries.caution: Different categories overlap by definition; they must not be blindly added together as though they were independent allocations.

entries.summary: A driver-reported GPU execution-engine class or instance associated with client work.
entries.details: DRM fdinfo can expose engine busy-time or cycle counters and, where supported, engine capacity or maximum-frequency information.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes activity reported for different kinds of GPU execution engines.
entries.caution: Engine names and available counters are driver-specific and may not be reported at all.

entries.summary: A cumulative DRM client counter reporting time attributed to a particular GPU engine where supported.
entries.details: The counter is intended for usage accounting and can be sampled over time by monitoring tools.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides raw evidence from which interval activity could be derived without pretending the cumulative value itself is a percentage.
entries.caution: A cumulative busy-time value is not a live utilisation percentage.

entries.summary: Memory capacity/usage information reported for the GPU device itself rather than for one DRM client.
entries.details: Some drivers expose device-specific memory attributes through PCI/sysfs. GPU Inspector keeps these values separate from DRM fdinfo per-client memory accounting.
entries.why_it_matters: It prevents whole-device memory figures from being confused with one process client’s buffers.
entries.caution: Device-level memory sysfs attributes are driver-specific; GPU Inspector does not synthesize them for drivers that do not report them.

entries.summary: A Linux terminal endpoint managed by the kernel TTY subsystem.
entries.details: TTY devices include consoles, serial terminals, pseudo-terminal endpoints and other terminal-style character devices exposed through the TTY layer.
entries.why_it_matters: TTY identity explains which terminal endpoint a process or session is associated with.
entries.caution: A TTY device existing does not mean a user is logged in through it or that a process currently has it open.

entries.summary: A pseudo-terminal: a software terminal pair used by terminal emulators, shells and remote/session tools.
entries.details: Linux commonly exposes pseudo-terminal slave endpoints through devpts under /dev/pts while a corresponding master side is managed through the PTY subsystem.
entries.why_it_matters: PTYs are the ordinary terminal mechanism behind many graphical terminal windows and remote shell sessions.
entries.caution: A numeric /dev/pts node identifies a slave endpoint; its existence alone does not establish a specific master-process relationship.

entries.summary: The terminal associated with a process session for job-control and terminal-generated signal semantics.
entries.details: Process state exposed by procfs can identify a controlling-terminal device number for a process.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes a process session terminal relationship from merely having a terminal device open as a file descriptor.
entries.caution: No controlling terminal does not imply that a process is a daemon, and an open TTY file descriptor is not necessarily the controlling terminal.

entries.summary: A registered kernel TTY driver family that provides terminal devices.
entries.details: /proc/tty/drivers reports registered driver names, device prefixes, major/minor ranges and driver types.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains which terminal device families the running kernel currently exposes.
entries.caution: Registry presence is not proof that a particular device instance is active or in use.
