entries.summary: A kernel TTY processing layer that defines how terminal input/output is interpreted between a TTY driver and userspace.
entries.details: /proc/tty/ldiscs reports registered line disciplines.
entries.why_it_matters: Line disciplines are part of the terminal stack and can affect input processing semantics.
entries.caution: A registered line discipline is not proof that it is currently attached to any particular TTY.

entries.summary: The pseudo-filesystem that exposes pseudo-terminal slave device nodes, normally at /dev/pts.
entries.details: Allocated PTY slave endpoints typically appear as numeric entries beneath the devpts mount.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the filesystem-facing representation used to access PTY slaves.
entries.caution: A devpts node is an endpoint, not a complete description of the process or session using it.

entries.summary: The conventional pseudo-terminal master multiplexer device used to allocate a new PTY master/slave pair.
entries.details: Applications opening /dev/ptmx can request a new pseudo-terminal; the slave is commonly exposed through devpts.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains the allocation endpoint behind many PTY sessions.
entries.caution: Inspection of /dev/ptmx presence does not allocate a PTY; an inspector should not open it merely to enumerate terminals.

entries.summary: An identifier grouping processes into a POSIX process session.
entries.details: Process-session information is visible in procfs process state and is used with process groups for job-control relationships.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish terminal/job-control grouping from login-manager sessions.
entries.caution: A process session ID is not the same concept as a systemd-logind session ID.

entries.summary: A POSIX grouping of related processes used for job control and signal delivery.
entries.details: A process group has a process-group ID and normally exists within a process session.
entries.why_it_matters: Shell job control and controlling-terminal behavior are expressed in terms of process groups.
entries.caution: A process group is not a cgroup and should not be interpreted as a resource-control boundary.

entries.summary: The xdg-desktop-portal frontend service that exposes the public portal API to applications.
entries.details: The frontend routes portal requests to implementation backends selected for the current desktop/configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: It separates the stable application-facing API from desktop-specific implementation services.
entries.caution: Frontend presence does not prove that every portal interface has a usable backend.

entries.summary: A desktop-specific implementation service for one or more XDG Desktop Portal interfaces.
entries.details: Installed backends declare implementation interfaces and a D-Bus name in .portal descriptor files.
entries.why_it_matters: Backend selection explains why the same portal API can behave differently across desktop environments.
entries.caution: An installed backend is not necessarily selected, running or functional for the current session.

entries.summary: A metadata file describing an installed XDG Desktop Portal backend.
entries.details: Descriptor fields can include DBusName, Interfaces and legacy UseIn information.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides offline evidence of which backend implementation interfaces are installed.
entries.caution: Descriptor declarations are metadata; they do not prove the corresponding service is running or usable.

entries.summary: A backend-side D-Bus interface in the org.freedesktop.impl.portal namespace.
entries.details: Backend descriptors declare which implementation interfaces a backend provides.
entries.why_it_matters: Configuration can select different backends for different portal implementation interfaces.
entries.caution: A declared implementation interface is not proof that a portal request will succeed at runtime.

entries.summary: The configuration used by xdg-desktop-portal to choose implementation backends.
entries.details: Desktop-specific and generic portals.conf files participate in a documented lookup order and can specify a default backend preference plus per-interface overrides.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the current authority for backend preference rather than the legacy UseIn descriptor key.
entries.caution: A configured backend preference is not proof that the backend is installed, running or capable of completing a request.

entries.summary: The default backend preference defined in the [preferred] section of portal configuration.
entries.details: It supplies the fallback backend choice for implementation interfaces that do not have a more specific override.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains the general backend-selection path for a desktop/session.
entries.caution: Default preference can be superseded by interface-specific configuration and still depends on installed backend availability.

entries.summary: A portals.conf preference that chooses backend order for a particular portal implementation interface.
entries.details: Interface-specific entries override the general default preference for the named implementation interface.
entries.why_it_matters: Different portal functions can therefore be implemented by different backends on the same desktop.
entries.caution: Selection preference is configuration evidence, not a runtime success guarantee.

entries.summary: A legacy .portal descriptor field historically used to associate a backend with desktop environments.
entries.details: Modern xdg-desktop-portal backend selection uses portal configuration rather than relying on UseIn as the main selection mechanism.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains older backend metadata that may still appear in installed descriptor files.
entries.caution: Do not treat UseIn as the current authoritative backend-selection result.

entries.summary: The well-known D-Bus service/interface namespace used for the public XDG Desktop Portal API.
entries.details: Applications call portal interfaces through the frontend service on the user/session bus.
entries.why_it_matters: It identifies the application-facing portal endpoint.
entries.caution: Seeing the bus name does not prove every portal interface has a selected and usable backend.

entries.summary: The namespace used by XDG Desktop Portal backend implementation interfaces.
entries.details: Desktop-specific backends implement interfaces in this namespace for the frontend to call.
entries.why_it_matters: It distinguishes backend implementation APIs from the public org.freedesktop.portal.* APIs exposed to applications.
entries.caution: Implementation interfaces are backend-facing contracts, not direct evidence that a user-facing portal request is available.

entries.summary: A hardware or firmware-backed security device implementing TPM functions such as protected keys, PCRs and measured-boot support.
entries.details: Linux exposes TPM devices through the kernel TPM subsystem and device/sysfs interfaces.
entries.why_it_matters: TPM state can provide evidence used by measured-boot and attestation workflows.
entries.caution: TPM presence alone does not establish that the machine is trusted, uncompromised or correctly provisioned.

entries.summary: The kernel TPM resource-manager interface, commonly exposed as /dev/tpmrmN for TPM 2.0 devices.
entries.details: It virtualizes transient TPM resources for multiple userspace clients while the raw TPM node remains a lower-level interface.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why a system can expose both /dev/tpmN and /dev/tpmrmN.
entries.caution: Device-node presence is interface evidence, not proof that a userspace TPM stack is configured or in use.

entries.summary: A TPM register whose value is extended by measurements rather than ordinarily overwritten directly.
entries.details: PCR values are grouped into hash-algorithm banks and can represent the accumulated result of a measurement sequence.
entries.why_it_matters: PCR snapshots are central evidence in measured-boot and attestation workflows.
entries.caution: A PCR value is a time-specific snapshot; by itself it does not say whether the system is good, expected or trusted.

entries.summary: A set of TPM PCRs using a particular hash algorithm, such as SHA-256.
entries.details: A TPM can expose multiple banks, and the same PCR number can therefore have values in different hash algorithms.
entries.why_it_matters: Bank identity is required to interpret which digest algorithm a PCR value belongs to.
entries.caution: Do not compare PCR values from different banks as though they were the same register value.

entries.summary: A boot process in which firmware/software components are measured and measurements are recorded/extended into TPM PCRs.
entries.details: Firmware can also provide an event log describing the sequence associated with those measurements.
entries.why_it_matters: Measured boot supplies evidence that can later be compared against an expected policy.
entries.caution: Measurement is not the same as enforcement, and an event log/PCR set does not automatically establish trust.

entries.summary: A firmware-produced log describing measured-boot events associated with TPM PCR extensions.
entries.details: Linux can expose the firmware event log through securityfs for userspace inspection.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain how PCR state was constructed during boot.
entries.caution: Log presence or successful parsing does not prove the measurements are complete, expected or trustworthy.

entries.summary: The kernel securityfs exposure of the TPM firmware measurement log, commonly under /sys/kernel/security/tpm*/.
entries.details: binary_bios_measurements is a kernel-exposed event-log data source when firmware/kernel support makes it available.
entries.why_it_matters: It identifies the local evidence source used by read-only measured-boot inspectors.
entries.caution: A missing or unreadable securityfs path can reflect platform support, mount state or permissions; it should not be treated as proof that no measurements occurred.

entries.summary: The kernel subsystem that represents keyboards, pointers, touch devices, game controllers and other input devices through common interfaces.
entries.details: Input devices expose identity, capability and relationship data through sysfs and can expose event interfaces through evdev.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides a common model across many physical buses and device types.
entries.caution: Subsystem membership does not imply a particular desktop classification or that live events are currently being generated.

entries.summary: A device registered with the Linux input subsystem.
entries.details: Kernel input devices can report names, bus/vendor/product identifiers, physical paths, properties and capability bitmaps.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the basic inventory object behind input event nodes and capability inspection.
entries.caution: A single physical device can expose multiple Linux input devices or event nodes.

entries.summary: A character-device interface, normally /dev/input/eventN, exposing Linux input events for an input device.
entries.details: The event node corresponds to kernel input capabilities but can also carry live user input when opened for reading.
entries.why_it_matters: It identifies the userspace event interface associated with an input device.
entries.caution: Enumerating node metadata is different from reading events; inspection tools should not capture live input unless explicitly designed to do so.

entries.summary: Kernel-exported bitmaps describing which event/code families an input device supports.
entries.details: sysfs exposes capability sets for event types, keys/buttons, relative and absolute axes, switches and other input features.
entries.why_it_matters: Capabilities let an inspector describe what a device can report without capturing live events.
entries.caution: Capability support does not prove that a particular event is active, configured by the desktop, or currently occurring.

entries.summary: A Linux input event family such as key/button, relative-axis, absolute-axis or switch events.
entries.details: The event-type capability bitmap indicates which families a device can emit.
entries.why_it_matters: Event types provide the first level of structure for interpreting input capabilities.
entries.caution: An advertised event type is capability evidence, not live-event activity.

entries.summary: A key or button code that an input device reports as supported by its capability bitmap.
entries.details: Keyboard keys, mouse buttons, gamepad buttons and other switches can be represented in the EV_KEY code family.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps distinguish device capabilities without recording actual key/button presses.
entries.caution: Supported keys/buttons do not reveal what the user has pressed.

entries.summary: An input axis whose events report movement relative to a prior position, commonly pointer motion or wheel movement.
entries.details: REL_* capability bits describe which relative axes a device can emit.
entries.why_it_matters: Relative-axis support helps characterize pointer-like input devices.
entries.caution: Capability presence does not reveal current pointer movement.

entries.summary: An input axis whose events report positions in a defined coordinate/range space, used by devices such as touchscreens, touchpads and tablets.
entries.details: ABS_* capability bits identify the absolute axes exposed by a device.
entries.why_it_matters: Absolute-axis support helps describe touch/tablet/game-controller capabilities.
entries.caution: The capability bitmap alone does not provide current axis values or desktop calibration policy.

entries.summary: Kernel input properties that describe structural traits of an input device in addition to event-code capabilities.
entries.details: Properties can help userspace distinguish characteristics such as pointer/direct-input behavior.
entries.why_it_matters: They provide useful classification evidence without requiring live event capture.
entries.caution: Properties are kernel-exposed hints/capabilities, not a complete desktop policy classification.

entries.summary: An optional device-supplied unique identifier exposed by some Linux input devices.
entries.details: The sysfs uniq attribute can contain a persistent hardware identifier depending on the device/driver.
entries.why_it_matters: It can help distinguish otherwise similar devices when legitimately needed.
entries.caution: Because it can be identifying and persistent, an inspector should avoid making it a prominent public-facing inventory field by default.

entries.summary: The identifier used to refer to an installed desktop entry within the XDG applications search path.
entries.details: Desktop-file IDs are derived according to the Desktop Entry specification and participate in precedence when entries with the same ID exist in multiple data directories.
entries.why_it_matters: Handler/default configuration refers to desktop applications by desktop-file ID rather than arbitrary filesystem path.
entries.caution: The winning desktop entry depends on XDG search-path precedence; a lower-priority file can be shadowed.

entries.summary: The desktop-entry key that defines the command template used to launch an application or action.
entries.details: Exec supports field codes defined by the Desktop Entry specification.
entries.why_it_matters: It is registration evidence for how a desktop entry proposes to launch an application.
entries.caution: Reading Exec is not the same as executing it; an inspector should never launch the command merely to display registration metadata.

entries.summary: An optional desktop-entry key naming an executable whose availability can be used to determine whether an entry should be considered launchable.
entries.details: Desktop environments can use TryExec as an availability check without running the application.
entries.why_it_matters: It can explain why a registered desktop entry is hidden or ignored when its executable is unavailable.
entries.caution: Checking path/PATH availability must not execute the referenced program.

entries.summary: A desktop-entry key used to mark an entry as deleted/disabled for precedence purposes.
entries.details: A higher-priority desktop entry with Hidden=true can suppress a lower-priority entry with the same desktop-file ID.
entries.why_it_matters: It matters when resolving which registration is effective across XDG data directories.
entries.caution: Hidden is not the same as NoDisplay and should not be collapsed into a generic visibility flag.

entries.summary: A desktop-entry key indicating that an application should not normally be shown in menus even though the entry can still be used for other purposes.
entries.details: NoDisplay affects presentation rather than acting as the same precedence/deletion mechanism as Hidden.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain entries that are valid handlers but intentionally absent from ordinary application menus.
entries.caution: NoDisplay and Hidden have different semantics.

entries.summary: A desktop-entry key restricting display/use of an entry to named desktop environments.
entries.details: Desktop environment identifiers determine whether the condition matches the current desktop.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains desktop-specific application visibility/registration behavior.
entries.caution: OnlyShowIn is not equivalent to Hidden or NoDisplay and depends on current desktop identity.

entries.summary: A desktop-entry key excluding an entry from named desktop environments.
entries.details: It is the exclusion counterpart to OnlyShowIn.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why an otherwise installed desktop entry may not apply to the current desktop.
entries.caution: NotShowIn is not equivalent to Hidden or NoDisplay.

entries.summary: A named secondary action declared by a desktop entry, with its own label and Exec command.
entries.details: Actions provide additional launch operations associated with an application entry.
entries.why_it_matters: They are registration metadata distinct from the main application launch command.
entries.caution: An action being declared does not prove its command is currently executable or should be run by an inspector.

entries.summary: A standardized media-type identifier used to describe the format/content class of a file or data object.
entries.details: Desktop entries can declare supported MIME types and mimeapps.list can associate types with application desktop IDs.
entries.why_it_matters: MIME types are the keys used when resolving default and associated desktop applications.
entries.caution: A declared MIME type association does not prove the application can successfully open every object of that type.

entries.summary: A relationship between a MIME type and one or more desktop applications in the freedesktop MIME Applications model.
entries.details: Associations can arise from desktop-entry declarations and mimeapps.list added/removed/default configuration.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains which applications are candidates or defaults for a content type.
entries.caution: Association is desktop registration evidence, not proof that an application is installed correctly or can open a particular file.

entries.summary: The freedesktop.org specification defining application associations and defaults for MIME types.
entries.details: It defines mimeapps.list lookup/merge behavior and Default Applications, Added Associations and Removed Associations sections.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the authority for resolving desktop MIME handler preferences across XDG configuration layers.
entries.caution: Resolution involves precedence and fallback; it should not be reduced to a simplistic first-file-only rule.

entries.summary: A freedesktop configuration file used to record preferred/default, added and removed application associations for MIME types.
entries.details: Multiple user/system and desktop-specific mimeapps.list files can participate in resolution according to documented XDG precedence.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the primary configuration evidence for desktop MIME handler selection.
entries.caution: One file in isolation may not represent the effective result when higher/lower-precedence files and fallbacks participate.

entries.summary: The mimeapps.list section specifying preferred default desktop applications for MIME types.
entries.details: Defaults are ordered desktop-file IDs and resolution can fall back when a candidate is unavailable or invalid.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains which application the desktop should prefer for a content type.
entries.caution: A configured default reference can point to a missing desktop file and should not be silently treated as valid.

entries.summary: The mimeapps.list section adding desktop applications to the association list for MIME types.
entries.details: These entries augment associations beyond those declared by desktop files or inherited through other configuration layers.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain why an application appears as a handler candidate.
entries.caution: Added association is not the same as making an application the default.

entries.summary: The mimeapps.list section suppressing particular desktop applications from MIME associations.
entries.details: Removed associations participate in the specification-defined merge/resolution process.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why a desktop entry declaring a MIME type may nevertheless be excluded as a handler.
entries.caution: Removal from MIME association does not uninstall or delete the desktop entry.

entries.summary: An alternate MIME type name mapped to a canonical type by the shared MIME-info database.
entries.details: Aliases let desktop MIME resolution treat equivalent media-type names consistently.
entries.why_it_matters: Alias context helps explain handler resolution when configuration uses a non-canonical type name.
entries.caution: An alias is naming metadata, not a desktop application association by itself.

entries.summary: A shared MIME-info inheritance relationship indicating that one MIME type is a subclass of another.
entries.details: Desktop association logic can use installed MIME inheritance context when considering handlers.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains why a handler for a parent type may be relevant to a more specific subtype.
entries.caution: Subclass inheritance is content-type metadata and does not automatically make an application the configured default.

entries.summary: The revision identifier reported for the microcode currently loaded by a CPU.
entries.details: On supported x86 systems Linux can expose per-CPU microcode revision evidence through sysfs, with other local evidence depending on the platform.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides direct local evidence of the revision the running kernel reports as loaded.
entries.caution: Revision numbering and interpretation are vendor/model-specific; a revision value alone does not prove that it is the latest or sufficient for a mitigation.

entries.summary: The Linux kernel mechanism that applies supported CPU microcode updates, including early loading during boot.
entries.details: On x86 the kernel documents vendor firmware locations and early/runtime loading mechanisms.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains how local microcode firmware can become the revision reported by running CPUs.
entries.caution: The existence of a reload control or firmware files is not proof that a particular update was applied; inspection should not write the reload interface.

entries.summary: The conventional Linux firmware directory containing Intel CPU microcode blobs, commonly /lib/firmware/intel-ucode/.
entries.details: Files in this directory are local firmware inputs available to the kernel/distribution microcode-loading path.
entries.why_it_matters: Their presence can explain what microcode payloads are locally installed.
entries.caution: File presence does not prove that a blob is compatible, newer, or currently loaded.

entries.summary: The conventional Linux firmware directory containing AMD CPU microcode blobs, commonly /lib/firmware/amd-ucode/.
entries.details: Files in this directory are local firmware inputs available to the kernel/distribution microcode-loading path.
entries.why_it_matters: Their presence can explain what microcode payloads are locally installed.
entries.caution: File presence does not prove that a blob is compatible, newer, or currently loaded.

entries.summary: A hierarchical firmware/platform description of devices and their properties used extensively on ARM, RISC-V and embedded systems.
entries.details: Linux can expose the firmware-provided tree through /sys/firmware/devicetree/base or compatible paths on systems that boot with a Device Tree.
entries.why_it_matters: It preserves platform-description evidence that complements ACPI/DMI on systems using a different firmware model.
entries.caution: Device Tree describes hardware/platform relationships; it is not automatically a live inventory of which drivers successfully bound to every described node.

entries.summary: A hierarchical node in a Device Tree representing a device, bus, CPU, memory region or other platform object.
entries.details: Nodes contain named properties and child nodes, and their full path identifies their position in the tree.
entries.why_it_matters: Node hierarchy is the basic structure used to inspect firmware-provided platform description.
entries.caution: A node existing does not prove that a matching kernel driver is active.

entries.summary: A Device Tree property containing one or more compatibility strings that identify the programming/model binding expected for a node.
entries.details: The ordered string list is used by operating-system driver/binding logic to match supported hardware descriptions.
entries.why_it_matters: It provides important firmware identity/binding evidence for a node.
entries.caution: A compatible string is not proof that a driver actually bound successfully on the running system.

entries.summary: A Device Tree property used for certain node classes in the Devicetree model.
entries.details: Where present, device_type is firmware-provided metadata associated with a node.
entries.why_it_matters: It can provide additional structural context for selected Device Tree nodes.
entries.caution: Do not invent device_type for nodes where firmware does not report it, and do not use it as a substitute for live driver state.

entries.summary: A numeric handle used by Device Tree properties to reference another node.
entries.details: Phandle-based references encode relationships such as clocks, interrupts, regulators and other platform connections.
entries.why_it_matters: They allow properties to refer to nodes without embedding full paths.
entries.caution: A raw phandle value requires the corresponding Device Tree context to resolve correctly.

entries.summary: A conventional Device Tree node containing firmware/bootloader-provided parameters selected for the operating system.
entries.details: The exact properties are platform-dependent and can include boot-related information.
entries.why_it_matters: It is a useful navigation point when inspecting firmware-to-kernel handoff data.
entries.caution: Properties under /chosen are descriptive boot evidence; their presence and meaning depend on the platform and binding.

entries.summary: A conventional Device Tree subtree describing memory regions reserved for firmware, devices or special-purpose use.
entries.details: Child nodes can describe reserved address ranges and usage constraints for the platform.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains firmware-described memory reservations that should not be treated as ordinary allocatable RAM.
entries.caution: Device Tree reservation description is not a substitute for the kernel live memory map or NUMA inventory.

entries.summary: The Linux kernel framework that provides registered cryptographic and related transformation implementations to kernel consumers.
entries.details: The Kernel Crypto API exposes multiple transformation classes and can have several implementations registered for the same generic algorithm name.
entries.why_it_matters: Crypto Registry is inspecting this registration layer rather than measuring application-level cryptographic activity.
entries.caution: The presence of an implementation in the Crypto API does not prove that any current workload is using it.

entries.summary: The procfs view that lists cryptographic implementations currently registered with the Linux Kernel Crypto API.
entries.details: The interface is arranged as blank-line-delimited records. Crypto Registry preserves each reported record separately, including multiple implementations that share the same algorithm name.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the direct source for Crypto Registry inventory and per-entry metadata.
entries.caution: It is a registration inventory, not a record of which algorithms are currently active in a workload.

entries.summary: The presence of a cryptographic implementation in the Kernel Crypto API registry.
entries.details: Registered implementations are available for matching/allocation through the Crypto API according to their names, types and other registration properties.
entries.why_it_matters: It explains what a Crypto Registry row proves: availability to the kernel Crypto API.
entries.caution: Registration is not evidence that a specific process, service or kernel subsystem is currently using that implementation.

entries.summary: The Kernel Crypto API term for an algorithmic transformation that can be requested and instantiated through the API.
entries.details: The Crypto API uses transformation terminology across cryptographic operation classes and related data-transform mechanisms.
entries.why_it_matters: It is the kernel-side abstraction behind many entries exposed in the Crypto Registry.
entries.caution: A transformation class describes API semantics; it does not by itself identify the selected implementation or current use.

entries.summary: The generic algorithm name reported by a Kernel Crypto API registration.
entries.details: Several implementations can register the same generic name. A caller requesting that name can therefore be matched to one of multiple registered implementations.
entries.why_it_matters: Crypto Registry intentionally keeps same-name records separate so implementation differences remain visible.
entries.caution: The generic algorithm name is not necessarily a unique implementation identifier.

entries.summary: The implementation-specific driver name reported for a Kernel Crypto API registration.
entries.details: The driver name distinguishes a concrete implementation from the generic algorithm name and can identify a particular software or hardware-backed implementation.
entries.why_it_matters: It lets Crypto Registry distinguish multiple registrations that implement the same algorithm name.
entries.caution: A reported driver name identifies the registered implementation; it does not prove that the implementation is currently selected by a workload.

entries.summary: The Kernel Crypto API class/type reported for a registered implementation.
entries.details: The Crypto API supports multiple operation classes, including symmetric ciphers, AEAD, message digests and random-number generators, with additional API classes depending on kernel support.
entries.why_it_matters: Crypto Registry uses the reported type as a category/filter while preserving the kernel-provided value.
entries.caution: Type names and available classes depend on the running kernel and implementation; missing fields should not be invented.

entries.summary: A registration priority used by the Kernel Crypto API when choosing among implementations that provide the same generic algorithm name.
entries.details: For a generic algorithm request, the Crypto API can select the registered implementation with the highest applicable priority.
entries.why_it_matters: It helps explain why several same-name Crypto Registry rows can coexist and which implementation is preferred for generic allocation.
entries.caution: Priority is selection metadata, not a security score, quality rating or proof of current use.

entries.summary: A software-defined machine presented with virtual processors, memory and devices by a virtualisation stack.
entries.details: Virtualisation Inspector inventories registered local libvirt/QEMU virtual machines, not every virtual machine on the host or remote machines.
entries.why_it_matters: Distinguishes a registered guest from host capabilities and from the current Linux system running as a guest.
entries.caution: A VM definition does not prove the VM is running, its disk exists, or an OS is installed.

entries.summary: A software or hardware-assisted layer that provides execution environments for virtual machines.
entries.details: Linux KVM supplies kernel virtualisation facilities while QEMU can provide a machine model and device emulation; libvirt manages supported instances.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps separate the components reported in Host Capabilities and the VM inventories.
entries.caution: A detected CPU flag or installed virsh executable does not establish an operational hypervisor.

entries.summary: A machine emulator and virtualisation platform that can run guests using software emulation or an accelerator such as KVM.
entries.details: The applet interrogates only local libvirt QEMU connections, not arbitrary unmanaged QEMU processes.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains the QEMU backend named by local libvirt connection URIs.
entries.caution: QEMU presence alone does not prove KVM acceleration or a currently running guest.

entries.summary: The Linux kernel virtualisation facility exposed through KVM-specific interfaces.
entries.details: The applet reports CPU capability flags, the /dev/kvm node, loaded KVM modules and nested-module parameters without performing a KVM capability ioctl.
entries.why_it_matters: These separate signals explain what the kernel and current user expose for hardware-assisted virtualisation.
entries.caution: No individual signal is a complete functional KVM availability test.

entries.summary: CPU features commonly associated with Intel VMX or AMD SVM hardware-assisted virtualisation.
entries.details: The applet reads vmx and svm flag tokens when exposed by /proc/cpuinfo.
entries.why_it_matters: These flags provide one host capability signal without changing system settings.
entries.caution: Their presence or absence does not alone establish whether KVM can successfully run a VM.

entries.summary: The character-device interface through which userspace accesses the KVM subsystem.
entries.details: Virtualisation Inspector checks whether the node is a character device and whether read/write access is reported for the current user; it does not open it or issue ioctls.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why a present device and the current user's access are separate reported facts.
entries.caution: A present or accessible /dev/kvm node is not proof that a VM can be created.

entries.summary: Dynamically loaded kernel modules associated with KVM, including kvm, kvm_intel and kvm_amd.
entries.details: The applet checks /proc/modules for these specific names.
entries.why_it_matters: Supports inspection of kernel virtualisation components without trying to load them.
entries.caution: A module absent from /proc/modules may be built into the kernel or otherwise not represented as a dynamic module.

entries.summary: Running a VM that can itself act as a virtualisation host for another VM.
entries.details: The applet reads the nested parameter under /sys/module/kvm_intel or /sys/module/kvm_amd when available.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains the reported nested-virtualisation setting in Host Capabilities.
entries.caution: A parameter value marked enabled does not test whether nested guests can actually start.

entries.summary: A virtualisation management library and daemon/API ecosystem for supported hypervisors.
entries.details: The applet uses an optional virsh client to query selected local libvirt/QEMU connections.
entries.why_it_matters: Separates management-layer records from CPU and kernel capability signals.
entries.caution: A libvirt client being installed does not prove that any libvirt service is available or accessible.

entries.summary: A libvirt command-line query made using virsh with a read-only connection.
entries.details: Virtualisation Inspector uses fixed local URIs and virsh --readonly for explicit list, dominfo, dumpxml and snapshot metadata scans.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains how the applet obtains local VM metadata without providing management controls.
entries.caution: Read-only commands can still contact or socket-activate a local libvirt service; scans are explicit.

entries.summary: A local libvirt QEMU connection to a per-user session instance.
entries.details: The applet queries this URI separately and reports accessibility, domain count and acquisition status.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why a user session can have a different VM inventory from the system instance.
entries.caution: An empty accessible session inventory does not mean the system connection has no VMs.

entries.summary: A local libvirt QEMU connection to the system-wide instance.
entries.details: The applet queries this URI only on request and reports its access limitations independently.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains host-managed domain inventory distinct from a per-user session inventory.
entries.caution: A permission or authentication failure must not be interpreted as zero system VMs.

entries.summary: The outcome of attempting to query a particular local libvirt endpoint.
entries.details: The applet distinguishes accessible, partial, unavailable, restricted, failed and not-yet-scanned results when supported by acquisition.
entries.why_it_matters: Shows whether a reported VM count is actually based on a successful query.
entries.caution: An unscanned or inaccessible endpoint is an unknown inventory, not an observed empty inventory.

entries.summary: The libvirt object representing the configuration and, when active, runtime state of a managed virtual machine.
entries.details: The applet obtains registered local domain UUIDs and combines independent dominfo, selected XML and snapshot observations.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains the Virtual Machines inventory and its source-connection field.
entries.caution: A domain entry can exist while the guest is shut off; metadata may be partial.

entries.summary: A universally unique identifier used by libvirt to identify a domain.
entries.details: The applet obtains UUIDs from libvirt and checks that a returned domain XML UUID matches the requested domain before accepting its details.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps avoid misattributing configuration from one domain to another.
entries.caution: A UUID identifies a domain record; it is not evidence of the guest OS or its current contents.

entries.summary: The libvirt-reported operational state of a domain, such as running, paused or shut off.
entries.details: The applet obtains state from dominfo and presents it separately from configured CPUs, memory and devices.
entries.why_it_matters: Prevents configuration metadata from being mistaken for live guest activity.
entries.caution: An unavailable runtime-state query is not the same as a shut-off VM.

entries.summary: A libvirt domain whose definition is maintained beyond a single transient execution.
entries.details: The applet reports the persistent property provided by dominfo.
entries.why_it_matters: Distinguishes stored VM definitions from temporary domain lifecycles.
entries.caution: Persistence is not the same as currently running or automatically starting.

entries.summary: A libvirt-reported flag indicating whether a domain is configured for automatic start under its driver rules.
entries.details: The applet reports the autostart property supplied by dominfo; it does not enable or disable it.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains configuration metadata found in the Virtual Machines view.
entries.caution: Autostart enabled is not proof that the VM started successfully at boot.

entries.summary: A CPU execution unit assigned or configured for a virtual machine.
entries.details: The applet reads configured vCPU counts from domain XML where available and may show dominfo or current-attribute values separately.
entries.why_it_matters: Helps interpret CPU allocation settings without confusing them with physical host cores.
entries.caution: A configured vCPU count does not measure current guest CPU usage.

entries.summary: Memory amounts declared by a libvirt domain configuration, including current and maximum memory fields.
entries.details: The applet normalises reported XML memory units and separates configuration from any dominfo Used memory field.
entries.why_it_matters: Allows users to compare VM allocations while preserving provenance.
entries.caution: Configured memory is not the same as guest resident memory or host physical RAM consumption.

entries.summary: Structured XML describing libvirt domain identity, configuration and devices.
entries.details: The applet first attempts inactive configuration XML and can fall back to reported domain XML, marking which form was acquired and accepting only matching UUIDs.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why next-boot configuration and current running configuration can differ.
entries.caution: XML is selected metadata rather than a verified representation of the running guest or its disk contents.

entries.summary: Libvirt CPU model/mode, topology and optional host-CPU affinity settings for a domain.
entries.details: The applet selects available CPU mode, model, topology and vCPU pinning declarations from domain XML.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains CPU-related details shown for a selected VM.
entries.caution: These settings describe the domain configuration; they do not measure runtime CPU performance.

entries.summary: Virtual or assigned devices declared for a libvirt domain.
entries.details: The applet presents already-acquired disks, network interfaces, selected other devices and snapshots in Devices... without performing a fresh scan.
entries.why_it_matters: Separates device configuration from the physical-device inventory of Hardware Topology.
entries.caution: A configured device or device path is not proof that the underlying resource is currently usable.

entries.summary: A libvirt domain XML disk record describing an assigned block device or storage source.
entries.details: The applet reports target, bus, source, format and readonly declaration when present in selected XML.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains the Disk section of a VM's Devices... dialog.
entries.caution: A disk source path in XML does not establish that a file or block device exists, is accessible or is healthy.

entries.summary: A libvirt domain XML interface describing a guest network attachment.
entries.details: The applet exposes selected interface kind, MAC, source network/bridge, model and target information where reported.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains the Network Interfaces section of a VM's Devices... dialog.
entries.caution: Configured network attachment does not prove traffic, connectivity or a live guest interface.

entries.summary: A libvirt record describing a named domain snapshot and its reported metadata.
entries.details: The applet explicitly queries snapshot names and XML for a selected domain, showing names, parent, creation time and reported state when acquired.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains the Snapshots section of the selected VM's Devices... dialog.
entries.caution: A listed snapshot is not a guarantee that its backing data is present, complete or restorable.

entries.summary: An attempt to identify whether the Linux system running the inspector is itself a VM guest.
entries.details: The applet invokes systemd-detect-virt --vm and combines its output with separately labelled DMI and CPU flag evidence.
entries.why_it_matters: Keeps guest-environment inspection distinct from the host's registered VM domains.
entries.caution: No VM detected by the tool does not prove the machine is physical or outside all virtualisation environments.

entries.summary: DMI/SMBIOS manufacturer and product strings exposed by the current Linux environment.
entries.details: The applet reads selected /sys/class/dmi/id values as supporting evidence for guest identification.
entries.why_it_matters: Explains why manufacturer, product and BIOS strings appear in Guest Environment.
entries.caution: DMI strings are descriptive and may be missing, generic or spoofed; they are not conclusive proof of virtualisation.

entries.summary: A CPU feature indicator that can be exposed when the current Linux system runs under a hypervisor.
entries.details: The applet checks /proc/cpuinfo for the hypervisor flag as supporting evidence in Guest Environment.
entries.why_it_matters: Provides a separate signal from systemd-detect-virt and DMI strings.
entries.caution: The flag alone is not an authoritative guest identity, and its absence does not prove bare metal.
